# Learning Grove · Grove Readers (ages 7–10): side stories and fun quests

## S1. The Wardens’ Walk

- `s1-step1`: Walk beside Moss to the stream lantern, at his speed. · _Moss walks very slowly. Stay next to him. If you get ahead, he stops and waits for you to notice._
- `s1-step-boats`: Play Briar’s game: float a lit leaf-boat from the stream lantern all the way to the pond. · _Tap the water behind the boat to push it along. Keep it off the reeds. Leaves are free, so try as often as you like._
- `s1-step2`: Walk with Moss to the lantern by the old wall. · _Hush’s post is on the north side of the Grove, by the tumbled stone wall. Go on a quiet evening._
- `s1-step3`: Walk with Moss to his own lantern, by the pond. · _Go at dusk, just after sunset. Moss likes the light then._
- `s1-step4`: Moss won’t visit the Long-Grass post while it stands empty. He’ll tell you when. · _This story finishes in chapter 9. Carry on with the main story until then._

#### `s1-ask`

_The Keepers wander home with their empty cups. Three lanterns glow. The fourth post, by the long grass, is dark._  
_Moss hasn’t gone back up the hill. He sits by your boot, staring at the dark post._  
**You**: Twenty-two years?  
**Moss**: Not tonight. Ask me something else. Anything else.  
**Moss**: I told you the tale. A tale is only the part that fits in a song. The rest doesn’t fit anywhere.  
**Moss**: At each post I keep one small memory that isn’t in the tale. Four posts. Four small things.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): oral history: how spoken stories carry the past  
> **Moss**: Nobody wrote the old days down. They were kept like this: one of us telling the next one.  
> _People do this too. When someone tells what they remember and others pass it on, it’s called oral history._  
> _Oral means spoken. Long before there were books, most people kept their past this way._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what oral history is: memories passed on by telling, before and alongside writing._

**Moss**: Hazel used to walk round them with me every Lantern Night. Slowly. I’d like to do it again.  
**Moss**: At my pace. I am older than the trees, and the trees are not in a hurry either.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): a quarter of the speed takes four times as long  
> _Moss walks at a quarter of your speed. That means he covers one step for every four of yours._  
> _On your own, you could reach the stream lantern in 3 minutes. How long will it take beside Moss?_  
> - ✅ 12 minutes → Twelve. Four times as slow means four times as long. Three, four times over. You’ve been listening.
> - 7 minutes → You added four. Slowness doesn’t add, I’m afraid. It multiplies. Four lots of three minutes: 3, 6, 9, 12. Twelve minutes. Bring patience.
> - 3 minutes → If I walked at your speed, yes. I don’t. I never have. A quarter of the speed takes four times as long. Four lots of three: twelve minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that a quarter of the speed means four times the time (4 × 3 = 12)._


**Choices**

- **Walk beside him.**
    - You walk. It takes a long time to cross the grass. Halfway, you realise that is the point.
    - **Moss**: Good. You didn’t sigh. Hazel sighed for the first ten years.
- **Offer to carry him.**
    - **Moss**: Certainly not. I have legs. They are very short and very old, but they are mine.
    - **Moss**: Ask me again another year. I may surprise us both.
- **Ask which post comes first.**
    - **Moss**: Briar’s, by the stream. She hated waiting more than anything, except being sad.
    - **Moss**: She was very good at not being sad. It was most of what she did.

#### `s1-briar`

_The stream lantern hisses softly in the damp air. Moss looks at it for a long while before he speaks._  
**Moss**: Briar. The songs call her Joy. That’s a big word. Mostly, she laughed.  
**Moss**: She laughed at frogs. At weather. At me, constantly. When she was scared, she laughed loudest of all.  
**Moss**: Fading is how an Eternal dies. When it was Briar’s time, she walked up the hill laughing.  
**Moss**: She said she’d thought of a joke and wanted to tell it to the view.  
_For a moment the lantern light turns old and gold, and you hear a voice that isn’t his._  
**Briar**: If I’m not down by supper, eat mine. If I’m not down by spring, plant something nice.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): reading between the lines: what a character really means  
> _Briar says, “If I’m not down by spring, plant something nice.” What did she really mean?_  
> - ✅ She knew she wasn’t coming back, and wanted to be remembered with something lovely. → Yes. She knew. She just said it in a way that let us smile. That was Briar all over.
> - She wanted someone to tidy the garden. → Ha. She’d have liked that answer. But no. She knew she wasn’t coming down that hill. She asked for a flower so we’d have something lovely to remember her by.
> - She was hungry and wanted her supper saved. → She was always hungry, to be fair. But listen to the second half. “If I’m not down by spring.” She knew she wouldn’t be. The flower was her way of saying goodbye gently.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred a character’s real meaning from what she said, not just the words themselves._

**Moss**: Nobody had to plant anything. Something yellow came up where she sat. The first memorial flower.  
**Moss**: Typical. She always got the last word.  
**Moss**: I never found out what the joke was. Some evenings I sit up there and try to guess.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): remembering someone who has died  
> **Moss**: When someone you love dies, the missing doesn’t stop. It changes shape.  
> **Moss**: Telling their stories helps. So does a flower. So does guessing at their jokes, on a quiet evening.  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that sadness after a death is normal, and that remembering together helps._


#### `s1-boats-ask`

**Moss**: She had a game. Of course she had a game. Leaf-boats, each with a candle stub a grown-up lit, from her post down to mine.  
**Moss**: If yours reached the pond still lit, you had to laugh out loud. Those were her rules.  
**Moss**: There were eleven rules. Nine of them were about laughing.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): subtraction word problem within 20  
> **Moss**: Eleven rules. Nine about laughing. So how many were about anything else at all?  
> - ✅ 2 → Two. One said only a grown-up lights the candles. One was about not pushing Moss in. She needed that one.
> - 20 → That’s eleven and nine added together. We want what’s left over. Start at nine and count up to eleven: ten, eleven. Two rules. One was about not pushing me in.
> - 3 → Close. Count up from nine: ten, eleven. That’s two steps, so two rules. One said only a grown-up lights the candles, and one was about not pushing me in.
> _For grown-ups: Solved 11 − 9 = 2 by counting on from the smaller number._

_He brings out a dock leaf from somewhere, folded very neatly, with a stub of candle standing in it._  
**Moss**: I have never once got one to the pond. Not in all the years. She said I watched it too hard.  
**Moss**: I’ve been watching it less hard, on purpose, for a very long time. It hasn’t helped.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, ask): why a wide, flat boat is steadier  
> **Moss**: Before you fold yours. Which boat is less likely to tip over: wide and flat, or tall and narrow?  
> - ✅ Wide and flat → Right. A wide boat spreads its weight over lots of water, and its low middle is hard to tip. Tall and narrow wobbles at the first ripple. Ask me how I know.
> - Tall and narrow → That’s how I fold mine. Every year. Watch what happens to it. Wide and flat is steadier. The weight is spread out and low down, so a ripple can’t tip it.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two boat designs and explained why a wide, low boat is more stable._


**Choices**

- **Fold yours wide and flat.**
    - **Moss**: Briar’s way. Flat as a pancake and twice as smug.
- **Give yours a sail.**
    - **Moss**: A sail. Nobody has ever thought of a sail.
    - **Moss**: …I don’t know if that’s allowed. She’d have allowed it. She’d have been furious she didn’t think of it first.

#### `s1-boats`

_The stream takes the boats as if it has been waiting all year. Moss’s tips over at once, with great dignity._  
**Moss**: Every year.  
_Yours wobbles past the stepping stones, spins once at the reed bend, and slides out onto the pond._  
_The candle is still lit._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): what a flame needs to keep burning  
> **Moss**: Briar always said a flame needs three things: something to burn, air, and heat.  
> **Moss**: Splash it, and the water cools it and shuts out the air. Keep it dry, and it carries on. Like yours.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fire needs fuel, air and heat, and that water puts it out by cooling it and blocking air._

_Your Nubbin, who has run beside it the whole way along the bank, sits down hard in amazement._  
**Moss**: Well? Rules are rules.  
_You laugh. It comes out louder than you meant, and it rolls right across the water._  
**Moss**: …There. That’s the sound. I haven’t heard it at this post in a very long time.  
_Behind you, Moss’s boat drifts back to the bank upside down, as if it would quite like another go._  
**Moss**: Next Lantern Night. And the one after. Somebody ought to. It’s a tradition now.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): traditions: how a group remembers together  
> _Something a family or a town does again every year, the same way, is called a tradition._  
> **Moss**: Traditions are how a valley remembers without anybody having to write it down. Boats included.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a tradition is and how it helps a community keep its memories._


#### `s1-wall-ask`

_A few evenings later, Moss is waiting at the gate. He has clearly waited a while, and would like you to know it._  
**Moss**: The old wall next. Hush’s. Feed them first. I’ll wait. I am, you’ll have noticed, good at it.  
_Byte is leaning on the wall with a notebook, trying to look casual. It clearly took a lot of planning._  
**Byte**: Is he talking? Right now? Ask him something only he would know. For proof.  
**Moss**: Tell the pale one it’s the other shoe this time.  
_Byte looks down at both shoes. Byte goes very quiet, and leaves._  
**Moss**: Hush was the quiet one. People think quiet means resting. Hush wasn’t resting. She was listening.  
**You**: Listening to what?  
**Moss**: Whatever you weren’t saying. Come on. North side of the Grove. Mind the step.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions: north, east, south, west  
> **Moss**: Hush’s wall is on the north side. Face north with me. Now: which way is east?  
> - ✅ To my right → Right. Facing north, east is on your right hand, west on your left, and south behind you. Going round clockwise: north, east, south, west. Hush’s post never moves, which helps.
> - To my left → That’s west. Easy to swap them. Face north and hold out your right arm. That points east. Clockwise: north, east, south, west.
> - Behind me → Behind you is south, the opposite of north. East is on your right. Go round clockwise: north, east, south, west.
> _For grown-ups: Practised the four compass directions and where east and west are when facing north._


#### `s1-hush`

_The lantern by the old wall burns lower than the others, steady and quiet, like a candle in an empty room._  
**Moss**: After the White Year, some of the stilled ones never moved again. They sat where they were put down.  
**Moss**: The rest of us were busy. Mending. Hatching. Getting the valley warm. Hush sat with the still ones.  
**Moss**: Every one. Every day. She didn’t try to wake them. She kept them company, so they weren’t alone.  
_Moss stops. When he goes on, his voice is smaller._  
**Moss**: The last of them faded on a winter morning, under this wall. Faded means it died. Hush was beside it.  
_The memory rises slowly, like breath on cold glass._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, notice): similes  
> _“Like breath on cold glass” is a simile. A simile compares two things using “like” or “as”._  
> _It tells you how the memory appears: slowly, softly, and a little bit misty._  
> _For grown-ups: Spotted a simile and explained what the comparison shows._

**Hush**: That’s the last of them, Moss. Somebody kept them. I think I’d like to be kept now.  
**Moss**: She called grief a kind of keeping. You hold it, so it doesn’t get dropped all over the valley.  
**Moss**: She held it a very long time. Then she put it down. I’ve never thought that was weakness.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): think question: what grief is for  
> **Moss**: Hush called grief a kind of keeping. I’ve wondered about that for a long time. What do you think she meant?  
> - Being sad about someone is a way of still loving them. → That’s a fair answer. I think so too. The sad part is the love, with nowhere to go.
> - Somebody has to remember them, so they’re not forgotten. → That’s a fair answer. Hush would have nodded at that. Keeping them in mind is keeping them.
> - I’m not sure. Grief just feels heavy. → That’s an honest answer, and honest is always fair. It is heavy. Maybe that’s why she called it keeping. You carry it, and one day you’re allowed to put it down.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what grief means; there was no wrong answer._


#### `s1-pond-ask`

_Moss is on the hill when you look for him, and by the pond when you stop looking. That seems to be how it works._  
**Moss**: Mine. I’ve been putting it off. Not because it’s sad. Because it’s mine, and I talk about myself too much.  
**Moss**: Sit. No, closer. There. That’s where she sat.  
**You**: Hazel?  
**Moss**: Hazel. Before she was anybody’s gran. Before she was anybody’s anything.  
_The pond lantern hums. Above it, the sky has gone the deep blue that comes just after sunset. It is dusk._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, notice): dusk: why the sky stays light after sunset  
> **Moss**: Dusk. My favourite light. The Sun has already gone below the edge of the world.  
> **Moss**: But its light still glows in the sky for a while after. That’s why it isn’t dark straight away.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that dusk is the time after sunset when sunlight still lights the sky._


**Choices**

- **Sit where she sat.**
    - The grass there is worn, very slightly, in the shape of someone who came back to the same spot for forty years.
    - **Moss**: She’d say you were sitting in it wrong. You aren’t.
- **Ask him why he chose her.**
    - **Moss**: Patience. I’m getting there. Rush me and I’ll start from the Spring Age, and we’ll be here till May.

#### `s1-hazel`

_The pond lantern burns clean and warm. Moss looks at the water, not at you._  
**Moss**: She came here young. Clever, cross, and in a terrible hurry. She wanted the Nubbins to love her by Tuesday.  
**Moss**: They didn’t. So she sat by this pond every day and grumbled to the nearest thing that would listen. Me.  
**Moss**: I didn’t say a word, all winter. She wriggled and fidgeted the whole time, and never once asked me to talk.  
_The light turns old and gold. Snow, in the memory, and a young woman on a frozen bank, in a coat too big for her._  
**Young Hazel**: I haven’t the faintest idea what I’m doing. I don’t suppose you have either.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): two points of view on the same event  
> _To young Hazel, it looks as if Moss is just sitting there, doing nothing. What was he really doing all winter?_  
> - ✅ Waiting to see if she’d keep coming back. → Exactly. From where she sat, nothing was happening. From where I sat, everything was.
> - Ignoring her. → That’s how it looked to her. It’s a fair guess from her side of the pond. From my side, I was watching to see if she’d keep coming back. Same winter, two very different stories.
> - Sleeping. → I have been accused of that. Often. No. I was watching to see if she’d keep coming back. She thought nothing was happening. Something was.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two characters’ points of view on the same events._

**Moss**: Then, at the first thaw, I looked up at her and said, “You’ll do.”  
**Moss**: She laughed so hard she fell in the pond. It was only ankle-deep. She has never let me forget it.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-3, notice): ice floats, so ponds freeze from the top  
> **Moss**: Ice floats. So a pond freezes from the top down, like a lid.  
> **Moss**: Under the lid the water stays liquid, and the fish carry on all winter. Hazel landed on a thin bit of lid.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that ice floats, so ponds freeze from the top and life survives underneath._

**Young Hazel**: You sat with me all winter. Why?  
**Moss**: Because you kept coming back. That’s all it ever takes. Most people don’t.  
_The memory fades. The pond is a pond again, with your face in it, and his._  
**Moss**: Her third rule. Sit down next to them and wait. She thinks she invented it. I’ve never had the heart to say.  

#### `s1-wait`

_You look across the Grove at the fourth post, by the long grass. Moss doesn’t._  
**Moss**: Not that one. Not while it’s empty.  
_Over the lane, some children are skipping and chanting, in the sing-song voice children keep for old rhymes._  
_“Cinder held them close and tight, / kept them warm one winter night;”_  
_“when the morning came to call, / they did not move at all.”_  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.4, ask): rhyme and rhythm help words last  
> _That rhyme is older than anyone in the valley. What helps children remember it for so long?_  
> - ✅ The rhyme and the steady beat. → Yes. Tight and night, call and all. Rhymes and a beat are easy to remember, especially when you skip to them. That’s why so many old stories were kept as songs and rhymes.
> - It’s written in a famous book. → Nobody wrote it down. The children learn it from older children, by ear. What makes it stick is the rhyme and the beat: tight, night, call, all. You can skip to it.
> - It’s very long. → It’s actually very short, which helps. But the real glue is the rhyme and the beat. Tight, night, call, all. Words that rhyme and bounce are easy to remember.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how rhyme and rhythm make a verse easy to remember and pass on._

**Moss**: They’ve got the words right. They’ve got her wrong.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): think question: can a story be true and still unfair?  
> **Moss**: The words are right. She did hold them too tight. So can a story be true, and still be unfair to someone?  
> - Yes. If it only tells the worst part. → That’s a fair answer. A true story with the rest left out can still mislead.
> - No. If it’s true, it’s fair. → That’s a fair answer too. Truth matters most. I’d only say: a true part isn’t always the whole. That’s why I want you to hear the rest.
> - It depends who’s telling it. → That’s a fair answer. Historians say the same: always ask who told it, and what they left out.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a true story can still be one-sided; there was no wrong answer._

**Moss**: Everybody remembers her winter. Somebody should remember the rest of her. I’ll tell you. When it’s home.  
**You**: When what’s home?  
**Moss**: Feed them. Go to bed. Ask me again when I ask you.  

#### `s1-cinder`

_Three nights before the longest night. Frost reaches out of the long grass in thin white fingers._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, notice): metaphors  
> _Frost doesn’t really have fingers. “Thin white fingers” is a metaphor: it says one thing is another._  
> _It makes the frost feel as if it is reaching for something. Which it is._  
> _For grown-ups: Recognised a metaphor and what feeling it creates._

_Moss is waiting at your door. He is so faint you can see the doorstep through him._  
**Moss**: All four home. I said I’d tell you. You can carry me this time. Don’t make a face.  
_You carry him to the fourth post. He weighs almost nothing, like a bird’s nest with opinions._  
**Moss**: Everyone remembers Cinder in the snow. I’m going to tell you about the day before.  
**Moss**: Hot. The hottest day anyone could remember. The Nubbins lay flat in the long grass like dropped gloves.  
**Moss**: Cinder spent the whole day carrying them into the shade, one at a time. They kept wandering back out.  
_The light goes old and gold, then red at the edges. You smell hot grass and hear a voice, fierce and fond._  
**Cinder**: Out of the sun, you silly things. You’ll burn. Come here. Come here. I’ve got you.  

> **Lesson** (science, K-PS3-1, ask): why shade is cooler than sunshine  
> **Moss**: She knew what she was doing, carrying them into the shade. Why is shade cooler?  
> - ✅ Something blocks the sunlight, so less of it reaches the ground to warm it. → Yes. Sunlight warms whatever it lands on. Block it, and that patch stays cooler.
> - Shade is made of cold air. → It feels that way. But shade is just a place the sunlight can’t reach. Sunlight warms whatever it lands on. Under a tree, less sun lands, so it stays cooler.
> - Trees blow cool wind. → A nice idea. Trees do rustle. But the cool comes from blocking the sunlight. Sunlight warms the ground it lands on. Shade is where it can’t land.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that shade is cooler because it blocks sunlight that warms the ground._

**Moss**: She was never gentle. But she was never once tired of them. Not once, in all the years.  
**Moss**: That night the first snow came. In summer. And it didn’t stop.  
_The memory goes white, and is gone. Frost glitters at the foot of the post._  
**Moss**: Cinder-love, they call it now. A love that holds too tight. It’s fair. It isn’t all of her.  

#### `s1-complete`

**Moss**: There. Now two of us remember her warm. That’s twice as many as yesterday.  
_He nudges something across the frost to your boot: an acorn on a loop of faded string, worn smooth as a pebble._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): the life cycle of an oak  
> _An acorn is an oak tree’s seed. Planted, it sprouts into a seedling, then a young sapling, then an oak._  
> _An oak can live for hundreds of years and drop acorns of its own. Moss would approve of the pace._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the life cycle of an oak tree, from acorn to seedling to sapling to tree._

**Moss**: Hazel tied that on me, the spring after our first winter. The first gift anyone had given me in a very long time.  
**Moss**: Wear it. Then something of hers is walking about the Grove, and something of mine.  
_Hanging on the post is a soft hat with a little lantern stitched into the brim, and a note in big loud letters._  
_“SAW YOU TWO DOING THE ROUNDS IN THE DARK, SO I MADE YOU THIS. IT PROBABLY DOESN’T EXPLODE. —SPARKS”_  
_That night you write it all down: four posts, four small things. You call the pages The Tale of the Four._  
_Now there is a written record, as well as Moss’s memory._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, ask): spoken memories and written records  
> _Moss remembers. Your journal records. Why might a valley want both?_  
> - ✅ Writing lasts even when the teller is gone, and telling keeps the feeling in it. → Yes. Historians use both: what people wrote, and what people remember and tell.
> - It doesn’t. Writing is always better. → Writing does last. But a written page can’t answer questions or do Briar’s laugh. Historians use both: what people wrote down, and what people remember and tell.
> - It doesn’t. Telling is always better. → Telling is wonderful. But tellers grow old, and memories slip. Writing it down keeps it safe. Historians use both, side by side.
> _For grown-ups: Compared oral history with written records and why both matter._

_Moss falls asleep on your windowsill before you finish, which he has never done before._  

### Glossary

- **oral history**: The past as people remember it and tell it out loud, passed from one person to the next.
- **memorial**: Something that helps people remember someone who has died, like a flower or a stone.
- **dignity**: Staying calm and proud, even when something silly or hard is happening.
- **tradition**: Something a group does again and again, often every year, in the same way.
- **casual**: Relaxed and not bothered, or pretending to be.
- **grief**: The deep sadness you feel when someone you love has died.
- **simile**: A comparison that uses “like” or “as”, such as “quiet as a mouse”.
- **dusk**: The time just after sunset, when the sky is still glowing but getting dark.
- **grumbled**: Complained in a low, cross voice.
- **thaw**: When ice and snow melt because the weather is warming up.
- **metaphor**: Saying one thing is another to describe it, such as “the frost’s white fingers”.
- **record**: Something written or saved so that people can find out about it later.

## S2. Wisp

- `s2-step1`: Sit up after dark by Sable’s fruit, and keep very still. · _Leave fruit at the edge of the long grass, then wait nearby at night without moving._
- `s2-step2`: Keep an eye on Wisp. When the weather turns, find where he sleeps. · _This picks up in the chapter 6 rain. The warm things went somewhere warm._
- `s2-step3`: Keep winning Sable’s trust. Wisp is never far from her. · _This picks up in chapter 7. Once Sable leans on you, visit Luna’s night garden after dark._

#### `s2-fruit`

_Morning. The fruit you left for Sable is gone._  
_That should be good news. But Sable is curled in the long grass looking thinner, not fatter._  
_There is frost on the grass round her, though it is nearly midsummer._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS2-3, notice): what frost is and when it forms  
> **Luna**: Frost is water from the air that freezes onto cold grass, in tiny ice crystals.  
> **Luna**: It only forms when the ground is at freezing or colder: 0°C (32°F). In midsummer, that’s very strange.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that frost is frozen water from the air, and forms at 0°C (32°F) or below._

**Luna**: You noticed. Good.  
**Luna**: I saw her eat one piece last night. Then something else came out of the dark and took the rest.  
**Luna**: Not shared. Took.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): sharing versus taking  
> **Luna**: “Not shared. Took.” Do you know what I mean by the difference?  
> - ✅ Sharing is when the owner chooses to give. Taking is grabbing without asking. → That’s it. Sable didn’t choose. That’s what bothers me.
> - There’s no difference. The fruit’s gone either way. → In the morning it looks the same, doesn’t it? An empty dish. But sharing is when the owner chooses to give. Taking is when nobody asks. Sable didn’t get a choice.
> _For grown-ups: Explained the difference between sharing (a choice) and taking (no choice)._

**You**: Another Nubbin?  
**Luna**: A grey one. Thinner than her. He moves like he’s always expecting a boot.  
**Luna**: Sit up tonight. Leave the fruit where you always do, and keep still. Still as a post.  
**Luna**: He wants something here. I’d like to know what, before he takes it.  

#### `s2-thief`

_Past midnight. Sable creeps out of the grass to the fruit and takes one bite._  
_Then the grass parts again. Something comes through: grey, thin as a stick, one ear torn to a fringe._  
_He shoulders her aside, not hard, and drags the fruit towards the dark. Sable lets him._  
_Then he sees your lantern. He creeps up to it and presses his cheek against the warm glass._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): heat moves from warmer things to cooler things  
> _Heat always moves from a warmer thing to a cooler thing._  
> _The candle warms the glass. The glass warms his cold cheek. He has found the warmest thing in the Grove._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that heat flows from warmer objects to cooler ones._

_He is shaking. He keeps shaking, even there._  
_Then he sees you._  
**Wisp**: Hsss. Hers. Not yours. Not hands.  
_And under the hiss, much smaller, comes another voice._  
**Wisp**: …she ate. she ate today. good.  
_He is gone before you can breathe out. Sable stares at the place where he went for a long time._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a character’s words reveal about him  
> **Luna**: He has two voices. The hiss and the whisper. What does the little whisper tell us about him?  
> - ✅ He cares whether Sable has eaten. → Yes. The hiss says “go away”. The whisper says “she ate, good”. Both are him.
> - He only wants the fruit. → That’s what the hiss would have us think. But listen to the whisper again: “she ate today. good.” He’s glad she ate. He cares about her.
> - He’s angry at everyone. → The hiss is angry, yes. But the whisper is glad Sable ate. Underneath the hiss, he cares about her.
> _For grown-ups: Used a character’s words to work out his hidden feelings._

**Luna**: Greys don’t talk. They don’t. I’ve known a dozen.  
**Luna**: Something’s talking through the cracks in that one. Two somethings.  
**Luna**: Call him Wisp. He’ll hate it. Everyone should have a name they hate a little.  

#### `s2-missing`

_Over the next days, things go missing from the Grove. Not just fruit now. Warm things._  
**Fern**: Someone’s had my left glove. Left me the right. I can’t decide if that’s cruel or considerate.  
_A sock off the line. A candle stub from the cottage window. The tea cosy, which nobody admits to missing._  
_And the round stone Hazel kept by the hearth for warming eggs. Its dish is empty._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): insulation: materials that keep warmth in  
> **Clover**: He only takes warm things. Which of these keeps warmth in best, by trapping air?  
> - ✅ The woolly glove and the tea cosy → Yes. Wool and padding hold lots of tiny pockets of still air. Heat moves through still air very slowly. That’s insulation. And the stone? Warmed by a fire, a stone holds its heat and lets it out slowly.
> - The candle stub → A lit candle makes heat, true. But it doesn’t keep heat in. Wool and padding do. They trap tiny pockets of still air, and heat moves through still air slowly. That’s insulation.
> - A metal spoon → Metal lets heat rush straight through it. A spoon in hot tea gets hot fast. Wool and padding keep warmth in. They trap tiny pockets of still air. That’s insulation.
> _For grown-ups: Sorted materials by how well they keep heat in, and learned the word insulation._

**Clover**: He’s cold. That’s all it is. Can’t we feed him too? I can see the light through his ears.  
**Luna**: Shoo him off, Clover. I mean it.  
**Luna**: Every time Sable gets near a hand, he hisses at it. And she listens. She was taught to listen to that voice.  
**Clover**: He was taught too. Somebody taught him.  
**Luna**: …I know. It doesn’t make him any quieter.  
_In the fork of the fruit tree, Wisp licks his torn ear and watches you, like something that has been right before._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, do): share equally into two groups  
> **Clover**: Just in case. Twelve fruit. Two piles. If we feed him, it’s got to be fair.  
> _(Put the fruit into two equal piles.)_  
> **Clover**: Six and six. Twelve shared between two is six each. Nobody can say that isn’t fair.  
> Check: `edu:share:fruit:6-each`
> _For grown-ups: Divided 12 into 2 equal groups of 6._


**Choices**

- **Put down two piles of fruit: one each.**
    - Wisp waits until you are far away and eats his pile. Then he eats most of hers.
    - **Clover**: That’s not quite how I pictured it. But he did eat.
- **Clap your hands and shoo him off.**

    - **Luna**: Not the hands. Never the hands. Use your voice next time.
- **Sit down where you are, and wait.**

#### `s2-rain`

_It has rained for a day and a night. The stream is over its stones, brown and loud._  
_Behind the cottage, where the chimney bricks hold the day’s heat, the woodpile has slumped into a pool._  
_Under it is a nest, or what is left of one: Fern’s glove, the sock, the tea cosy, all sodden through._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): why wet things can’t keep you warm  
> **Clover**: A soaked glove can’t keep anything warm. The water fills up all the little air pockets.  
> **Clover**: And water carries heat away much faster than air does. That’s why wet and cold is the worst cold.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that wet materials lose their insulation because water carries heat away faster than air._

_And Wisp, on the last dry log, shaking so hard the water ripples round him. Hazel’s egg stone is in his paws._  
**Wisp**: mine. warm. mine.  
**Wisp**: …was warm. was.  
_He tries to stand, and his legs fold. He is too cold to hiss._  
**Clover**: The bathhouse is warm. Hazel kept it warm for exactly this. Please.  
**Luna**: If you carry him, he’ll fight. Hold him anyway. Hold him like you expected it.  
_Across the yard, in the long grass, Sable is watching. She has seen hands pick up a Nubbin before._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): seeing a moment from someone else’s side  
> _Sable has seen hands pick up a Nubbin before, and it didn’t end well. How might she feel, watching now?_  
> - ✅ Scared, because last time hands meant something bad. → That’s what I think too. So whatever you do, do it gently. She’s learning what hands are for.
> - Happy that someone is helping. → Maybe, a little, underneath. I hope so. But last time she saw hands lift a Nubbin, it went badly. She’s probably scared. So be gentle where she can see.
> - She doesn’t care. → She’s watching very hard for someone who doesn’t care. I think she’s scared. Last time hands lifted a Nubbin, it went badly. Be gentle where she can see.
> _For grown-ups: Imagined how a character might feel based on what has happened to her before._


**Choices**

- **Pick him up. Hold on.**
    - He fights, then stops fighting. He weighs less than the stone he won’t let go of.
    - In the steam of the bathhouse his fur lifts and his eyes go sharp. He looks at your hands, and bites one, hard.
    - **Wisp**: Hsss. Hands. Hands, hands.
    - He scrambles to the warmest corner with the stone, and glares until his tail stops dripping.
    - **Clover**: He’s warm now. Look at him. Warm right through.
    - He is. And he is still shaking.
- **Fetch a blanket, and let Clover lift him.**
    - Clover wraps him up like a loaf and carries him in at a run, talking to him the whole way.
    - In the steam of the bathhouse his fur lifts and his eyes go sharp. He bites her, hard, through the blanket.

    - He scrambles to the warmest corner with the stone. He is warm now, right through.

#### `s2-number`

**Clover**: Warm. Dry. Fed. And look at him.  
**Luna**: …Then it was never the cold.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): how fear shows in the body  
> **Clover**: He’s warm and dry now, and still shaking. Why?  
> - ✅ He’s frightened. → Yes. Fear lives in the body too. It can make you shake, breathe fast and feel your heart thump. Getting warm fixes cold. It doesn’t fix scared. That takes much longer.
> - He’s still a bit cold. → That’s what we thought. But he’s warm right through now. Feel the air in here. It’s fear. Fear can make a body shake, breathe fast and thump inside. Warmth doesn’t fix that.
> - He’s excited about the stone. → He does love that stone. But look at his ears, flat back. He’s frightened. Fear can make a body shake, even somewhere warm.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fear shows in the body (shaking, fast breathing, a racing heart)._

_Nobody says anything for a while. The rain drums on the bathhouse roof._  
_High on Wisp’s side, half washed off, is a number someone once painted on in grey._  
**Luna**: That paint. I’ve seen that paint before. Square numbers, very neat.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): noticing clues  
> _Luna is collecting clues: grey paint, square numbers, very neat. Small details that hint at a bigger answer._  
> _Good readers do the same. They notice the small things the story puts in on purpose._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how small details in a story can be clues to something bigger._

**Luna**: I’m going to ask around. Don’t tell Sable. I know that’s silly.  
_When you come out, Sable is by the bathhouse door. She sniffs your hands very carefully, and doesn’t run._  

#### `s2-night`

_Night, from Luna’s garden. The moonflowers are open. Two grey shapes sit at the edge of the Grove._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-2, notice): night-flowering plants and their pollinators  
> **Luna**: Moonflowers open at dusk, not in the day. They’re big and white, so they show up in the dark.  
> **Luna**: Moths that fly at night visit them for nectar, and carry pollen from flower to flower.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that some flowers open at night and are pollinated by night-flying moths._

**Luna**: Get down. Listen.  
_Wisp is close to Sable, closer than he lets anyone get. Tonight his voice is all whisper._  
**Wisp**: hands are for throwing. they all throw. in the end.  
**Wisp**: come back to the dark. no hands there. the dark never threw anyone.  
_Sable doesn’t answer. She looks at Wisp, then at your window. She moves towards neither._  
**Luna**: Moss says the cold leaves them half a voice. And he’s spending all of it talking her out of the Grove.  
_Clover has crept up behind you in a dressing gown, holding a bag of fruit as if it might go off._  
**Clover**: You don’t feed him because he’s earned it. You feed him because you’re you.  
**Luna**: He bit the hand that carried him, Clover.  
**Clover**: He was cold. I’d have bitten too.  
**Luna**: She leaned on a shin this week. A shin. Do you know how far that is, for her?  
**Luna**: One more month of that voice in her ear and she’ll be back under a hedge. She won’t come out twice.  
**Luna**: I’m not choosing against him. I’m choosing her. Somebody has to.  
**Clover**: And where does he go? Back to the dark. On his own. Talking to nobody.  
_Neither of them looks at you. They both very carefully don’t._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think question: mercy  
> _Being kind to someone who hasn’t earned it is called mercy. Luna and Clover both love Sable._  
> _Should you keep feeding someone who bit you? What do you think?_  
> - Yes. Kindness shouldn’t depend on being thanked. → That’s a fair answer. It’s mine, too. He was taught to bite. Maybe he can be taught something else.
> - No. Sable has to come first. → That’s a fair answer. Somebody has to put her first. It doesn’t mean you don’t care about him.
> - Let Sable choose. It’s her life too. → That’s a fair answer, and a brave one. I’d only wonder: is that a big choice to hand someone so small? It’s still a fair answer.
> - I don’t know. They’re both right. → That’s a fair answer. Sometimes two people are both right, and you still have to choose. That’s what makes it hard.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about mercy and a hard choice between two good reasons; there was no wrong answer._


**Choices**

- **Keep feeding him. Even after the bite.**
    - In the morning you put down two piles of fruit, not one. And the next morning, and the one after.
    - Wisp eats his with his back to you. On the fourth morning, he eats it facing you.
    - **Wisp**: hands are for throwing. hands are for… not hers. maybe not hers.
    - Sable sees. Sable sees everything. She comes one step closer than she did yesterday.
    - It isn’t free. Your other sock goes missing on the fifth morning, and the hiss is still there most nights.
    - **Luna**: He’s still talking to her. I can hear him. I hope you’re right.
- **Drive him off. Sable needs the quiet.**
    - You walk at him, steady, not fast, until he backs into the long grass. Then further. Then gone.
    - **Wisp**: Hsss. See? See? Hands.
    - Sable watches him go and doesn’t follow. She doesn’t look at you for the rest of the night, either.
    - But near dawn she eats her whole pile, every scrap, and sleeps in the open where you can see her.
    - **Luna**: It was the sensible thing. I keep telling myself so.
    - **Clover**: I know it was. I’m still not speaking to you till Thursday.
- **Let Sable decide.**
    - You put down one pile of ten fruit between them, and step back.
    - Sable looks at it, then at you. Then she pushes half the pile across the grass with her nose, to Wisp.
    - **Wisp**: …hers. she gave. hers.
    - He eats it at the very edge of the Grove. When he has finished, he doesn’t leave. He just doesn’t come in.
    - **Luna**: Well. That’s a better answer than either of ours.
    - **Clover**: Or we’ve just handed the smallest one here the biggest choice, because we couldn’t make it.
    - **Luna**: …Yes. That too.

#### `s2-complete`

_Morning. Frost on the grass at the edge of the Grove, in two small circles where two grey things slept._  
_Wisp is curled in one of them, the egg stone between his paws. It has been cold for weeks. He keeps it anyway._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, ask): warm things cool to match their surroundings  
> **Moss**: That stone was warm by Hazel’s fire once. It’s been cold for weeks. Where did its warmth go?  
> - ✅ Out into the cooler air and ground around it. → Yes. Heat leaks from warm things into cooler things, until they’re all the same. He keeps it anyway.
> - Wisp ate it. → He’d try, if he could. He can’t. The heat leaked out into the cooler air and ground, a little at a time, until the stone matched them.
> - It’s still inside, hiding. → A lovely thought. Not quite. Heat always moves from warm to cool. It leaked out into the air and ground until the stone matched them.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that warm objects lose heat to cooler surroundings until they match._

**Moss**: He’ll never give that back, you know. Not if he lives to be as old as me.  
**Moss**: Feed them before you feed yourself. She never said only the good ones. I checked. I was there.  
_…_  
**Moss**: Grey things remember who fed them. That’s all I’ll say. I’m old, and I’ve seen it go both ways.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, notice): theme: the big idea a story keeps returning to  
> _A theme is the big idea a story keeps coming back to._  
> _This story keeps asking one question: who deserves kindness? Moss’s answer is in Hazel’s rule._  
> _For grown-ups: Identified the theme of a story: who deserves kindness, and mercy._


### Glossary

- **fringe**: A ragged edge of loose threads or strands, like the end of a scarf.
- **hearth**: The floor in front of a fireplace.
- **insulation**: Material that slows heat from escaping, such as wool, feathers or padding.
- **sodden**: Completely soaked with water.
- **clue**: A small detail that helps you work something out.
- **mercy**: Kindness shown to someone, even when they haven’t earned it.
- **theme**: The big idea or message a story keeps coming back to.

## S3. The Cycle

- `s3-step1`: Ask one Sun Keeper and one Moon Keeper what really happened at Midsummer. · _Fern, Marina, Sparks, Clover and Pixel are Sun. Luna, Ember, Byte, Dusty and Nova are Moon. Ask one from each side._
- `s3-step2`: Help Sparks and Byte develop the old Midsummer photo-finish plates. · _From chapter 6, go to Sparks’s workshop. Rock the tray on Byte’s steady count, not on Sparks’s “feeling”._
- `s3-step3`: Show the plates to Fern and to Ember. · _Fern is usually in her orchard. Ember is at the Circuit fence most evenings._
- `s3-step4`: Host the Lantern Moot at the pond, after the Long Night. · _In chapter 11, tap the pond and choose Call a Moot. All ten Keepers come._

#### `s3-stands`

_The Circuit stands are split down the middle: Sun Keepers on the left, Moon Keepers on the right, an empty bench between._  
**Fern**: Don’t sit there. That’s the gap. Nobody sits in the gap.  
**You**: Why not?  
**Fern**: Because it’s the gap. Hazel sat in it every race, on purpose, to annoy everyone.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fairness: staying on nobody’s side  
> **Fern**: Go on, guess. Why do you think Hazel really sat in the gap?  
> - ✅ To show she was on nobody’s side, and they were all still one valley. → That’s what she said. Also to annoy everyone. Mostly the first thing.
> - She got there late. → Hazel was never late in her life. Early, and cross about it. No, she sat there on purpose: to show she wasn’t on either side. One valley, she used to say.
> - It was the best seat. → Byte says it’s the worst seat. He’s checked. She sat there to show she was on nobody’s side. To remind us we’re one valley.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how staying neutral can help people in a quarrel remember what they share._

_At the front stand two tea urns: same make, same tea, same shop. One has a sun painted on it, and one a moon._  
**Sparks**: Midsummer, years back, Fern’s Bramble went over the cliff rail, Sun says Ash barged her, Moon says rigged, OK bye.  
_Sparks sits down very fast and studies the race card as if it holds the meaning of life._  
**Sparks**: I didn’t say any of that. That was the wind.  
_This is a feud: a quarrel that has gone on for years. Both sides pretend not to listen. Both are bad at it._  
_Up in the owners’ box, Corvin isn’t watching the start line. He’s watching the stands._  

**Choices**

- **Sit in the gap, like Hazel did.**
    - You sit in the gap. Five heads turn from the left, and five from the right.
    - **Fern**: Oh, you’re hers all right.
    - **Byte**: That is the worst seat. You can’t see the cliff bend. I’ve checked.
- **Sit with the Sun side.**
    - **Sparks**: YES. Sun gets the new Keeper! Sun gets the new Keeper!
    - Across the gap, Luna writes something in a very small notebook.
- **Sit with the Moon side.**
    - **Byte**: Welcome. Our biscuits are better. I ran a blind taste test. It was mostly blind.
    - **Fern**: Traitor. Lovely to see you. Traitor.

#### `s3-two-stories`

_You get two stories. They agree about the weather and nothing else._  
_Sun says: Ember’s Ash came round the cliff bend like a cannonball, and Fern’s Bramble went over the rail._  
_Moon says: the cliff-bend flag was in the wrong place, so Ash went wide where the flag told her to._  
**Byte**: I have a chart. Both stories, colour-coded. The colours are also disputed.  
**Byte**: Two hundred and fourteen grievances in all. Three are about the race. The rest are about the urns.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.B.3, ask): reading a scaled bar graph  
> **Byte**: This year’s chart. Each square stands for 5 grievances. Urns: 9 squares. Biscuits: 4 squares.  
> **Byte**: How many more grievances about the urns than about the biscuits?  
> - ✅ 25 → Correct. Five more squares, and each square is 5. Five fives are 25. I’ve underlined it twice.
> - 5 → That’s the difference in squares. Good start. But each square stands for 5 grievances. 5 squares × 5 = 25 more grievances.
> - 45 → That’s all the urn grievances: 9 squares × 5 = 45. Biscuits have 4 × 5 = 20. So the difference is 45 − 20 = 25.
> _For grown-ups: Read a bar graph where each square stands for 5, and found a difference (25)._

**Ember**: After Midsummer, nobody would race Ash. Not Sun. Not Moon. Do you know who would?  
**Ember**: Him. He said he’d make her a champion.  
_Nobody, on either side, talks about Bramble after the rail. The story just stops there, like a path at a cliff._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): evidence: how to settle what really happened  
> _Two stories, and they can’t both be right. What would help find out what really happened?_  
> - ✅ Evidence: something recorded at the time, like a photo. → Yes. Evidence doesn’t take sides. A photo taken on the day can’t change its mind afterwards.
> - Whoever shouts loudest. → That’s how they’ve done it for years. It hasn’t worked. Loud isn’t the same as right. You need evidence: something recorded at the time, like a photo.
> - A vote. → Votes are good for deciding what to do. They can’t decide what already happened. For that, you need evidence: something recorded at the time, like a photo.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that evidence recorded at the time is better than opinion for finding out what happened._


#### `s3-plates`

_Sparks turns up at your gate looking like she has swallowed a secret, and it’s fizzing._  
**Sparks**: OK. OK OK OK. Confession. I’ve got the photo-finish plates from Midsummer. From the camera on the cliff bend. Mine.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): how a photo finish and old glass plates work  
> **Sparks**: A photo-finish camera takes a picture right on the line, for when a race is too close for eyes.  
> **Sparks**: Old cameras caught the picture on a glass plate. You develop it in trays of chemicals, in the dark. Then it appears.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a photo finish is and how old photographs were developed on glass plates._

**Sparks**: I never developed them. If it was Ash, Fern would never forgive Ember. If it wasn’t, I’d never forgive me.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s motive  
> _Sparks has had these plates for years. Why do you think she never developed them?_  
> - ✅ She was scared of what they would show, and who would get hurt. → …Yes. Not knowing was horrible. Knowing felt worse. Until now.
> - She forgot about them. → I wish. I thought about them every single race. She was scared. Whatever the plates showed, someone she loved would be hurt.
> - She was too busy. → I’m always busy. That wasn’t it. She was scared of what they’d show. Whatever it was, someone she loved would be hurt.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out why a character avoided doing something (her motive)._

**Sparks**: Trouble is, my darkroom timer’s broken. And the only person in the valley with a timer that works is…  
_She can’t say it. She points up the lane to the Moon end, at a cottage with labels on its windows._  
**Sparks**: Him.  

**Choices**

- **Fetch Byte. Tell him it’s for science.**
    - **Byte**: Science? You should have opened with that. I’ll bring three timers. One to check the other two.
- **Fetch Byte. Tell him Sparks asked nicely.**
    - **Byte**: She did not.
    - You admit she did not.
    - **Byte**: I’ll come anyway. Someone has to see it done properly.

#### `s3-flag`

_Sparks’s darkroom is red and cramped and smells of vinegar. Byte times, Sparks rocks the trays, and they argue in whispers._  
**Byte**: Red lamp only. The plates don’t react to dim red light. Anything brighter and they’re ruined.  
**Byte**: Rock on the count. One, and two, and— that was not two. That was one and a half.  
**Sparks**: I rock on FEELING, Byte.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): time as equal groups  
> **Byte**: Each plate needs 3 minutes in the tray, one plate after another. There are 3 plates. How long altogether? Quickly. Precisely.  
> - ✅ 9 minutes → Nine. Three lots of three. I’ll set the timer three times.
> - 6 minutes → That’s 3 + 3. We have three plates, not two. 3 + 3 + 3, or 3 × 3. Nine minutes.
> - 33 minutes → That’s how long it FEELS. It’s three lots of three minutes. 3 × 3 = 9. Nine minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Used multiplication as equal groups to find a total time (3 × 3 = 9 minutes)._

_The first plate swims up out of the dark: an enormous, blurry, perfectly lit thumb._  
**Byte**: Your thumb.  
**Sparks**: It’s a GOOD thumb.  
_The second plate comes up slower, on the count: the cliff bend at dawn, before the race. An empty course, and a flag._  
_And a man in a grey Circuit coat, pulling up the flag and moving it._  
**Byte**: Two posts nearer the edge. Look at the turf. Old hole there. New hole here.  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): what makes good evidence  
> _Byte says the turf proves the flag was moved. What makes the holes such good evidence?_  
> - ✅ You can still see them, and they don’t belong to either side. → Exactly. Holes don’t have opinions. Holes don’t own an urn.
> - Byte says so, and he’s clever. → I am. But that’s not evidence. That’s just me. The holes are evidence because anyone can look and check. They don’t take sides.
> - Holes are always suspicious. → Dusty would disagree. Strongly. The holes are good evidence because anyone can see them and check. They don’t take sides.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that good evidence can be checked by anyone and doesn’t depend on who is speaking._

**Sparks**: Nobody on either side moved that flag. Nobody. It was a steward.  
_The last plate is the finish, with the owners’ box behind it. Corvin isn’t watching the race. He’s watching the stands._  
**Byte**: The flag sent them wide. Ash went wide because the course told her to. Bramble went wide because Ash did.  
**Sparks**: We’ve been fighting about the wrong thing for years. Byte. We have two URNS.  
**Byte**: The urns were your idea.  
**Sparks**: They were a GOOD idea at the TIME.  

#### `s3-courier`

_Sparks wraps the plates in a tea towel with a sun on it. Byte wraps a second tea towel, with a moon on it, round that._  
**Sparks**: You show them. They both like you. It’s very annoying.  
**Byte**: A neutral courier. I approve. I’d like that noted somewhere.  
_Neutral: on nobody’s side. Courier: someone who carries things. You are, it seems, both._  
_The plates are heavier than they look. Glass, and years of not knowing._  
**Sparks**: Be careful with them. And with Fern. And with Ember. Mostly with Ember.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): sharing hard news kindly  
> **Sparks**: This news is going to hurt them both. What’s a kind way to share it?  
> - ✅ Somewhere quiet, gently, and give them time to take it in. → Yes. That. Do that. I’d have shouted it across the Circuit.
> - Shout it across the Circuit so everyone knows at once. → That’s what I’d do. That’s why I’m not doing it. Hard news is easier to hear somewhere quiet, said gently, with time to take it in.
> - Leave the plates on their doorsteps without a note. → Then they’d find out alone. Nobody should find out alone. Hard news is kindest somewhere quiet, said gently, with someone there.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to share upsetting news gently and kindly._


**Choices**

- **Show them together, at the same time.**
    - Getting Fern and Ember into one place takes a week. You manage it by telling each that the other won’t come.
    - **Fern**: You absolute snake. Hazel did that to me once.
- **Show them one at a time.**
    - You go to Fern first, then to Ember. Each asks, before anything else, whether the other one has seen it yet.

#### `s3-truce`

_Fern looks at the plates for a long time. So does Ember. Neither looks at the other._  
**Ember**: I don’t need to be forgiven. I need to know who to be angry at.  
**Ember**: Him. It’s always him. He had Ash by the autumn.  
**Fern**: All those years. I hated you because of a flag. That’s… honestly very efficient of him.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): think question: saying sorry for a mistake you didn’t know you made  
> _Fern blamed Ember for years, and it wasn’t Ember’s fault. Fern didn’t know._  
> _Should Fern say sorry? What do you think?_  
> - Yes. She hurt Ember, even by mistake. → That’s a fair answer. Fern would probably agree. A mistake still leaves a bruise.
> - No. She was tricked. The one who moved the flag should say sorry. → That’s a fair answer. Ember says nearly the same: she wants to know who to be angry at.
> - They could both say sorry for the years they lost. → That’s a fair answer, and a generous one. Sometimes “sorry” just means “I wish it had been different.”
> _For grown-ups: Thought about apology and blame when someone was tricked; there was no wrong answer._

**Ember**: There should be a Moot. Everyone. Both sides. Out in the open.  
**Fern**: After midwinter. When there’s time to do it properly. And one urn.  
**Ember**: One urn.  
_It’s the first thing they’ve agreed on in years: a truce. They both look faintly ill about it._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): meetings where people settle things together  
> _“Moot” is a very old English word for a meeting where people come together to talk things out._  
> _Long ago, English villages held moots to settle quarrels and agree on rules, out in the open._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the old word “moot” and how communities met to settle disagreements fairly._


#### `s3-invitations`

_Pixel has been put in charge of the invitations. So there is a planning meeting about the invitations._  
**Pixel**: Gold ink or silver? Gold is Sun. Silver is Moon. Black is a funeral. I’ve tested twelve inks. Everything means something.  
**Clover**: Green? Nobody’s green.  
**Pixel**: …Clover, that’s genius. Green. Nobody’s green.  

> **Lesson** (art, ask): mixing colours to make green  
> **Pixel**: Problem. I have twelve inks and none of them is green. Which two paints do I mix?  
> - ✅ Yellow and blue → Yellow and blue. Green! I knew that. I wanted to see if you knew that.
> - Red and blue → That makes purple. Lovely, but very royal. Nobody wants to be royal. Yellow and blue make green.
> - Red and yellow → That makes orange. Very Sun. Too Sun. Yellow and blue make green.
> _For grown-ups: Practised colour mixing: yellow and blue paint make green._

_Dusty has offered to dig a hole for the one urn. Nobody asked for a hole, and nobody has the heart to say so._  
**Nova**: I’ve been to this valley four times and I still don’t know if I’m Sun or Moon. Somebody said it’s my scarf.  
**Nova**: I’ve decided I’m weather.  
**Luna**: Ember says she’s coming “to make sure it’s done right”. That’s Ember for yes.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): division word problem: how many packs are needed  
> **Pixel**: Ten Keepers, plus one for you. Eleven invitations. Green cards come in packs of 4. How many packs do I buy?  
> - ✅ 3 packs → Three. Two packs is only 8, not enough. Three packs is 12, with one spare. For mistakes. I make mistakes.
> - 2 packs → Two packs is 8 cards. Three people wouldn’t get one. Imagine the grievances. Three packs is 12. Enough for eleven, with one spare.
> - 11 packs → That’s 44 cards! I’d be writing until spring. Each pack has 4. Three packs is 12, enough for eleven, with one spare.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out how many packs of 4 are needed for 11 cards (3, with one spare)._


#### `s3-moot`

_Evening at the pond. Ten Keepers, one urn, green invitations, and nobody sure where to stand._  
_Dusty has dug the hole. The one urn stands in it, so that it is exactly level with nobody. Dusty is very proud._  
**Gran Hazel**: A Moot! I haven’t been to a Moot since my hair was brown. Isn’t this awkward. I love it.  
_You set the plates on the bench by the pond, between the two groups. Sun and Moon come to look, and then everyone._  
**Sparks**: It was the flag. I had it in a box the whole time. I’m loud about everything except the one thing.  
**Fern**: Bramble went over that rail because a man moved a flag. Not because of Ash. Not because of anyone here.  
_Pixel pours the last of the sun urn and the last of the moon urn into the one urn. Byte tastes it, gravely._  
**Byte**: Same tea. It was always the same tea. I’d like that read into the record.  
**Sparks**: Byte, I swear by every lantern in this valley—  
**Byte**: Into the record.  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): planning a fair test  
> **Byte**: For the record, I tested it properly first. Which test is fairest, to prove two teas are the same?  
> - ✅ Same cups, same amount, same heat, and the taster doesn’t know which is which. → Yes. Change nothing except the thing you’re testing. And hide the labels, so nobody tastes what they expect. That’s a fair test. I did it eleven times. Same tea, every time.
> - Ask Sparks which one she likes best. → Sun. Obviously. Sun. Exactly why not. She knows which is which. A fair test hides the labels and keeps everything else the same.
> - Taste the sun tea hot and the moon tea cold. → Then you’re testing hot against cold, not sun against moon. A fair test changes only one thing. Same cups, same amount, same heat, labels hidden.
> _For grown-ups: Learned what makes a fair test: change one thing, keep the rest the same, and test blind._

**Ember**: So. Midsummer. A Cup. Everybody runs. Same course, new flags, and I check them.  
**Fern**: We check them.  
**Byte**: I’ll check the checking.  
**Gran Hazel**: And who’s keeping the Moot, love? Somebody has to bang the spoon.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): ending a quarrel by talking openly  
> **Gran Hazel**: Disagreeing is fine, love. Valleys are full of it. It’s the whispering behind urns that does the damage.  
> **Gran Hazel**: Say it to their faces, kindly, with the evidence on the table. That’s how a feud ends.  
> _For grown-ups: Heard how talking openly and honestly, with facts, can end a long quarrel._


**Choices**

- **Bang the spoon on the urn.**

    - **Pixel**: Ribbons! Gold and silver, stitched down the middle in green. One for every Nubbin who runs the Cup.
    - **Gran Hazel**: Moot-Keeper. Told you it’d suit.
- **Give the spoon to Fern and Ember to share.**
    - Fern and Ember hold the spoon between them and bang the urn together. Both miss, and the whole pond cheers.
    - **Pixel**: Ribbons! Gold and silver, stitched down the middle in green. One for every Nubbin who runs the Cup.
    - **Gran Hazel**: You’re still the Moot-Keeper, love. Somebody had to bring the spoon.

### Glossary

- **feud**: A long, bitter quarrel between two people or groups.
- **grievance**: A complaint about something you feel was unfair.
- **evidence**: Facts or things you can see and check that show what is true.
- **develop**: To grow or build up; with photos, to treat film or plates with chemicals so the picture appears.
- **steward**: Someone whose job is to look after a place or an event, like a race.
- **neutral**: Not on either side in a quarrel.
- **courier**: Someone who carries messages or packages from one person to another.
- **truce**: An agreement to stop fighting or quarrelling.
- **moot**: An old word for a meeting where people gather to talk things out and decide together.
- **fair test**: An experiment where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same.

## S4. The Wellspring

- `s4-step1`: Check the water line Hazel painted on the rock by the falls. · _The falls are past the pond, on the Hollow side. Tap the white mark on the rock beside the pool._
- `s4-step2`: Send a swimmer up the outflow to see what’s above the falls. · _Choose Swim at the top of the pool. If none of your Nubbins can swim yet, Marina gives one a lesson first._
- `s4-step3`: Walk the ledge path behind the falls with Marina. · _Meet Marina at the pool in the evening. Stay close behind her on the ledge, and don’t stop to look down._
- `s4-step4`: Open the sluice gate on the Circuit’s dam, after dark. · _Go at night with Marina and a strong Nubbin. Move on the snore, freeze on the whistle. The sluice sticks._

#### `s4-pools`

**Marina**: You won. Good. Come and see something that isn’t winning.  
_Past the ridge, Marina’s tide pools step down the rock like a row of bowls. Half of them are dry._  
_In the rest, the anemones have shut up tight, like fists._  
**Marina**: They get what the stream gives them. This summer it’s giving them less. And what does come down is cold.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, notice): tides and the Moon’s pull  
> **Marina**: Real tide pools sit on the seashore. The sea fills them up, then drains away, about twice a day.  
> **Marina**: That’s the tide. The Moon’s pull makes the oceans bulge on two sides of the Earth. As the Earth turns, we pass through both bulges each day.  
> **Marina**: Mine are too high up the rock for any tide. They only get the stream. So when the stream fails, so do they.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the Moon’s pull causes the tides, which rise and fall about twice a day on most coasts._

**Marina**: Cold. In July.  
**Marina**: Hazel painted a line on the rock by the falls, years back. Where the water ought to come to. Go and look.  
**You**: Why not look yourself?  
**Marina**: I’ve looked forty times. I want someone else to tell me I’m wrong.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): when worry wants a second opinion  
> _Marina has checked forty times. Why do you think she wants someone else to look?_  
> - ✅ When you’re worried, a second pair of eyes helps you know if it’s real. → That’s it. After forty looks you stop trusting your own eyes. Worry does that.
> - She’s too lazy to walk to the falls. → Forty times. To the falls. Lazy. She’s worried. When you’re very worried, asking someone else to check helps you know what’s real.
> - She wants to win an argument. → I’d love to lose this one. She’s worried. Asking someone else to look is a good way to check whether a worry is real.
> _For grown-ups: Recognised that asking someone else to check can help when we are worried._

**Marina**: Take a Nubbin. They like the falls. Mind the moss on the rocks. Not that Moss. The slippery kind.  

#### `s4-line`

_The falls are loud and white. On the dark rock beside the pool, someone has painted a thick white line._  
_The water sits a hand’s width below it. Above the water the rock is pale and dry, where it should be dark and wet._  
_Your Nubbin dips a paw in, pulls it out, and looks at you as if you did this._  
**Marina**: A hand. A whole hand.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.MD.A.1, do): measuring length in centimetres  
> **Marina**: Mind you, a hand isn’t a proper measure. Everybody’s hand is a different size.  
> **Marina**: Here. Hazel’s measuring stick. Put the zero at the water and read the mark at the white line.  
> _(Line the stick up and read the number at the white line.)_  
> **Marina**: Ten centimetres. Write it down. Numbers don’t argue, Hazel used to say.  
> Check: `edu:measure:water-line:10cm`
> _For grown-ups: Measured a length in centimetres with a ruler, starting from zero._

_Marina has followed you after all. She is standing at the edge of the pool with her shoes in her hand._  
**Marina**: Something upstream is taking it. Something big enough to take a hand of water off the falls.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): reading signs that water levels have changed  
> _Wet rock looks darker than dry rock. The pale band is where the water used to reach and doesn’t any more._  
> _People who study rivers look for bands like this. The rock remembers where the water was._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned to read marks on rock as evidence of a change in water level._

**Marina**: Hazel traded me fruit for swimming lessons. For her Nubbins, not her. She swam like a dropped teapot.  
**Marina**: Lesson one: they float better than you’d think. Lesson two: they don’t think, so let them.  
_She wades in to her knees and holds your Nubbin under the chin, the way you’d steady a cup._  
_It kicks once, amazed, and doesn’t sink._

**Marina**: And stay where I can see you. That’s the rule for Nubbins and Keepers alike.  

> **Lesson** (health, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, notice): water safety  
> **Marina**: Real rule, for real water: never swim without a grown-up watching. Not once. Not even a good swimmer.  
> **Marina**: Rivers and pools can be colder, deeper and faster than they look. Cold water steals your strength quickly.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the water-safety rule: only swim with a grown-up watching, as water can be colder and deeper than it looks._
