#### `s4-dam`

_Your swimmer comes back down the outflow and shakes itself all over you, the way Nubbins do when water has been rude._  
_Caught in its fur: a grey thread, and a flake of fresh mortar._  
_Round the bend upstream you find it. A wall of new grey stone across the stream, with a sluice gate in it, shut._  
_Behind the wall the water lies flat and still and very blue, all the way up to the Circuit’s new swimming lanes._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS2-2, ask): how a dam changes the water downstream  
> **Marina**: So. Why are my pools drying up?  
> - ✅ The dam holds the water back, so less flows down to the falls and the pools. → Yes. A wall that holds back a river is a dam. The lake it makes behind it is a reservoir. Everything downstream gets whatever the dam lets through. Right now, that’s not much.
> - The sun has dried it all up. → The sun takes a little, every summer. Not a whole hand. The dam holds the water back, so less flows down to us. The lake behind it is called a reservoir.
> - The Nubbins have been drinking it. → They do drink a lot. Not that much. The dam holds the water back, so less flows down to us. The lake behind it is a reservoir.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how a dam holds back water and changes the land and life downstream._

_Each lane has a rope, a number, and a neat sign: NO SPLASHING._  
**Marina**: No splashing. It’s water. Splashing is what it’s for.  
**Marina**: A swimming course. My pools are dying for a swimming course.  
**Marina**: I’ve written to the Circuit three times. I got three forms back. Received. Filed. Very tidy.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): temperature difference (subtraction within 100)  
> _Marina dips her old thermometer in the stream. It reads 8°C (46°F)._  
> **Marina**: Hazel wrote down the July water every year. Last July: 17°C (63°F). How many degrees Celsius colder is it now?  
> - ✅ 9 degrees → Nine. 17 take away 8. That’s not summer water. That’s spring water.
> - 25 degrees → That’s 17 and 8 added together. We want the difference. Count up from 8 to 17: two to get to 10, then seven more. Nine degrees colder.
> - 11 degrees → Close. Count up from 8: two to get to 10, then seven more to 17. Two and seven is nine. Nine degrees colder.
> _For grown-ups: Found the difference between two temperatures (17 − 8 = 9) by counting on._


#### `s4-ledge-ask`

**Marina**: Before we do anything about that wall, I want to show you something. Not because it helps.  
**Marina**: Because somebody besides me ought to know the way. Hazel knew it. Hazel’s away.  
_Beside the falls, half hidden by ferns, a narrow ledge runs straight into the roar._  
_Behind the curtain of water, the rock has been worn back into a long, dark hollow._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, notice): erosion: how water carves rock  
> **Marina**: Falling water wears rock away. That’s called erosion. Soft rock wears away faster than hard rock.  
> **Marina**: Here the top is hard and the rock beneath is soft. Over a very long time the soft part washed out, and left a hollow.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how erosion by falling water carves soft rock faster than hard rock, making hollows behind waterfalls._

**Marina**: The ledge path. Back to the rock, eyes on my heels.  
**Marina**: Don’t look at the water. It doesn’t like being stared at.  

#### `s4-ledge`

_Behind the falls the world turns to noise and spray. The rock under your hand is wet and soft with moss._  
_Halfway along, the ledge bends into the dark. From round the bend comes a breath of air: warm, and smelling of stone._  
**Marina**: That’s the spring breathing. Where the first ones came up, if you believe Moss. I do, mostly.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): warm springs: heat from under the ground  
> **Marina**: There are warm springs in the real world too. Rain soaks down deep, where the rock is hot.  
> **Marina**: The water warms up down there and rises back to the surface. Where warm water meets cold air, you see a mist.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that warm springs are heated by hot rock deep underground._

_Marina stops at the bend. She doesn’t go on._  
**Marina**: Further is for when it’s needed. Hazel’s rule. I’ve kept it twenty years.  
**Marina**: But now you know the way this far. That’s all a path is, really. Somebody else knowing it.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): passing on knowledge of places: walking and maps  
> **Marina**: So. What’s the best way to make sure a path like this is never forgotten?  
> - ✅ Walk it with someone, and draw a map as well. → Both. Walking teaches your feet. A map keeps it when there’s nobody left to walk it with you.
> - Walk it with someone. → That’s how Hazel taught me. It’s the best way to learn it. But add a map as well. A map remembers the way when there’s nobody left to walk it with you.
> - Draw a map. → A map is a good keeper. It doesn’t forget. But walk it too. A map can’t tell you which rock wobbles. Both together is best.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how knowledge of a place is passed on, by showing someone and by maps._


#### `s4-sluice`

**Marina**: Three letters. Three forms. I’m done writing.  
**Marina**: We’re not breaking anything. Breaking is loud, and it gets you talked about. We’re opening a gate that ought to be open.  
_At night the dam is just a dark wall and the sound of held water. The sluice is a great wooden door in new stone._  
_Beside it, in a tidy hut, the Circuit’s night steward sits bolt upright in his chair, fast asleep, clipboard on his chest._  
_He snores in a perfect rhythm. In, out, and a thin little whistle. The clipboard rises and falls._  
**Marina**: I’ve watched him three nights. Move on the snore. Freeze on the whistle. The whistle’s when they wake.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): a repeating pattern and its rule  
> **Marina**: In, out, whistle. In, out, whistle. If we count every sound, what will the 9th sound be?  
> - ✅ Whistle → Whistle. Every third sound is a whistle: 3rd, 6th, 9th. So on the 9th, we freeze.
> - In → Let’s count it: in 1, out 2, whistle 3, in 4, out 5, whistle 6, in 7, out 8, whistle 9. Every third sound is a whistle. 3, 6, 9. Freeze on 9.
> - Out → Count it with me: in, out, whistle is 1, 2, 3. Then 4, 5, 6. Then 7, 8, 9. The whistle lands on every multiple of 3. The 9th is a whistle. Freeze.
> _For grown-ups: Found the rule of a repeating pattern (every third sound) and used it to predict the 9th._

**You**: “They”?  
**Marina**: Stewards. They’re all the same steward, as far as I can tell.  
_You creep to the sluice on a snore and try it on the next one. It doesn’t move. It is, without any doubt, stuck._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): think question: is it right to open the gate without asking?  
> _Marina asked three times, politely, and nobody listened. The gate isn’t hers._  
> _Is it right to open it without permission? What do you think?_  
> - Yes. The pools are dying, and the gate should never have been shut. → That’s a fair answer. It’s mine. Living things come before tidy swimming lanes.
> - Only if we leave a note saying what we did and why. → That’s a fair answer. Doing it openly, with your name on it, is a kind of honesty.
> - No. We should keep asking, louder, and get more people to ask too. → That’s a fair answer. Lots of things change that way. I’m just not sure the pools can wait.
> _For grown-ups: Weighed rules, fairness and urgency in a hard choice; there was no wrong answer._


**Choices**

- **Lift, then push.**
    - You lift, and push, the way the Grove gate taught you. The sluice groans, gives, and swings.
    - **Marina**: Where did you learn that?
    - **You**: Home.
- **Let your strongest Nubbin have a go.**
    - Your Nubbin puts its back into it and shoves, and nothing happens. Then it slips, lifts by accident, and the whole thing swings.
    - **Marina**: Hazel’s trick. Even the Nubbins know it.
- **Pin a polite note to the gate first.**
    - You write: “Sluice opened for the tide pools, with thanks, from Hazel’s Grove.” Then you lift, and push, and it swings.
    - **Marina**: Polite. He’ll hate that more than anything.

#### `s4-water`

_Water pours through the gap, dark and loud, and goes tumbling off towards the falls as if it’s late for something._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): water flows downhill  
> _Which way does the water go, now the gate is open?_  
> - ✅ Downhill, towards the falls. → Yes. Gravity pulls water down, so it always flows to the lowest place it can reach. Downhill means the falls.
> - Uphill, back to the swimming lanes. → Water can’t flow uphill on its own. Gravity pulls it down. It always runs to the lowest place it can reach. Here, that’s the falls and the pools.
> - It stays where it is. → It stayed put while the gate held it. Now nothing does. Gravity pulls water downhill, to the lowest place it can reach: the falls and the pools.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that gravity makes water flow downhill to the lowest place it can reach._

**Marina**: Listen.  
_Below you, the falls change their sound: fuller and louder, the way the rock remembers them._  
_In the hut, the steward stirs, says “Received,” quite clearly, and goes back to sleep._  
**Marina**: Filed, I expect.  
**Marina**: Somebody will shut it again, probably. Then somebody will open it again. That’s most of keeping.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, notice): theme: what “keeping” means in this story  
> _“That’s most of keeping.” Looking after something isn’t done once. It’s done again and again._  
> _That idea comes up all through the Grove’s stories. A big idea a story keeps returning to is its theme._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed a theme (caring for something is ongoing work) that runs through the stories._


#### `s4-complete`

_A week later the tide pools are full to the brim. The anemones have opened, as if surprised to be asked._  
**Marina**: Look at them. Showing off.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): how anemones survive in tide pools  
> **Marina**: Anemones look like flowers, but they’re animals. Those are tentacles, not petals.  
> **Marina**: When the water drops, they pull in tight to keep from drying out. Under water, they open up to catch bits of food.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sea anemones are animals that close up to stay moist and open their tentacles to feed._

_In the deepest pool, wedged between two stones, something round and pearl-white is catching the light._  
_Your swimmer has seen it too. It dives before anyone can stop it: one kick, two, and a long silver string of bubbles._  
_It comes up with the thing balanced on its head, extremely pleased with itself, and sneezes. It is an egg._  
**Marina**: …Oh. Oh, you beauty.  
**Marina**: Once in a long while one comes down from behind the falls. Hazel saw one in forty years. It’s yours. You opened the gate.  
**Marina**: And your swimmers can dive here whenever they like. As deep as they want. I’ll teach them the rest.  
**Marina**: Take some shells for the Grove. Take the pool weed too; it’s lucky. It isn’t lucky. It smells. Take it anyway.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> **Marina**: I’ve filled 4 bags with 6 shells each. How many shells is that for the Grove?  
> - ✅ 24 → Twenty-four. Four sixes. Don’t spend them all at once.
> - 10 → That’s 4 and 6 added. But it’s 4 bags with 6 in each. 6, 12, 18, 24. Four lots of six is 24.
> - 20 → Close. Count in sixes, one for each bag: 6, 12, 18, 24. Four lots of six is 24.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied equal groups (4 × 6 = 24) by counting in sixes._

_Up at the dam, someone has hung a neat painted sign on the open sluice: OPEN BY ORDER. It doesn’t say whose._  

### Glossary

- **anemone**: A soft sea animal with a ring of tentacles that looks a bit like a flower.
- **tide**: The rise and fall of the sea, caused mostly by the pull of the Moon.
- **centimetre**: A small unit of length. A hundred centimetres make one metre.
- **outflow**: The place where water flows out of a pool or lake.
- **reservoir**: A lake made by holding water back, often behind a dam.
- **sluice**: A gate that can open or close to control how much water flows through.
- **erosion**: The slow wearing away of rock or soil by water, wind or ice.
- **rhythm**: A pattern of sounds or beats that repeats.

## S5. Fossil’s Last Walk

- `s5-step1`: Carry Fossil to the cliff where Dusty found her egg. · _The cliff is east, past the stream. Walk, don’t run. She’s very old, and she likes to look at things._
- `s5-step2`: Take Fossil to Hazel’s first tree and shake it once. · _It’s the low, crooked tree across the stream. Build a gentle shake, not a huge one. One fruit only._
- `s5-step3`: Hold Fossil up in the shallows of the pond. · _Bring Fossil to the pond’s edge and choose Swim. One of your swimmers can hold her, or Marina will._
- `s5-step4`: Sit with them until dark. · _Stay still near Fossil and your youngest Nubbin until night falls. If you wander off, she’ll wait._

#### `s5-list`

_Dusty is at the gate with a very old Nubbin in the crook of one arm and a much-folded bit of paper in the other hand._  
_The Nubbin is the colour of sand. When she blinks, she does it slowly, as if each blink costs something._  
**Dusty**: This is Fossil. I dug her egg out of the cliff when I was eleven. Don’t say the name isn’t original. I was eleven.  
**Dusty**: She’s very old now. She’s fading. Not her glow. Her. You’ll have seen it, if you’ve looked.  
**Dusty**: Twenty years. You’d think I’d have run out of things to say to her. I’ve got a list.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): addition word problem within 100  
> _Dusty was 11 when they dug out Fossil’s egg. That was 20 years ago. How old is Dusty now?_  
> - ✅ 31 → Thirty-one. Don’t say it like that. Thirty-one is young. For a cliff.
> - 9 → Ha. I wish. That’s 20 take away 11. Twenty years have passed since Dusty was 11, so we add: 11 + 20 = 31.
> - 30 → Nearly. Don’t round me down, I’ve earned that year. Start at 11 and add 20: 21, 31. Dusty is 31.
> _For grown-ups: Added 11 + 20 = 31 to work out an age from a starting age and years passed._

_Dusty unfolds the paper. It has been folded and unfolded so often it has gone soft as cloth._  
**Dusty**: Three things. My back’s gone; I can’t carry her and do the things. Would you?  
**Dusty**: One, the cliff. Two, Hazel’s first tree. Three, the water. She used to swim like she was late for something.  
_Fossil looks up at you, unhurried, and holds out her arms the way very small children do._  
**Fossil**: …  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): life cycles: being born, growing, growing old, dying  
> _Every living thing has a life cycle. It is born, it grows, it grows old, and in the end it dies._  
> _Fossil is near the end of hers. That is why Dusty has a list._  
> **Dusty**: Old isn’t over. Old is when you do the things that matter. While you can.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that every living thing has a life cycle that includes growing old and dying, in plain, gentle words._


**Choices**

- **Lift her with both hands, like an egg.**
    - You lift her the way you’d lift a full cup. She settles against you, approving.
    - **Dusty**: That’s it. That’s exactly it.
- **Let her ride on your shoulder.**
    - She climbs up, slowly, and sits on your shoulder like a very old queen inspecting something ridiculous.
    - **Dusty**: Oh, she likes you. The last person who tried that got their ear nibbled.

#### `s5-cliff`

_At the foot of the cliff the rock is striped like a cake: brown, red, grey, brown. Each stripe is a layer._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS1-1, do): rock layers: the oldest is at the bottom  
> **Dusty**: Every stripe was mud or sand once, laid down flat, one on top of the last. Over ages, it pressed into rock.  
> **Dusty**: Go on. Tap them in order. Oldest first.  
> _(Tap the layers from oldest to newest.)_  
> **Dusty**: Bottom to top. The bottom one was laid down first, so it’s the oldest. Everything above came later.  
> Check: `edu:order:rock-layers:oldest-first`
> _For grown-ups: Ordered rock layers by age, learning that lower layers are usually older than the ones above._

**Dusty**: Here. I was twelve. It was raining. I used a trowel.  
_Fossil leans out and taps the rock, twice, very firmly._  
**Dusty**: …Eleven. Fine. Eleven. And it was sunny.  
_Tap._  
**Dusty**: A spoon. It was a spoon. A big spoon. You try digging out a whole egg with a spoon. It took two days.  
_Fossil lays her head against the rock and leaves it there a while. Dusty doesn’t say anything at all._  
**Dusty**: I tell it wrong on purpose. Every time. Twenty years, and she’s never once let me get away with it.  
_By her head a little fern grows out of a crack, curled tight. Pressed into the stone beside it is a much older one._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS4-1, notice): fossils show what lived long ago  
> **Dusty**: That’s a fossil. A real one. Not her. The fern.  
> **Dusty**: Long ago a fern was buried in mud. Very slowly the mud turned to stone, and kept the fern’s shape.  
> **Dusty**: Fossils tell us what lived here before any of us. Ferns, it turns out. Ferns were here first.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a fossil forms and that fossils show us what lived long ago._


#### `s5-tree-ask`

**Dusty**: Next, Hazel’s first tree. The crooked one over the stream. Shake it once. She was very specific.  
**Dusty**: Well. I was. On her behalf.  
_Fossil falls asleep on the way. She wakes exactly as you reach the tree, as if she set an alarm._  
_The tree is low and crooked, and its trunk is wider than you can reach round._  
**Dusty**: Hazel planted it the year she came. Forty years old. Twice as old as Fossil.  
**Dusty**: If it ever came down, you could count the rings in the stump: one ring for every year it grew. Let’s not find out.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): comparing two ages by subtracting  
> **Dusty**: The tree is 40. I’m 31. How many years older than me is it?  
> - ✅ 9 years → Nine. Count up from 31 to 40. It’s still taller than me, too. Rude.
> - 71 years → That’s us added together. We’d need a very big cake. To compare, subtract: 40 − 31. Count up from 31 to 40: nine years.
> - 10 years → Nearly. Count up from 31 to 40. 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40. Nine steps. Nine years.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two ages by subtraction (40 − 31 = 9), counting on to check._


#### `s5-tree`

_Every Nubbin you own has followed you here. They sit in a row under the branches with their mouths open._  
**Dusty**: Once. Not twice. Twice is just weather.  
_You shake it, once. One fruit drops: small, wrinkled, an odd yellow-brown, like an apple that has heard bad news._  
_It misses every open mouth in the row and lands in Fossil’s lap, as if it knew the way._  
**Dusty**: That’s the one. Hazel gave her one the day she hatched. She ate it in one go and was sick on my shoe.  
_Fossil takes the fruit in both hands but doesn’t eat it yet. She holds it, and smells it, and closes her eyes._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): smell and memory  
> _Smell is one of the senses most closely tied to memory._  
> _One sniff of something from long ago can bring the past rushing back, as if you were there again._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the sense of smell is strongly linked to memories._

**Dusty**: Hazel stood where you are and said, “Well, she’s yours now. Good luck to you both.” I think she meant me.  
_Fossil eats a third of it, very slowly. Then she hands the rest to Dusty, who eats it, though it is horrible._  
**Dusty**: Tastes like being eleven.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): fractions of a whole  
> _Fossil ate one third of the fruit. What fraction did Dusty eat?_  
> - ✅ Two thirds → Yes. Three thirds make a whole. Fossil had one, so Dusty had the other two. Two horrible thirds.
> - One third → That’s Fossil’s share. A whole fruit is three thirds. Take away Fossil’s one third, and two thirds are left for Dusty.
> - One half → Halves would be two equal parts. This fruit was cut into three equal parts: thirds. Fossil ate one third, so Dusty ate the other two thirds.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that a whole is three thirds, so taking away one third leaves two thirds._


#### `s5-water-ask`

**Dusty**: Last one. The water. She can’t swim on her own any more.  
**Dusty**: Marina taught her, years back, with Hazel’s lot. Says she was the only one who swam sideways on purpose.  
_Marina is already at the pond, sleeves rolled up, as though somebody sent for her._  
_Dusty is very bad at secrets._  
**Marina**: I was passing. With a towel. As you do.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): using clues to find a character’s real motive  
> _Marina says she was “just passing”. Sleeves rolled up. A towel. What’s really going on?_  
> - ✅ Dusty asked her to come and help, and she’s pretending it’s nothing. → Yes. The towel and the sleeves are the clues. Nobody just passes with a towel.
> - She was going for a swim anyway. → Possible. But look at the clues: sleeves rolled up for lifting, a towel ready, and Dusty bad at secrets. Dusty asked Marina to come. She’s pretending it’s nothing.
> - She’s lost. → Marina knows every rock in this valley. She’s not lost. The towel and sleeves are clues: Dusty asked Marina to help, and she’s pretending it’s nothing.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in the text to work out a character’s real reason for being there._

**Dusty**: Course you were.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): quiet kindness  
> _Sometimes kind people pretend a big favour is nothing. That way, the other person doesn’t feel they owe them._  
> _Dusty knows. Marina knows Dusty knows. Nobody says so. That’s a kind of kindness too._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed a quiet kind of kindness: helping without making a fuss about it._


**Choices**

- **Let one of your swimmers hold her.**
    - Your swimmer wades out and waits, very serious, as if it has been given the most important job in the valley.
    - **Marina**: Paw under the chin. Like a cup. There you go.
- **Ask Marina to hold her.**
    - Marina wades in to her waist and holds out her hands.
    - **Marina**: Come on then, old girl. Same as always.

#### `s5-water`

_You lower Fossil into the water, and it takes her weight. For a moment she is stiff and heavy. Then she is light._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): water pushes up on things in it  
> **Marina**: Water pushes up on anything that’s in it. That push holds up some of her weight.  
> **Marina**: That’s why she suddenly feels light. The water is helping to carry her.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that water pushes upwards on objects in it, which makes them feel lighter._

_Then, very slowly, she kicks._  
**Dusty**: Look at her. That’s the stroke. The little sideways one. Like she’s late for something.  
**Dusty**: To the reeds and back, Fos. Then you can be smug about it.  
_She swims to the reeds and back. It takes a long time, and nobody hurries her._  
_When you lift her out she is shivering, and her eyes are bright. She isn’t looking at Dusty. She’s looking at the Grove._  

> **Lesson** (health, ask): why bodies shiver  
> **Marina**: Towel. Quick. Why do you think she’s shivering?  
> - ✅ Her body is shaking its muscles to make heat after the cold water. → Yes. Shivering is your muscles working fast to warm you up. A towel and a cuddle help it along.
> - She’s scared. → Look at her eyes. Bright. Not scared. Shivering after cold water is the body shaking its muscles to make heat. A towel helps.
> - She’s excited. → She might be, a little! But the shiver is from the cold. Shivering is the body shaking its muscles to make heat. A towel helps it along.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that shivering is the body making heat by moving muscles quickly._

**Dusty**: …That’s not the list. She’s got a list of her own.  

#### `s5-secret`

_You set Fossil down on the bank. She walks across the Grove on her own, one slow step at a time._  
_Not to Dusty, and not to you. She goes to your youngest Nubbin, who is busy falling over a fruit, and sits beside it._  
**Dusty**: …Oh.  
_Your youngest stops falling over and looks at Fossil, and Fossil looks back. Then they just sit._  
**Dusty**: She did this for me once. I was small and I’d had a bad day. She just sat. Didn’t fix anything. Didn’t try.  
**Dusty**: Nobody ever taught her that. She just knew, years before I did.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): being there for someone  
> **Dusty**: She didn’t fix my bad day. Not one bit of it. So why do you think it helped?  
> - ✅ Because I wasn’t alone with it any more. → That’s it. You can’t always fix it. You can always sit next to it.
> - It didn’t help. Only fixing things helps. → I thought that too, when I was small. But some things can’t be fixed. Having someone beside you means you’re not alone with them. That helps more than you’d think.
> - Because she was warm. → She was. Still is, just about. But mostly it helped because I wasn’t alone with it any more. Someone was there.
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how being with someone helps, even when you can’t fix their problem._


#### `s5-gift`

_The sun goes down behind the western hill. Fossil doesn’t move, nor does your youngest, and after a while nor do you._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, ask): the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west  
> _The sun is setting behind the western hill. Which direction does the Sun set in?_  
> - ✅ West → Yes. Each day the Sun rises in the east, crosses the sky, and sets in the west.
> - East → East is where it rises, in the morning. It crosses the sky all day and sets in the west. That’s why the hill is called the western hill.
> - North → Not north. The Sun rises in the east, crosses the sky, and sets in the west. That’s why the hill it sets behind is called the western hill.
> _For grown-ups: Recalled the daily pattern of the Sun: rising in the east and setting in the west._

_The sky turns orange, then pink, then a deep, quiet blue._  
_One by one, the first stars come out over the pond._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-1, notice): why stars only show at night  
> _The stars were there all day. The Sun’s bright light hid them._  
> _Once the Sun has set and the sky grows dark, the stars can shine through._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that stars are in the sky all the time but are hidden by daylight._

_When it’s dark, the old Nubbin gets up and touches her nose to your youngest’s nose._  
_Then Fossil walks back to Dusty, slowly, the way she does everything._  
_Your youngest sits up straighter than you’ve ever seen it sit._  
_On its stats sheet, under Stamina, are new words: “A gift from Fossil.”_  

#### `s5-home`

_Dusty picks Fossil up to carry her home, bad back or not. The ball above her head is very pale now._  
_It doesn’t glow. It only gets paler, the way a sky does at the end of the day._  
**Dusty**: Thank you. I mean it. I don’t say that much. Ask anyone. They’ll tell you I never say it.  
**Dusty**: I think it thins slower with someone walking beside it. I’d like to think so.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): think question: what helps when someone we love is very old  
> _Fossil is very old. Dusty knows she won’t be alive much longer, and it hurts._  
> _What do you think helps, when someone you love is near the end of their life?_  
> - Doing the things they love, together. → That’s a fair answer. It’s why I made the list.
> - Telling them what they mean to you. → That’s a fair answer. I should do more of that. I’m bad at it. Ask anyone.
> - Just being there, like Fossil did. → That’s a fair answer. She taught me that one herself.
> - I don’t know. It just feels sad. → That’s a fair answer, and an honest one. It is sad. Being sad about it is allowed.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about ageing and saying goodbye; there was no wrong answer. Feelings of sadness were named as normal._

_Fossil reaches out to you. In her fist is a curled seed from the fern at the foot of the cliff._  
**Dusty**: She wants you to plant it. Fossil-fern. Grows out of rock, if you’re patient. Course it does.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): real ferns grow from spores, not seeds  
> **Dusty**: Mind you, real ferns don’t make seeds. They make spores, tiny as dust, in brown dots under their leaves.  
> **Dusty**: The wind carries the spores off, and new ferns grow where they land. This is a Grove fern. It ignores rules.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that real ferns reproduce with tiny spores rather than seeds._

**Dusty**: And have this. Don’t argue. I bought it the week after I dug her out. Never needed it like I needed the spoon.  
_Dusty’s trowel. The handle is worn pale where a hand has held it for twenty years._  
_They go out through the gate together. Dusty lifts and pushes without thinking._  
_On the western hill, Moss watches the gate long after it has closed._  

### Glossary

- **crook**: The bend on the inside of your elbow.
- **life cycle**: The stages a living thing goes through: being born, growing, growing old and dying.
- **layer**: A flat sheet of something lying on top of or under another, like the stripes in a cliff.
- **fossil**: The shape of a plant or animal from long ago, preserved in rock.
- **specific**: Exact and particular, with no room for mistakes.
- **fraction**: A part of a whole, such as one half or one third.
- **smug**: Very pleased with yourself, and showing it.
- **spore**: A tiny speck, like dust, that ferns and mushrooms use to grow new ferns and mushrooms.

## S6. Ash’s True Name

- `s6-s1`: Ember has asked you over. Go and see Ash. · _Ember’s house is past the dojo on the Moon side. Knock. She’ll pretend she wasn’t waiting._
- `s6-s2`: Find what Hazel wrote about the egg she gave Ember. · _In the cottage, tap the bookshelf by the stove. Hazel kept her record books on the bottom shelf._
- `s6-s3`: Take the register to Ember, and practise the three notes by the pond. · _Pick the pattern Hazel wrote: low, high, and a little one going up. There’s no timer, and a wrong try costs nothing._
- `s6-s4`: Be in Ember’s kitchen when she whistles to Ash. · _Go to Ember’s house after dark. Stand by the door and let her do it._

#### `s6-kitchen`

_A note under your door at dawn: COME OVER. Then PLEASE, crossed out, and written again._  
_Ember’s house is very tidy. It’s the kind of tidy you get when someone cleans because they’re angry._  
**Ember**: She’s out of that garden. Don’t ask how. I don’t care how, and I never will.  
_A grey Nubbin sits in the corner of the kitchen, facing the wall. Beside her is a full bowl._  
**Ember**: Ash.  
**Ember**: Ash, love. It’s me. Ash.  
_The grey Nubbin doesn’t turn. A drip falls from the tap. She doesn’t turn for that either._  
**Ember**: Four hundred and twelve times since yesterday. I counted. Tell Byte I counted and I’ll deny it.  
**Ember**: She eats when I leave the room. She sleeps standing up.  
**Ember**: It isn’t her name any more. To her it’s just a noise.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): use a character’s actions to work out her real feelings  
> _Ember says she doesn’t care. But look at her clues: the PLEASE on the note, and all that counting._  
> _How does Ember really feel about Ash?_  
> - ✅ She cares about Ash more than anything. → Yes. People sometimes hide big feelings behind cross words. Ember’s clues give her away.
> - She doesn’t mind either way. → That’s what she says. But nobody counts to four hundred and twelve about something they don’t mind. Her actions show she cares a lot.
> - She’s cross with Ash. → She does sound cross. But she’s cross because she’s worried. The PLEASE and the counting show how much she cares.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in what a character does, not just what she says, to work out her real feelings._


**Choices**

- **Sit on the floor near Ash, and wait.**
    - You sit for a long time. Ash doesn’t look at you, but she stops pressing quite so hard into the wall.
    - **Ember**: …Hazel used to do that. Sit on the floor as if it were a perfectly good chair. It drove me mad.
- **Say “Ash” yourself, gently.**
    - Ash doesn’t turn. Ember lets out a long breath. It might be relief.
    - **Ember**: See? It’s not me. It isn’t just me.
- **Ask what Corvin called her.**
    - **Ember**: Nothing. He didn’t call them anything. He just stood where they could see him.
    - **Ember**: Years of nobody saying her name. You’d forget too.

#### `s6-egg`

_Ember puts the kettle on. She doesn’t make any tea._  
_The kettle starts to whistle, thin and high. Ember doesn’t move to take it off._  
**Ember**: When she was tiny she answered to everything. Her name, my name, the kettle.  
_The whistle gets louder. At last Ember lifts the kettle off the stove, and the sound dies away._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, notice): sounds are made by vibrations  
> _Why does a kettle whistle? Steam rushes out through a tiny hole in the whistle on the spout._  
> _That makes the air there shake very fast. A fast shake like that is called a vibration, and vibrations make every sound._  
> _No vibration, no sound. When the steam slowed down, the whistle stopped._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sounds are made by vibrations, using Ember’s whistling kettle._

**Ember**: I named her Ash a week after I got her. Before that she was just the egg from Hazel’s.  
**Ember**: Go home. Thanks for coming. Don’t make it a thing.  

#### `s6-fern`

_Fern is leaning on the fence between your gardens, eating an apple. It is clearly from your tree._  
**Fern**: You’ve been at Ember’s. You’ve got the look. The look of someone told not to make it a thing.  
**You**: Ash won’t answer to her name.  
**Fern**: Ember asked you over? Ember doesn’t like anyone. She doesn’t like me, and I’m delightful.  
**Fern**: …Poor Ash. Poor Ember. Don’t tell her I said “poor”.  
**You**: Ash came from one of Hazel’s eggs.  
**Fern**: Then she’s in the book. Hazel wrote down every egg she ever gave away, and the first sound each one made.  
**Fern**: “For the record,” she said. Whose record, I said. “Theirs,” she said.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): choose the right meaning of a multiple-meaning word  
> _“Record” is a word with more than one meaning._  
> _When Hazel says “for the record”, which kind of record does she mean?_  
> - ✅ Writing something down so it’s remembered. → That’s it. A record is a written note of what happened. Hazel kept a record of every egg.
> - The fastest time ever, like a race record. → That’s a real meaning too! Sparks loves those. But Hazel means writing things down, so they’re remembered.
> - A music disc that plays songs. → Ha. Hazel did have a few of those. But here a record means a written note, kept so nobody forgets.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out which meaning of a multiple-meaning word (“record”) fits the sentence._

**Fern**: Bottom shelf, behind the jam. Don’t eat the jam. Nobody knows what the jam was.  

#### `s6-register`

_Behind the jam: a fat book, soft at the corners. On the cover, in Hazel’s writing: “EGGS.”_  
_Underneath, smaller: “Do not lend this to Byte.”_  
_Halfway through, a new section begins, under a heading she has underlined twice: “Given away.”_  
_Forty years of eggs, in pencil, with the weather. You can’t help reading the others on the way._  
**Gran Hazel**: “Egg 7. Given to Sparks, aged six. First sound: a bang. Not from the egg. From Sparks.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “Egg 23. Given to Byte, who asked for a receipt. Gave him one. First sound: a hiccup. He wrote that down too.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “Egg 41. Given to Ember, aged fifteen, very serious. Promised to feed it before herself. Meant it.”  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): find the difference between two numbers by counting on  
> _Byte’s egg was number 23. Ember’s egg was number 41._  
> _How many more eggs had Hazel given away by Ember’s egg than by Byte’s?_  
> - ✅ 18 → Yes! 41 − 23 = 18. Count on from 23: 7 more makes 30, then 11 more makes 41. 7 + 11 = 18.
> - 28 → Close, but let’s check. From 23, count on 7 to reach 30, then 11 more to reach 41. 7 + 11 = 18.
> - 64 → 64 is 41 + 23, so that’s adding them. We want the difference: 41 − 23 = 18.
> _For grown-ups: Found the difference between two numbers by counting on (41 − 23 = 18)._

**Gran Hazel**: “First sound: three notes. Low, high, and a little one at the end, like a question.”  
_Hazel has drawn the notes as three dots: one low, one high, and a tiny one trailing upwards._  

> **Lesson** (music, notice): written music shows high and low notes  
> _Hazel’s dots work just like written music._  
> _In written music, notes are drawn as dots. A dot higher up means a higher sound. A dot lower down means a lower one._  
> _So you can see a tune’s shape before you hear it: low, high, and a little step up._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that written music shows high and low notes by how high the dots sit._


#### `s6-practise`

_Ember reads the page twice. Then she shuts the book on her own thumb, on purpose._  
**Ember**: And if I do it and she doesn’t turn round?  
**Ember**: Right now she’s lost. If I call her real name and she still doesn’t turn, she’s gone. I’d rather have lost.  
_She follows you to the pond anyway, the register under her arm, scowling at the water._  
**Ember**: I can’t sing. Don’t ask me to sing. I can whistle.  
**Ember**: You first. I’m not doing it till I know it doesn’t sound stupid.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, do): feel your own voice vibrate  
> _Before you whistle, warm up like a singer. Hum a long “mmmm” and rest your fingers on the front of your throat._  
> _Can you feel the buzz? That’s your voice box vibrating. Now hum a high note, then a low one._  
> Check: `edu:hum:throat-buzz`
> _For grown-ups: Felt their own throat vibrate while humming, to learn that sound comes from vibration._

_Your Nubbins gather on the bank to watch. It is the most interesting thing to happen all week._  
**Ember**: Low, high, little one. Like a question. If a duck answers, we’re stopping.  

> **Lesson** (music, notice): pitch: high and low notes  
> **Ember**: Low, high. That’s pitch. How high or low a sound is.  
> _Fast vibrations make high notes. Slow vibrations make low notes. A good whistle can slide from one to the other._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word pitch, and that faster vibrations make higher notes._

_There are no ducks on the pond. Ember checks anyway._  

**Choices**

- **Whistle: high, low, a little one.**
    - One of your Nubbins sneezes. Ember laughs once, before she can stop it.
    - **Ember**: That was a duck. The shape’s upside down. Again.
- **Whistle: low, a little one, high.**
    - The last note goes up and keeps going, like a kettle.
    - **Ember**: That’s not a question. That’s a complaint. Again.
- **Whistle: low, high, and a little one at the end.**
    - Low, high, and a small one tipped up at the end, like a question.
    - Every Nubbin on the bank turns its head at once. Your first one trots over to see who called.
    - **Ember**: …Oh.
    - **Ember**: Again. Slower. I want to hear it.

#### `s6-ember-tries`

_Ember puts two fingers in her mouth and whistles the three notes, quietly, to nobody._  
_Your Nubbins don’t come to her. They don’t know her yet._  
_From the far side of the pond, a duck nobody has ever seen before answers, loudly._  
**Ember**: No.  
_Ember glares at the duck until it leaves. It takes a while. It is a very confident duck._  
_It doesn’t matter. She heard herself do it._  
**Ember**: Tonight. Before I can think about it. You’re coming, and you’re not saying anything.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): what helps when you’re scared to try (think question)  
> _Ember was scared to try, in case it didn’t work. Now she’s going tonight, before she can talk herself out of it._  
> _What helps you when you’re scared to try something?_  
> - Doing it quickly, before I can worry. → That’s my way. Jump before you think. It works more often than it should. That’s a fair answer. For lots of people, the waiting is the scariest part.
> - Practising first, somewhere safe. → That’s a good answer. Ember practised by the pond first, to nobody, and it helped her a lot.
> - Having a friend with me. → That’s a good answer too. It’s why Ember wants you there tonight, even if she’d never say so.
> - Telling myself it’s all right if it doesn’t work. → That’s a wise answer. Trying is brave, even when it doesn’t go right the first time.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about ways to face a scary first try (a think question with no wrong answer)._


#### `s6-whistle`

_Ember’s kitchen after dark, with one lamp lit. Ash is in the corner, facing the wall._  
_Ember kneels a little way off, not too close. She has thought hard about the distance._  
**Ember**: If this doesn’t work, you walk me to the pond and we don’t talk. Agreed?  
**You**: Agreed.  
_She puts two fingers to her mouth. For a moment nothing comes out at all._  
_Then three notes. Low, high, and a small one at the end, like a question._  
_Ash’s ear moves. One ear, a very little._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): animals turn their ears to catch sounds  
> _Many animals, like cats, dogs and horses, can turn their ears towards a sound._  
> _It helps them hear it better and work out where it’s coming from. Ash is listening._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many animals move their ears to catch a sound and find where it comes from._

_Ember whistles it again, slower. Her hands are shaking, so it wobbles. But it’s still the right shape._  
_Ash turns round._  

> **Lesson** (music, notice): a tune is a pattern of notes  
> _Ember’s whistle was slower and wobblier than yours, and Ash still knew it._  
> _A tune is a pattern of high and low notes. Play it slow, fast or shaky, and the pattern stays the same._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a tune is a pattern of notes that stays recognisable at different speeds._

**Ash**: …pip. wirr. a?  
_She crosses the kitchen one careful step at a time and puts her grey head against Ember’s knee._  
**Ember**: Hello, you. It’s me. It was always me.  

**Choices**

- **Stay by the door, very quietly.**
    - You stay. Ember cries without making any noise at all. You suspect she has practised.
    - Ash lets her.
- **Let yourself out. This part is theirs.**
    - You lift the latch slowly so it doesn’t click.
    - Behind you, Ember whistles the three notes again, and again. Every time, Ash answers.

#### `s6-complete`

_Next morning Ember is at your gate. She lifts and pushes without thinking. She’s known the trick since she was fifteen._  
_Ash walks so close to Ember’s boots that Ember has to walk carefully. She is still grey._  
**Ember**: Clover says the grey stays. Clover says you can only make it lighter.  
**Ember**: She ate breakfast with me in the room. That’s lighter.  
**Ember**: She answers to both now. The whistle’s hers. Ash is the one I gave her. She can keep both.  
**Ember**: This was her first ribbon. I kept it in a drawer for years, like a soppy old thing. Give it to one of yours.  
**Ember**: And this. Two fingers, like that. Now blow. No. Less spit.  
_It takes four tries. On the fifth, your whistle carries across the Grove, and three of your Nubbins come running._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): mistakes are part of learning  
> _Four tries that didn’t work, and one that did. That’s how almost everyone learns to whistle._  
> _Getting it wrong while you practise isn’t failing. It’s part of learning._  
> _For grown-ups: Saw that practice and mistakes are a normal part of learning a new skill._

**Ember**: Don’t tell anyone I like you. I’ve got a reputation.  

> **Lesson** (music, do): sing a three-note pattern  
> _Your turn, for real. Whistle or hum Ash’s three notes: low, high, and a little one going up._  
> Check: `edu:hum:tune:low-high-question`
> _For grown-ups: Sang or whistled a three-note pattern from a description of its shape._


### Glossary

- **deny**: To say that something isn’t true, or that you didn’t do it.
- **vibration**: A very fast shaking, back and forth. Vibrations make sound.
- **delightful**: Very pleasant and lovely to be around.
- **receipt**: A slip of paper that shows you have been given, or paid for, something.
- **scowling**: Frowning in a cross or grumpy way.
- **pitch**: How high or low a sound is.
- **confident**: Sure of yourself, and not at all shy.
- **reputation**: What other people think someone is like.

## S7. Unverified

- `s7-s1`: Find Byte after Moss’s talk and hear what he’s writing. · _Byte stayed behind on the low wall by the long grass, with his notebook._
- `s7-s2`: See the timer Pixel has built for Null. · _Pixel’s workbench is behind the lantern shed. Follow the ticking._
- `s7-s3`: After a week of bells, go and see how Null is doing. · _Visit Byte’s house when the journal says a week has passed. A week is seven days._
- `s7-s4`: Spend an evening with Byte and Null with the timer off. Pet Null when it comes to you, and don’t count. · _Sit still near Byte and wait. Only pet Null once it comes close on its own._

#### `s7-unverified`

_After Moss’s talk, the Keepers drift home in twos and threes. Byte stays on the wall, writing very small and very fast._  
_Beside him sits a pale blue Nubbin with a flat, tidy ball above its head. It is watching the notebook._  
**Byte**: This is Null. Grown-up. Four years and some weeks. I know the weeks. Pixel says saying the weeks is unsettling.  
**Byte**: Moss says a Nubbin loved enough becomes an Eternal. “Enough.” That isn’t a unit.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): what a unit of measurement is  
> **Byte**: A unit is a fixed amount you measure with. Metres. Kilograms. Minutes.  
> **Byte**: Which of these is a real unit?  
> - ✅ A minute → Correct. A minute is always sixty seconds, everywhere, for everyone. That’s what makes it a unit.
> - Enough → That’s Moss’s word, and it’s my whole complaint. My “enough” and yours might be different. A minute is always sixty seconds.
> - A bit → A bit of what? A bit is a different size every time. A real unit, like a minute, is always the same.
> _For grown-ups: Learned what a unit of measurement is (a minute is always 60 seconds; “enough” is not a unit)._

_He shows you the page. Under everything Moss said tonight, in neat capitals: UNVERIFIED._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): use the prefix un- to work out a word  
> _UN-VERIFIED. “Un” at the start of a word means “not”. To verify something means to check that it’s true._  
> _So what does Byte mean when he writes UNVERIFIED?_  
> - ✅ Not checked or proved yet. → Exactly. I’m not saying Moss is wrong. I’m saying nobody’s checked.
> - Definitely wrong. → No, that would be “false”. Unverified just means not checked yet. It might be true.
> - Very important. → Not quite. “Un” means “not”, so unverified means not checked yet. Like “unopened” means not opened.
> _For grown-ups: Used the prefix un- to work out the meaning of “unverified”._

**Byte**: When Fossil faded, everybody just sat with her. Sitting isn’t a method.  
_Fossil was Dusty’s old Nubbin. “Fade” is the Grove’s word for die. Fossil died this summer, on the hill._  
**Byte**: Enough is an amount. Amounts can be put on a schedule. Pixel’s timer runs four lanterns to the second.  
**Byte**: Before you say it: no stone. I’m not Cinder. I’m using a clock. Completely different.  
**Moss**: Your shoelace is untied.  
_Byte looks down. It is. It always is._  
_He goes very quiet._  
**Moss**: Things on a timer learn to wait for the bell, Byte. Safe is not the same as well.  
_Byte writes it down carefully. Then, next to it: UNVERIFIED._  

**Choices**

- **I’ll help. What do you need?**
    - **Byte**: Fruit, a bed and a witness. You can be the witness. Witnesses don’t touch anything.
- **Moss is usually right, Byte.**
    - **Byte**: “Usually” is a percentage. I’d like to know which percentage.
    - On the wall, Moss appears to be asleep. He is very bad at appearing to be asleep.
- **Pet Null.**
    - Null leans into your hand, surprised, and then leans harder.
    - **Byte**: Don’t, you’ll spoil the… fine. Fine. Once.

#### `s7-minder`

_Pixel’s workbench: a clock face, three little brass bells, a feeding chute and a very small bed._  
**Pixel**: Hi. So. It’s my lantern timer, basically. Four lanterns or one Nubbin, same maths, Byte says.  
**Pixel**: Bell one, fruit drops. Bell two, bed warms. Bell three, ninety seconds of petting. Byte does the petting.  
**Byte**: Ninety-one seconds was too many. I tested it.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): change seconds into minutes and seconds  
> **Pixel**: Ninety seconds of petting. There are sixty seconds in a minute.  
> **Pixel**: So how long is ninety seconds?  
> - ✅ 1 minute and 30 seconds → Correct. Sixty seconds make one minute, and thirty are left over.
> - 9 minutes → That would be a very long pet! Nine minutes is 540 seconds. Ninety seconds is 60 + 30: one minute and thirty seconds.
> - An hour and a half → Ha, Null would love that. But hours are much bigger. Ninety seconds is 60 + 30: one minute and thirty seconds.
> _For grown-ups: Changed 90 seconds into 1 minute and 30 seconds, using 60 seconds = 1 minute._

**Pixel**: He wanted to call it the Accelerator. I wanted the Nap Box. We settled on the Minder, which neither of us likes.  
_The clock ticks. The chute fires a plum across the shed and hits Byte right on his clipboard._  
**Pixel**: That was calibration.  
**Byte**: That was a plum.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): a push is a force that starts and stops motion  
> **Pixel**: Pushes and pulls are called forces. The chute gave that plum a big push, so it flew.  
> **Pixel**: Then Byte’s clipboard pushed back and stopped it. Too much push. I’ll turn the spring down.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a push is a force that can start something moving, and another push can stop it._

_On the next tick, a piece of fruit drops neatly into the bowl, exactly on the beat._  
**Pixel**: I built the clock. Clocks don’t care what they count down to. I’m trying to care for it.  
**Byte**: Null eats on the bell, sleeps on the bell, is loved on the bell. If enough is an amount, this is enough.  

**Choices**

- **What if Null’s hungry before the bell?**
    - **Byte**: Null won’t be. The bell’s been set just right.
    - **Pixel**: …I asked him that too. It sounded better when he said it to me.
- **Does it have an off switch?**
    - **Pixel**: Lever. Left side. I always put a lever on.
    - **Pixel**: Nobody ever asks about the lever. Thank you for asking about the lever.

#### `s7-first-bell`

_Byte sets Null in the little bed. The first bell rings._  
_Null looks at Byte, then at the bell, then eats._  
**Byte**: Day one. Logging begins. Three bells a day. I’ll write down every single one.  
**Pixel**: Every one? For a whole week?  
**Byte**: Come back in a week. Seven days. Not six. Not eight.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiply equal groups  
> **Pixel**: Three bells a day, for seven days. How many bells is that?  
> - ✅ 21 → Twenty-one. Seven groups of three. I’ll rule a column for each.
> - 10 → That’s 3 + 7, adding. But it’s three bells every day, seven times over: 3 × 7 = 21.
> - 37 → Hmm, that’s the 3 and the 7 side by side. Seven days of three bells is 3 × 7 = 21.
> _For grown-ups: Multiplied equal groups (3 bells a day for 7 days = 21) to solve a word problem._

**Pixel**: It’s going to be fine. It’s a clock. Clocks are fine.  

#### `s7-week`

_A week later, Byte’s front room is all clipboards. Null sits in the little bed, perfectly upright, waiting._  
**Byte**: Best week of data I’ve ever had. Run, Swim, Power, all up. It’s never eaten so tidily.  
**Pixel**: Watch this.  
_Pixel rolls a ball across the floor, the way you would for any Nubbin. Null watches it go by and doesn’t move._  
_The bell rings, and Null eats. It doesn’t look at the fruit, only at the bell._  
_Its blue has gone thin at the edges, like a shirt washed too often. Not grey. Paler._  
**Byte**: It used to chase that ball into the stove. Why doesn’t it play?  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): why young animals play  
> **Pixel**: Young animals play all the time. Kittens pounce. Puppies chase. Lambs bounce about.  
> **Pixel**: Play is how they practise running, catching and getting along. Animal carers watch for it. It’s a sign an animal feels safe.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that young animals play to practise skills, and that play is a sign an animal feels safe._

**Pixel**: Byte. I think it’s waiting to be told.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.MD.D.10, ask): read a bar graph and compare two bars  
> _Pixel has been keeping a chart too. It shows how many times Null played each day._  
> _Day 1: ■■■■■ (5). Day 2: ■■■ (3). Day 3: ■ (1). Days 4 to 7: nothing at all._  
> _How many fewer times did Null play on Day 3 than on Day 1?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes. 5 take away 1 is 4. And after Day 3, the bars stop altogether.
> - 6 → That’s 5 + 1. We want the difference: 5 − 1 = 4 fewer times.
> - 1 → One is how many times it played on Day 3. The difference from Day 1 is 5 − 1 = 4.
> _For grown-ups: Read a bar graph and found the difference between two bars (5 − 1 = 4)._

_Byte turns his notebook back a week. There is Moss’s line, in his own neat capitals, and beside it: UNVERIFIED._  
**Byte**: He told me. In plain words. And I wrote “unverified” next to it.  
_He crosses it out and writes VERIFIED. Then he crosses that out too._  
_It isn’t something he wanted to be right about._  

**Choices**

- **Pull the lever.**
    - Pixel pulls it before you’ve finished saying it. The ticking stops, and the quiet is enormous.
    - **Pixel**: I always put a lever on.
- **Sit down beside Null, Byte. And wait.**
    - **Byte**: For how long?
    - **You**: Until it isn’t waiting for the bell.
    - **Byte**: That isn’t a unit of time.
    - But he reaches over and pulls the lever himself.

#### `s7-same-graph`

**Byte**: I wasn’t trying to own it. I was trying to keep it. Turns out those make the same graph.  
_Null sits in the bed, waiting for a bell that isn’t coming. For the first time, it looks a little lost._  
**Pixel**: A clock does the same thing every time. That’s what I love about clocks.  
**Pixel**: Null isn’t a clock. I don’t think I knew that was the problem until now.  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): how living things differ from machines (think question)  
> **Pixel**: Here’s what I keep wondering. A clock and a Nubbin both tick along, every day.  
> **Pixel**: What makes Null different from a machine?  
> - Null has feelings. A clock doesn’t. → That’s a good answer. A clock can’t be lonely, or happy, or bored. Null can.
> - Null grows and changes. Clocks stay the same. → That’s fair. Null hatched, grew up, and will change again. My clock just gets dusty.
> - Null wants things, like playing and friends. → That’s a fair answer, and I think it’s Moss’s answer too. A clock only does what it’s set to do. Null wants things of its own.
> - Maybe they’re not that different. → That’s an honest answer. Bodies do work a bit like machines: hearts pump, legs push. But a machine can’t want to chase a moth. I think that bit matters most.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how living things differ from machines (a think question with no wrong answer)._

**Byte**: Moss didn’t have a schedule or a single number. He was right anyway. I’ll have to think about that.  
**Pixel**: Tomorrow evening. No clock. We’ll all just sit there. We’re very good at sitting there.  

#### `s7-no-clock`

_Evening in Byte’s garden, and no bells. The Minder sits under a cloth on the step, with its lever down._  
_Byte has brought his stopwatch. He holds it the way some people hold a habit they’ve given up._  
**Byte**: I’m not timing. I’m just holding it. In case.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): changing a habit happens in small steps  
> _A habit is something you do so often you hardly notice. Byte has timed everything for years._  
> _Stopping a habit is hard. Holding the stopwatch without pressing it is his first small step._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that changing a habit is hard and usually happens in small steps._

**You**: In case of what?  
**Byte**: Unverified.  
_For a long time, nothing. Null sits in the grass, looking at the place where the bell used to be._  
_Then a moth goes past, and Null’s head turns. It watches the moth all the way to the hedge._  
**Byte**: Did you see that? That isn’t on any schedule.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): nocturnal animals  
> **Byte**: Fact: most moths fly at night. Animals that are busy at night are called nocturnal.  
> **Byte**: Bats, hedgehogs, most owls and most moths are nocturnal. That one is right on time.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word nocturnal and some animals that are active at night._

_Null takes one step after the moth, then looks back at you, as if checking that’s allowed._  

**Choices**

- **Nod. “Go on.”**
    - Null goes. It doesn’t catch the moth, but it falls into the hedge and comes out with a leaf on its head.
    - **Null**: …prrp!
- **Put the stopwatch down, Byte.**
    - Byte looks at it for a long moment. Then he lays it face down in the grass.
    - **Byte**: It’s still running. I just can’t see it. That’s a start.

#### `s7-lap`

_Near dark, at quarter past seven, Null comes back. It climbs into Byte’s lap without being asked, and falls asleep at once._  
_Byte doesn’t move for an hour._  
_You know it’s an hour because he doesn’t check. You check, a little._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): find a time one hour later  
> _Null fell asleep at quarter past seven. Byte didn’t move for one hour._  
> _What time was it when he finally moved?_  
> - ✅ Quarter past eight → Yes. One hour later, the hour hand moves on by one. 7:15 becomes 8:15.
> - Eight o’clock → Close! But we started at quarter past. One hour after 7:15 is 8:15, quarter past eight.
> - Half past seven → That’s only fifteen minutes later. One whole hour after 7:15 is 8:15.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a time one hour later (7:15 to 8:15)._

**Byte**: Its edges are bluer. Don’t tell me if I’m imagining it.  
**Pixel**: You’re not imagining it. I didn’t write it down. I just looked.  
**Byte**: Looking. Huh. Unverified. But I’ll allow it.  

#### `s7-complete`

_A few evenings later, Pixel knocks on your door and says nothing, which is how you know._  
_Null has curled up under Byte’s hedge, and the air around it has begun to glow._  
_When a Nubbin’s life comes to an end, it makes a cocoon. Some fade, which means they die. Some are reborn as a new egg._  
**Byte**: End-of-life check. Four years, eleven weeks, two days. I said I wouldn’t say the days.  
_Byte sits by the cocoon with his hand on it, and doesn’t count. You can see how hard that is._  
_The cocoon doesn’t thin. It glows warm and gold, and opens on an egg: small, blue, humming._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, do): put a moth’s life cycle in order  
> **Pixel**: It’s a life cycle. Egg, young, grown-up, cocoon, egg again. Round and round.  
> **Pixel**: Moths have a life cycle too. Here are its stages, all muddled: moth, egg, pupa, caterpillar.  
> **Pixel**: Can you put them in order, starting with the egg?  
> Check: `edu:order:moth-life-cycle`
> _For grown-ups: Put the stages of a moth’s life cycle in order (egg, caterpillar, pupa, adult moth)._

**Byte**: Not Eternal. Reborn. It gets to start again, with someone who remembers it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): two feelings at once  
> _Byte looks sad and happy at the same time._  
> _That happens. Sad to say goodbye to grown-up Null, glad it gets to start again. Two big feelings can both be true._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that it’s normal to feel two strong feelings, like sad and glad, at the same time._

**Byte**: Here. My stopwatch. Keep it, please. I’ll only look at it.  
**Pixel**: And the timer, with the bells off. It only counts lanterns now.  
_On your way home you notice Byte’s shoelace is tied. Nobody had to tell him. It won’t last._  

### Glossary

- **unit**: A fixed amount used to measure things, like a metre or a minute.
- **unverified**: Not yet checked or proved to be true.
- **calibration**: Adjusting a machine so it works or measures exactly right.
- **logging**: Writing down what happens, again and again, to keep a record.
- **data**: Facts and numbers collected so you can study them.
- **schedule**: A plan that says when things will happen.
- **habit**: Something you do so often that you do it without thinking.
- **nocturnal**: Awake and busy at night, and asleep in the day.
- **cocoon**: A soft case some creatures make around themselves while they change.
- **reborn**: Born again, to start a new life.

## S8. The Warren in the Hollow

- `s8-s1`: Follow Nova and the fireflies past Hazel’s camp. · _Walk while the fireflies drift. Stand still when they settle. They lead on past the flat stone._
- `s8-s2`: Leave fruit at the edge of the ring, a little at a time, until the Old Girl lets you in. · _Bring twelve pieces of fruit over three evenings: four each time. Set them down at the roots and step back._
- `s8-s3`: Bring Fern to the ring of roots in the Hollow. · _Fern is at her gate next door. Walk her past the falls to the Hollow. She’ll keep up, mostly._
- `s8-s4`: Sit at the edge of the ring with Fern, and let the Old Girl come to her. · _Sit down by the roots with Fern and wait. Don’t reach in._

#### `s8-further`

_You are still by the flat stone with Hazel’s notebook when Nova steps out of the trees. She doesn’t say hello._  
**Nova**: That’s the camp. It isn’t the whole of it.  
**Nova**: “Fed nineteen today,” she wrote. Did you count her bowls? Twelve.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): subtract within 20 to find what’s missing  
> **Nova**: Nineteen Nubbins fed. Twelve bowls at the camp.  
> **Nova**: How many Nubbins didn’t have a bowl here?  
> - ✅ 7 → Seven. 19 − 12 = 7. Seven mouths being fed somewhere else.
> - 31 → That’s 19 + 12. We want how many are left over: 19 − 12 = 7.
> - 9 → Count on from 12: 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19. That’s seven, not nine.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted within 20 to find a missing amount (19 − 12 = 7)._

**Nova**: Twelve bowls, nineteen mouths. She wasn’t feeding them all here. She was carrying food further in.  
_A firefly lands on the notebook, sits a moment, and lifts off into the dark beyond the camp. Then another._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): fireflies make their own light  
> **Nova**: Fireflies aren’t really flies. They’re beetles that make their own light, in their tails.  
> **Nova**: They flash to find each other in the dark. Hardly any heat. Just glow.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fireflies are beetles that make their own light to signal to each other._

**Nova**: They go the same way every night. I followed them once, years ago. I look in whenever I’m passing.  
**Nova**: I’ve never brought anyone. Bring fruit. Walk slowly. Slower than that.  

**Choices**

- **Lead on.**
    - **Nova**: I don’t lead. I follow fireflies. You can follow me following them.
- **Should my Nubbin wait here?**
    - **Nova**: No. They need to see you came with one that trusts you. It’s the only introduction that works.

#### `s8-ring`

_The fireflies stop above a ring of old roots, knotted out of the ground like a fence nobody built._  
_Inside sit dozens of grey Nubbins. Not in rows: in a ring, facing in. Some of them are touching._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): animals huddle in groups to survive the cold  
> **Nova**: Lots of animals huddle together to stay warm.  
> **Nova**: Emperor penguins stand in huge huddles all winter. They take turns on the cold outside edge, then shuffle back into the warm middle.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that some animals, like emperor penguins, huddle in groups to survive the cold._

_A stream runs close by, and the roots make a roof against the wind._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS3-1, ask): what a habitat gives the animals that live there  
> **Nova**: Hazel used to say a good home needs a few things. Look around the ring.  
> **Nova**: What does this place give the warren?  
> - ✅ Water, shelter, and each other. → Yes. The stream for water, the roots against the wind, and a ring of friends. And Hazel brought the food.
> - Nothing much. It’s just roots. → Look again. The stream gives water, the roots keep off the wind, and they have each other. That’s a lot.
> - Toys and beds. → Ha. No toys. But the roots are a kind of shelter, the stream gives water, and they keep each other warm.
> _For grown-ups: Named what a habitat provides: water, shelter, company (and food)._

_In the middle sits an old grey Nubbin whose left ear folds over at the tip. A scrap of faded ribbon is tied round it._  
**Nova**: They aren’t lost. They know exactly where they are. It’s everyone else they’ve lost track of.  
**Nova**: That one’s in charge. I call her the Old Girl. She’s never told me what she calls herself.  
**Nova**: This is their warren. It’s been their home for longer than I’ve known it.  

#### `s8-edge`

_You take one step towards the roots. Every grey head in the ring turns at once, and you stop._  
**Nova**: Nobody crosses. Not me. You don’t walk into someone’s house just because the door is made of roots.  
**You**: Then how did Hazel feed them?  
**Nova**: She left it at the edge and stepped back. Then she came again the next night. Patient. That’s the whole trick.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): respect an animal’s space and let it choose  
> **Nova**: So. How do you show a shy animal that you’re friendly?  
> - ✅ Leave food, step back, and come again tomorrow. → That’s it. Let them choose to come to you. The choosing is what makes it trust.
> - Walk in and pick one up. → They’d run, or bite. Grabbing teaches them hands are scary. Leave food, step back, and let them choose.
> - Shout hello so they know you’re there. → Loud noises frighten shy animals. Quiet, slow and patient works better. Let them choose to come to you.
> _For grown-ups: Learned to respect an animal’s space and let it choose to come closer._

_The Old Girl watches you. Her dark ball hangs very still above her head._  
_Close at her side sits a grey Nubbin thinner than all the rest. Its ear folds over at the tip, just like hers._  
**Nova**: Her youngest, I think. Doesn’t eat much. The others leave it the soft fruit.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): animals in groups look after each other  
> **Nova**: Groups look after their young. In a wolf pack, the grown-ups carry food back for the pups.  
> **Nova**: Here, the strong ones leave the soft fruit for the thin one.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that animals in groups help each other survive, like wolves bringing food to their pups._


**Choices**

- **Leave the softest fruit nearest the thin one.**
    - **Nova**: …That’s what Hazel did. Exactly that.
- **Put the fruit down, and sit a little way off.**
    - You sit. After a long time, a grey Nubbin creeps out, takes one piece, and carries it to the middle.
    - **Nova**: Good. Now do that for three nights.

#### `s8-gap`

_You come back three evenings running, with twelve pieces of fruit to share out between them._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, do): share into equal groups  
> _Twelve pieces of fruit, shared fairly over three evenings._  
> _Sort them into three equal piles at the roots. How many go in each pile?_  
> Check: `edu:share:fruit:12-into-3`
> _For grown-ups: Shared 12 into 3 equal groups (12 ÷ 3 = 4)._

_On the third evening the Old Girl gets up, slowly, and steps aside. There is a gap in the ring, one Keeper wide._  
**Nova**: Whenever I pass through the valley, I come and sit by these roots. She has never once done that for me.  
_Up close, her ribbon was brown once, with a leaf stitched on it. Five points, one curled stem._  
_You have seen that leaf before. It’s on Fern’s gloves, Fern’s gate, and Fern’s tea cosy._  
**Nova**: Hazel’s notebook. “The brown one let me touch her ear.” She isn’t brown. Her ribbon was.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): put clues together to make an inference  
> _Nova is putting clues together, like a detective._  
> _The leaf on the ribbon is Fern’s leaf. Who do you think the Old Girl might be?_  
> - ✅ A Nubbin Fern lost, long ago. → That’s what I think too. Fern sews that leaf on everything she loves.
> - Fern’s tea cosy. → Ha. No, she’s definitely a Nubbin. But the leaf is Fern’s. Fern must have tied it on, long ago.
> - Nobody special. → Maybe. But nobody sews a leaf on a ribbon for nobody. I think Fern lost her once.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in the story to make an inference about a character._


#### `s8-fern-gate`

_Fern is leaning on her gate, stitching a leaf onto a glove that already has three._  
**Fern**: You’re staring at my glove. It’s a leaf. I put them on everything.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, ask): find a line of symmetry  
> _Look at Fern’s leaf: five points, with a vein down the middle. Forget the curly stem for a moment._  
> _If you folded the leaf along that middle vein, would the two halves match?_  
> - ✅ Yes, they’d match. → Yes. The middle vein is a line of symmetry: each half is a mirror of the other. Lots of leaves are nearly symmetrical.
> - No, they’d be different. → Look again: two points on each side, and one at the top. Fold down the middle and they match. That fold is a line of symmetry.
> _For grown-ups: Found a line of symmetry in a leaf shape._

**Fern**: I put one on a ribbon once. Long time ago.  
_She pulls the thread tight, and keeps pulling after it’s tight._  
**Fern**: Six years ago. The Midsummer race. She went over the rail on the cliff bend. I stood at the bottom till dark.  
**Fern**: Everyone said she couldn’t have lived. Everyone was very kind about it. I hated it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): how to help a grieving friend  
> _People were kind to Fern, but their words didn’t help. When someone is very sad, words can’t always fix it._  
> _What often helps more is listening, and staying close._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that listening and staying close can help a grieving friend more than words._


**Choices**

- **Fern. I think I’ve found her.**
    - **Fern**: Don’t.
    - **Fern**: Don’t say that unless…
    - **You**: Bring fruit. Soft fruit.
    - She is through her own gate before you’ve finished, still holding the needle.
- **Will you help me carry fruit to the Hollow tonight?**
    - **Fern**: The Hollow? At night? With you?
    - **Fern**: …Fine. Someone has to carry things badly.
    - She doesn’t ask why. You don’t tell her. Not yet.

#### `s8-arrive`

_The fireflies drift ahead of you both, low over the path, like sparks from a slow fire._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): spot a simile  
> _“Like sparks from a slow fire.” When a writer says one thing is like another, that’s called a simile._  
> _What are the fireflies being compared to?_  
> - ✅ Sparks from a fire → Yes. Small, glowing and drifting. A simile uses “like” or “as” to paint a picture.
> - The path → The path is where they fly. The simile compares the fireflies to sparks: small, bright and drifting.
> - Fern → Ha. Fern is more like a tree-bumping machine. The fireflies are compared to sparks from a fire.
> _For grown-ups: Spotted a simile and said what it compares._

**Fern**: Is it always this dark? How did Hazel do this every night? She couldn’t see her own feet.  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, notice): we need light to see; eyes adjust to the dark  
> _We see things when light bounces off them into our eyes. In the dark, there’s very little light._  
> _But eyes slowly get used to it. After about half an hour in the dark, you can see far more than at first._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that we need light to see, and that our eyes slowly adjust to the dark._

_Fern walks into a tree, says sorry to it, and walks into the same tree again._  
**Fern**: I’m carrying the soft fruit. I insisted. I have sat on two of them.  
**Fern**: They’re still soft. Softer, if anything. That has to count.  
_At the stream she takes her boots off, wades across, and puts them back on the wrong feet. She doesn’t notice for a mile._  
_Then the path dips, the fireflies settle low, and for the first time all night, Fern stops talking._  

#### `s8-reunion`

_Fern stops at the roots, and every grey head turns._  
_She doesn’t notice them. She’s looking at the middle._  
_The Old Girl is already standing. Her folded ear is up. The scrap of brown ribbon hangs from it, leaf and all._  
**Fern**: Oh.  
**Fern**: Bramble? …Oh, you’ve gone grey. That’s all right, love. So have I.  
_For a long moment, nobody in the ring moves._  
_Then Bramble walks out through the gap, one careful step at a time, all the way to Fern’s boots._  
**Bramble**: …  
**Fern**: I stood at the bottom of that cliff till dark. I thought I’d left you there.  
**Fern**: I’m sorry I stopped looking. I’m so sorry I stopped looking.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): guilt, sorry and being kind to yourself (think question)  
> _Fern is saying sorry for something from six years ago. Everyone told her Bramble couldn’t have lived._  
> _Do you think Fern did something wrong by stopping looking?_  
> - No. She did her best with what she knew. → That’s a kind answer. Fern believed what everyone told her. Being kind to yourself matters too.
> - A bit, but she’s sorry, and that matters. → That’s a fair answer. Saying sorry, even late, is brave. And Bramble doesn’t seem to mind at all.
> - I’m not sure. → That’s an honest answer. Some things don’t have a clear right or wrong. Fern isn’t sure either, and that’s all right.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about guilt, saying sorry and being kind to yourself (a think question with no wrong answer)._

_Bramble sits down on Fern’s boots, both of them at once, and stays put._  
**Fern**: Right. Good. I’m going to cry now. Somebody hold my gloves.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): happy tears  
> _Fern is going to cry, and she’s happy. A reunion can make anyone cry._  
> _Tears can come with any big feeling, happy ones too. It’s all right to let them out._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that people cry with happy feelings too, and that tears are all right._

- **Hand Fern a ribbon from your pocket.**
    - **Fern**: You carry ribbons? Course you do. You’re Hazel’s.
    - Fern stitches a leaf onto it there and then, with shaking hands, and ties it under the old one.
    - **Fern**: She keeps both. She always was greedy.

#### `s8-one-short`

_Later, Bramble walks back to the middle of the ring. She has a job, and she goes back to it._  
**Fern**: She always did like being in charge.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): some animal groups have an experienced leader  
> **Nova**: Lots of animal groups have a leader. In an elephant herd, it’s usually the oldest female.  
> **Nova**: She remembers where to find water in a dry year, and her family follows her. Bramble’s a bit like that.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that some animal groups, like elephant herds, are led by an experienced older female._

_Bramble sits down and looks past you all, up the dark path, the way she looked the first night._  
**Nova**: The thin one. Her youngest. It isn’t at the ring tonight.  
**Fern**: Then we leave the soft fruit at the edge till it is.  
_Fern sets the softest plum down at the roots, and steps back. Patient, like Hazel._

**Gran Hazel**: This one? Found her at the edge of a ring of roots, too tired to stand. So I carried her.  
**Gran Hazel**: Her mother runs the place. Ear folds over at the tip. Opinions. I gather you’ve met.  
**You**: Fern found her. Her name’s Bramble.  
**Gran Hazel**: Did she. Oh, Fern. Did she.

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): think about a theme: looking after things for others  
> _“Nothing’s mine. I only carry things for a bit.”_  
> _What does Hazel mean?_  
> - ✅ We look after things for a while, then pass them on. → That’s it, love. The Grove, the Nubbins, the gate. You keep them for the next ones.
> - She doesn’t like owning things. → Ha. I own a great many teapots. No: I mean we only look after things for a while, then hand them on.
> - Her arms are tired. → They are, a bit. But I mean something bigger: we look after things for a while, then hand them on.

> **Lesson** (science, 1-LS1-2, notice): parents help their young survive  
> _Lots of animal mothers wash their babies, the way a cat licks her kittens clean._  
> _It keeps the baby clean and warm, and tells it: you’re mine, and you’re safe._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that animal parents care for their young, for example by washing them._

_Behind her, three strays stand up and look at you, as if waiting to see where you go next._
