**Sparks**: Pretty, isn’t it? Air resistance did half the work.  

#### `q05-complete`

_The white rabbit hops through the confetti, eating as it goes, and stops at your feet._  
_It looks up at you, then at your Nubbin, and very politely does not knock anyone into a bush._  
**Sir Rollo Brisket**: Extraordinary. I had a whole plan. It involved a lot of shouting.  
**Sir Rollo Brisket**: I suppose it was only ever minding its clover. We were the ones who kept walking up to it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): think question: fierce, or protecting its space?  
> **Sir Rollo Brisket**: Was that rabbit fierce, Keeper? Or were we just in its way?  
> - It was protecting its space. We kept bothering it. → That is a fair answer. I think so too. We walked up to it, one after another, all morning. Real wild animals need their space too. Watch them quietly from a distance, and never chase them.
> - It was a bit fierce, but only when someone came too close. → That’s a careful answer. Fierce, but fair. It never started anything. Lots of wild animals are like that. Give them space, watch quietly, and they leave you alone too.
> - It was hungry, and we got between it and its snack. → Ha! A fair answer. I would bump me into a bush too, if I were eating. Wild animals need to eat in peace. Watching quietly from a distance is the kindest way.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about an animal’s point of view and why we give animals their space._

**Sparks**: I made you a spare Hand Melon. For the mantelpiece. I took the fizz out, so it’s just pretty.  
_The rabbit follows you home. Your Nubbins adore it, and one of them is already trying on its ears._  
_Its name, you decide, is Snowdrop. It agrees by sitting on your foot._  

### Glossary

- **prey**: An animal that other animals hunt for food.
- **invention**: Something new that someone designs and makes to solve a problem.
- **odd**: In maths, an odd number can’t be split into two equal groups, like 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9.
- **air resistance**: The push of air against something moving through it, which slows it down.
- **extraordinary**: Very unusual and surprising.

## Q6. The Wooden Rabbit

- `q06-s1`: Build a giant wooden rabbit at the Workshop. · _The giant rabbit needs a lot of wood and a set of wheels. The fallen logs by the woods are a good start._
- `q06-s2`: Wheel the wooden rabbit to the stranger’s wall. · _Push it from behind and steer round the stream. It does not float._

#### `q06-intro`

_At the far end of the valley stands an old wall with a little tower on top. On the tower stands a stranger._  
_He has a magnificent moustache and an accent from somewhere very far away, or possibly from nowhere at all._  
**Sir Barnabus Parapet**: Hello down there, small Keeper with the small animals! I do not think much of your hat!  
**You**: I’m not wearing a hat.  
**Sir Barnabus Parapet**: And I do not think much of that either!  
_A ripe sun fruit sails over the wall and lands on your head. It goes everywhere._  
**Sir Barnabus Parapet**: Your boots go squelch, and your Nubbin smells of yesterday’s porridge!  
_He disappears behind the wall. You can hear him laughing and then, slightly worryingly, eating._  
_He reappears. He has thought of another taunt, and it has clearly cost him something._  
**Sir Barnabus Parapet**: And your Nubbin looks like a sock that has been told a secret!  
_Your Nubbin looks down at itself, then up at you, stricken. It looks as if it might cry._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): handling teasing and big feelings  
> _A taunt is something said on purpose to tease or upset you. Your Nubbin is upset._  
> _What would help it most right now?_  
> - ✅ Kneel down, tell it the truth kindly, and stay with it. → Yes. You tell it it looks nothing like a sock. It looks exactly like itself, which is better. Taunts say more about the person shouting than the person being shouted at. A friend beside you helps a lot.
> - Tell it to stop being silly. → Its feelings are real, even if the taunt is silly. Feelings shrink faster when someone listens. So you kneel down and tell it the truth: it looks nothing like a sock. It leans on your leg.
> - Shout something even worse at the stranger. → That’s tempting! But shouting back usually makes the shouting go on longer. First, look after your Nubbin. You kneel and tell it the truth: it looks nothing like a sock.
> _For grown-ups: Chose calm ways to handle teasing: comforting a friend, remembering that taunts aren’t true, and not shouting back._


**Choices**

- **Shout something rude back.**
    - **You**: Your… wall is… wonky!
    - **Sir Barnabus Parapet**: It is NOT wonky! It has CHARACTER!
- **Wipe off the fruit with dignity.**
    - You wipe off the fruit with great dignity. A second fruit arrives.

#### `q06-built`

_The wooden rabbit is finished. It is twice as tall as you, with big flat ears and a slightly anxious expression._  
_It is on wheels. It has a little door in its tummy. Nobody can remember why you added the door._  
_Your Nubbin climbs the measuring post beside it, to see how tall it really is._  
**You**: I’m 120 centimetres tall. So the rabbit must be…  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): doubling lengths; centimetres and metres  
> _You are 120 cm tall. The rabbit is twice as tall as you. How tall is the rabbit?_  
> - ✅ 240 cm, which is 2 metres and 40 centimetres. → Yes. Double 120 is 240. And 100 centimetres make a metre, so 240 cm is 2 m 40 cm. Taller than a grown-up. Taller than a door. Just right for a surprise.
> - 122 cm → That adds 2. “Twice as tall” means two lots of your height: 120 + 120. That’s 240 cm, or 2 metres and 40 centimetres, since 100 cm make 1 metre.
> - 60 cm → 60 is half of 120. The rabbit is bigger than you, not smaller! Twice as tall means double: 120 + 120 = 240 cm. That’s 2 m 40 cm.
> _For grown-ups: Doubled 120 cm to get 240 cm, then wrote it as 2 metres 40 centimetres (100 cm = 1 m)._

_Your Nubbin taps the post level with the tips of the ears, and squeaks._  
_The rabbit gazes down at you all, anxiously. It is going to need a lot of pushing._  

#### `q06-plan`

_The wooden rabbit stands outside the Workshop, wheels chocked, ears high._  
**You**: Right. We wheel it to his wall and leave it at the gate.  
_Your Nubbins nod seriously. They have been told it is a plan. They have not been told the plan._  
_Neither, you realise, have you._  
**You**: He’ll take it in, and then… something will happen.  
_You kick the wooden wedges away from the wheels and give it a push. It rolls off easily, squeaking._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): wheels reduce friction  
> _Without wheels, the rabbit would hardly budge. With them, one push gets it rolling._  
> _What do wheels do about friction, the force from surfaces rubbing together?_  
> - ✅ They roll instead of scraping, so there’s much less of it. → Exactly. Friction is the force that slows things when surfaces rub together. Dragging scrapes the whole bottom along the ground. A wheel just rolls, so there’s far less rubbing.
> - Wheels make it lighter. → It weighs just the same on wheels! What changes is the rubbing. Dragging scrapes along the ground: lots of friction. Rolling wheels rub much less, so it’s easier to push.
> - The rabbit wants to go. → It does look keen. But the real reason is friction: the force from surfaces rubbing together. Wheels roll instead of scraping, so there’s much less friction to push against.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that wheels make heavy things easier to move because rolling causes much less friction than scraping._

_That will do. It has wheels. Wheels are a sort of plan in themselves._  

#### `q06-gate`

_You leave the rabbit at the gate and hide behind a bush. The gate creaks. The stranger drags the rabbit inside._  
_Behind the bush, everyone looks at everyone. Slowly, it dawns that the rabbit was the whole plan._  
**You**: …Was somebody meant to be inside it?  
_Your Nubbins look at their feet. One of them looks at a different, unrelated bush._  
_You remember a very old story you once read, about a giant wooden horse._  
_In that story, the clever part was who was hiding inside. You have rather skipped the clever part._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): legends: how old stories carry the past  
> _It’s an ancient Greek legend. An army left a huge wooden horse outside the city of Troy, as if it were a gift._  
> _The people of Troy pulled it inside. That night, soldiers hidden in the horse crept out and opened the gates._  
> _A legend is a very old story that may be partly true. This one has been told for thousands of years._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard the ancient Greek legend of the wooden horse and learned what a legend is._


**Choices**

- **Start laughing.**
    - You laugh. Your Nubbins laugh. Behind the wall, the stranger laughs too, though not for the same reason.
- **Knock and ask for it back.**
    - **Sir Barnabus Parapet**: Ask for what back? I have no rabbit. I am a man alone with his wall.

#### `q06-complete`

_Next morning, the wooden rabbit is back outside your Workshop with a note pinned to one ear._  
_“Too big for the courtyard. Also, I found nobody inside it. Very poor attack. Nine out of ten for the ears.”_  
_Underneath, in smaller writing: “Your hat is still terrible.”_  
**You**: I’m still not wearing a hat.  
_Right at the bottom, very small, half rubbed out: “P.S. Nobody ever comes to the wall. Come again. Bring something to throw.”_  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): think question: a character’s motive  
> _Read the P.S. again._  
> _What do you think is the stranger’s motive: the real reason he shouts at everyone?_  
> - He’s lonely, and shouting is how he gets people to come. → That’s a fair answer, and the P.S. backs it up: “Nobody ever comes to the wall.” Sometimes people who tease are really asking for company, in a very clumsy way.
> - He thinks it’s a game, like throwing a ball. → That’s a fair answer. “Bring something to throw” does sound like he wants to play. Maybe he has never learned a gentler way to say “come and play”.
> - He’s just rude. → He certainly is rude! That’s a fair reading. Characters can be more than one thing, though. Rude, and maybe a little lonely too. Look at that P.S.
> _For grown-ups: Used a clue in the text (the P.S.) to think about why a character behaves the way he does._

_The little door in its tummy swings open. There is just room for you and a Nubbin to squeeze in and peek out._  
_It makes, everyone agrees, an excellent spot for photographs._  

### Glossary

- **taunt**: Something said on purpose to tease or upset someone.
- **stricken**: Suddenly very upset or hurt, and showing it on your face.
- **friction**: The force that slows things down when two surfaces rub together.
- **legend**: A very old story, passed down for a long time, that may be partly true.
- **motive**: The reason why someone does something.

## Q7. The Grand Palace of the Hill

- `q07-s1`: Gather 12 stone for the castle towers. · _Stone turns up in the riverbed and under the cliffs. Tap a sparkling rock to pick it up._
- `q07-s2`: Finish the castle’s two towers with Pixel. · _Place stones on the glowing spots at the top of each tower. Twelve in all: six for each tower._

#### `q07-intro`

_On top of the little hill, Pixel is kneeling beside a castle. It is about knee-high._  
_It has a gate, a drawbridge made from a lolly stick, and two towers that stop halfway up, as if they lost interest._  
**Pixel**: Keeper! Behold! The Grand Palace of the Hill!  
_Pixel turns to the valley, arms wide, and announces it again, louder, to everyone and no one._  
**Pixel**: Gaze upon it, all ye Grove! Marvel at its towers! Well. Marvel at the bottom halves of its towers.  
_Byte comes up the path with a cup of tea, looks at the castle, and does not slow down._  
**Byte**: Pixel, a footstool could beat that castle in a fight.  
**Pixel**: SHH.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): giving kind, honest feedback  
> _Byte’s feedback was true-ish, but it stung. Pixel worked hard on that castle._  
> _What could Byte have said instead?_  
> - ✅ “I like the drawbridge! How tall will the towers be?” → Yes. Notice something good, then ask a question. That’s honest and kind at the same time. Good feedback helps the maker want to keep going.
> - “It’s perfect.” → That’s kind, but is it honest? The towers do stop halfway. Try: notice something good, then ask a helpful question. “Lovely gate! What will the towers look like?”
> - Nothing at all. → Sometimes saying nothing is fine. But Pixel wanted a reaction! Kind, honest feedback works best: one thing you like, and one helpful question.
> _For grown-ups: Practised giving feedback that is honest and kind: notice something good, then ask a helpful question._

**Pixel**: It needs proper stone towers. Real ones. Little ones. Will you help? Byte clearly won’t.  
**Byte**: I am drinking my tea.  

**Choices**

- **Of course. Grand palace it is.**
    - **Pixel**: Thank you. Byte, write that down. Somebody believes.
- **It is quite small.**
    - **Pixel**: It is to SCALE. There is a difference.
    - **Byte**: There is not.

#### `q07-stone`

_You bring Pixel an armful of stone. Pixel weighs each piece in one hand like a jeweller._  
**Pixel**: This one is a tower. This one is a battlement. This one is… a nice stone. Keep that one.  
_A battlement is the bumpy top of a castle wall, with gaps for peeking through._  
_The stones from the riverbed are smooth and round. The ones from under the cliff are sharp and jagged._  
**Pixel**: Same rock, different lives. The river ones have clearly had a much more exciting time.  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-ESS2-1, ask): weathering and erosion: how rivers smooth stones  
> **Pixel**: Why do you think the river stones are so smooth and round, and the cliff stones so jagged?  
> - ✅ The river tumbles them about and wears the corners off. → Yes! Water rolls them along, knocking them together, for years and years. Every knock rubs off a tiny bit. Slowly, the sharp corners wear away, and they end up round.
> - Someone polished them. → Ha! Someone did. The river did. Very slowly. Water tumbles the stones together for years and years, wearing their sharp corners away.
> - They were born round. → Most started jagged, like the cliff ones. The river changed them. Flowing water knocks them together for years. Each knock wears a little more of the corners away.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that river stones are smooth because flowing water tumbles them for a long time and wears off their corners._

_Your Nubbin rolls a round one down the slope and chases after it._  

#### `q07-towers`

**Pixel**: Now. The towers. Hold this, hold that, and whatever happens, do not breathe on the east wing.  
_You build together. Pixel places, you hold, and your Nubbin hands up stones one at a time with great ceremony._  
_Every few minutes Pixel stands back, squints, and moves one stone a hair to the left._  
**Byte**: You moved that one back to where it was.  
**Pixel**: I moved it MORE to where it was.  
**Pixel**: It’s built to scale, you know. Every centimetre of my palace stands for 20 centimetres of a real one.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): scale: multiplying to find real sizes  
> **Pixel**: The palace gate is 10 centimetres tall. Each centimetre stands for 20 real ones. How tall is the real gate?  
> - ✅ 200 cm, which is 2 metres. → Yes! Ten lots of 20 is 200 centimetres. That’s 2 metres. A proper gate. Fine. I admit that is a real gate. In theory.
> - 30 cm → That adds 10 and 20. But scale means every centimetre becomes 20. So it’s ten lots of 20: 200 centimetres, or 2 metres.
> - 10 cm → That’s my model gate! The real one is much bigger. Each of the 10 centimetres stands for 20, so 10 × 20 = 200 centimetres. Two metres!
> _For grown-ups: Used a scale (1 cm stands for 20 cm) to work out a real size: 10 × 20 = 200 cm, or 2 metres._

_The towers rise, stone by stone. They reach your knee. Then a little over your knee._  
_A cloud passes. You lie flat in the grass, eye to eye with the gate. For one moment, the castle looks enormous._  

> **Lesson** (art, notice): perspective: near things look bigger  
> _Why did it look enormous? Things close to your eye look bigger than things far away._  
> _With your eye right by the gate, the castle filled your whole view, like a real one far off._  
> _Artists use this too. Draw near things big and far things small, and a flat picture seems deep. That’s perspective._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that things close to your eye look bigger, and that artists use this to show near and far._

_Then you sit up, and it is a model again. A very good one._  

#### `q07-finished`

_The last stone goes on. Two proud towers, a lolly-stick drawbridge, and a flag made from a sweet wrapper._  
**Pixel**: Grove! The Grand Palace is COMPLETE!  
_The valley echoes back, faintly: “…plete.” Pixel takes this as applause._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): echoes: sound bouncing back  
> _Pixel’s shout travelled out across the valley. When it hit the far hillside, it bounced back._  
> _A sound that bounces back like that is an echo. The further away the hill, the longer the wait._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that an echo is sound bouncing off a far, hard surface, like a hillside, and coming back._

_Far below, a Nubbin by the pond looks up, waves, and goes back to its puddle._  
**Byte**: You know it’s the same on both sides? Tower, gate, tower. Very tidy.  
**Pixel**: Symmetrical, Byte. The word is symmetrical. I did it on purpose.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, do): lines of symmetry  
> **Pixel**: Find my line of symmetry. Draw it so the two halves match exactly, like a mirror.  
> _Straight down the middle, through the gate. Tower on the left, tower on the right: a perfect match._  
> **Byte**: Except the flag. The flag is only on one side.  
> **Pixel**: The flag is a FEATURE.  
> Check: `edu:tap:symmetry-line:castle`
> _For grown-ups: Found the line of symmetry on the castle: the line that splits it into two matching halves._


#### `q07-complete`

_That evening, three Nubbins wander up the hill and stop in front of the castle._  
_One puts a leaf on its head like a crown. One stands on the drawbridge and points dramatically at nothing._  
_The third lies down and plays a dragon, or a cloud. It is hard to say. It commits completely._  
**Pixel**: They’re putting on a play. In my palace. This is the best day of my whole life.  
**Byte**: Still quite small, I’d say…  
_Byte stops, watches the leaf-crowned Nubbin take a very small bow, and sips the tea instead._  
**Byte**: It is a very good model.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): think question: why a character changes  
> _Byte thought the castle was too small. Now he says it’s very good._  
> _What do you think changed his mind?_  
> - Seeing the Nubbins play in it. → That’s a fair answer. When the castle made someone happy, it stopped mattering how big it was.
> - Seeing how happy Pixel was. → That’s a kind answer. Byte might grumble, but he cares about his friend.
> - He always liked it. He just didn’t want to say so. → Ooh, a clever reading. Some characters hide how they feel until the right moment.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what made a character change his mind, using what happened in the scene._


### Glossary

- **feedback**: What someone tells you about your work, to help you understand it or improve it.
- **battlement**: The bumpy top of a castle wall, with gaps to look or shoot through.
- **jagged**: With sharp, rough, uneven points and edges.
- **scale**: How much smaller (or bigger) a model is than the real thing, such as 1 cm for every 20 cm.
- **perspective**: Showing distance in a picture by drawing near things bigger and far things smaller.
- **echo**: A sound you hear again after it bounces back off something far away and hard.
- **symmetrical**: The same on both sides of a middle line, like a reflection in a mirror.

## Q8. The Aqueduct Committee

- `q08-s1`: Build an aqueduct from the falls to your crops. · _Craft aqueduct sections at the Workshop from stone and wood, then lay them from the top of the falls down to the crop beds._
- `q08-s2`: Harvest a crop from the aqueduct beds and take it to the committee. · _Ripe crops glow. Tap to harvest, then Give it to Reggie in the Keepers’ Hall._

#### `q08-intro`

_In the Keepers’ Hall, a meeting is in progress. There are four chairs, three Keepers and a lot of paper._  
_A banner on the wall says GROVE IMPROVEMENT COMMITTEE. Someone has crossed out IMPROVEMENT._  
_A committee is a small group that meets to talk things over and decide. This one mostly grumbles._  
**Reggie Thistlewood**: Order. Order. Item one: all this building the new Keeper keeps doing.  
**Frannie Quill**: Fences everywhere. Paths. Lanterns. Something with a drawbridge, I’m told.  
**Old Mags**: My cousin tripped over a fence post. A brand-new one.  
**Reggie Thistlewood**: Has one single bit of this building done anybody any good? Name one thing!  
_There is a pause. Frannie raises a hand._  
**Frannie Quill**: Reggie. The chair you are sitting on. The Keeper made it last week.  
**Reggie Thistlewood**: That is beside the point, Frannie. The point is the point.  
**Reggie Thistlewood**: Anyway. If you must build, Keeper, build something USEFUL. The crops are parched and my back is gone from carrying buckets.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): Roman aqueducts: life in the past  
> _An aqueduct is a channel that carries water a long way. “Aqua” is the Latin word for water._  
> _About 2,000 years ago, the ancient Romans built huge stone aqueducts to bring water to their towns._  
> _They had no pumps. The channel sloped gently downhill the whole way. Some of them are still standing today._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the ancient Romans built stone aqueducts, about 2,000 years ago, to carry water downhill to their towns._


**Choices**

- **Fine. I’ll build an aqueduct.**
    - **Reggie Thistlewood**: A what?
    - **You**: A sort of bridge, for water.
    - **Reggie Thistlewood**: Pfft. Sounds like more building.
- **Can I see the minutes?**
    - The minutes are the written notes of what a meeting decided.
    - These say, in full: “Met. Grumbled. Biscuits.”

#### `q08-water`

_The last section clicks into place. Water from the falls slides down the channel, glittering._  
_It runs the whole way by itself. Nobody pumps it. Nobody carries a single bucket._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): gravity makes water flow downhill  
> _No pump, no buckets. So what moves the water all the way from the falls to the crops?_  
> - ✅ Gravity. The channel slopes downhill. → Yes. Gravity pulls water down. The falls are higher than the crops, so the channel slopes gently down. As long as every section is a little lower than the one before, the water keeps going.
> - The Nubbins are pushing it. → They are mostly splashing in it! The water moves because of gravity. The falls are higher up, so the channel slopes downhill, and gravity pulls the water along.
> - Water just likes moving. → It does seem keen! But it only goes one way: down. Gravity pulls it. That’s why the channel must slope gently downhill from the falls all the way to the crops.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that an aqueduct needs no pump because gravity pulls water down a gentle slope._

_It spills into the crop beds. The crops have been wilting all week, drooping because they were short of water._  
_Within the hour they do a small, grateful droop-then-perk. Leaves lift. Stems stand up straight._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-LS2-1, notice): why plants wilt, and perk up with water  
> _Plants are made of tiny parts called cells. When there is plenty of water, the cells are full and firm._  
> _Like a balloon full of water, that firmness holds the stems and leaves up._  
> _When water runs short, the cells go floppy and the plant wilts. Water it, and up it comes again._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that plants droop when short of water and stand up again when water fills their cells._

_Your Nubbins jump about in the overflow, shrieking happily._  
**You**: It just… flows. Downhill, all on its own.  

#### `q08-invite`

_A note arrives, folded into a very small square._  
_“Emergency meeting. Re: the aqueduct. Bring something from the crops so we can examine it. Reggie.”_  
_Underneath, in different handwriting: “Bring biscuits too. Frannie.”_  
_A second note arrives a minute later: “Ignore the first note. Mine is the only real committee. Breakaways! Mags.”_  
_A breakaway is a group that splits off from a bigger one. By lunchtime there are three committees._  
_Nobody is sure who is in the third._  
**You**: Examine it for what?  
_Your Nubbin, dripping from the overflow, has no idea either, and does not mind._  
_The crop bed beside the aqueduct is already plump and shining. Little paths divide it into squares, one metre on each side._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.C.7, do): area of a rectangle by multiplying  
> _Count the squares in the bed. There are 4 rows, with 6 squares in each row._  
> _You could count them one by one, or multiply: 4 × 6 = 24._  
> _Each square is one square metre, so the bed’s area is 24 square metres. That’s a lot of crops._  
> Check: `edu:count:bed-squares:24`
> _For grown-ups: Found the area of a crop bed (4 rows of 6 one-metre squares = 24 square metres) by multiplying instead of counting one by one._


#### `q08-delivered`

_Reggie takes the crop, turns it over, sniffs it, and holds it up to the light for a suspiciously long time._  
**Frannie Quill**: Well?  
**Reggie Thistlewood**: Hmm. It’s very good.  
**Reggie Thistlewood**: I hate that it’s very good.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): a character’s feelings and motives  
> _Why would Reggie hate that the crop is good?_  
> - ✅ Because he said the building was useless, and now he has to admit he was wrong. → Exactly. Reggie likes the crop. What he hates is being wrong in front of everyone. Two feelings at once. Characters, like people, often have mixed feelings.
> - He doesn’t like vegetables. → He seems to like this one! Look: “It’s very good.” What he hates is having to admit he was wrong about the building. That’s much harder to swallow.
> - He’s just a grumpy person. → He is grumpy! But there’s a reason here too. He said building was useless. Now the proof is in his hand, and he has to admit he was wrong.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a character’s mixed feelings: Reggie likes the crop but hates admitting he was wrong._

_Frannie writes something in the minutes. Mags passes round the biscuits, looking smug._  
_Reggie takes two biscuits at once, which is how you can tell he is upset._  

#### `q08-complete`

**Reggie Thistlewood**: Item one. The aqueduct. All right. It waters the crops. I grant you the crops. But what ELSE has it done?  
**Frannie Quill**: The Nubbins love the spray. They’ve stopped asking me for baths.  
**Old Mags**: The frogs moved in. I like the frogs.  
**Frannie Quill**: It hums at night. Very soothing.  
**Old Mags**: My cousin can’t trip over it. It’s up in the air.  
**Reggie Thistlewood**: Fine. Crops, baths, frogs, humming, your cousin. Is that ALL?  
**Frannie Quill**: It keeps the path cool in summer.  
**Old Mags**: It’s pretty.  
**Frannie Quill**: And you’ve been filling your teapot from it since Tuesday, Reggie. We’ve all seen you.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.MD.D.10, ask): tally charts  
> _Frannie has been keeping a tally of every good thing anyone said about the aqueduct._  
> _Crops, baths, frogs, humming, cousin, cool path, pretty, teapot. How many tally marks?_  
> - ✅ 8 → Yes: one gate of five, and three more. Five and three make eight. Eight good things, Reggie. I’ve underlined it twice.
> - 5 → That’s one full gate of five. But there are three more after it: cool path, pretty, teapot. Five and three make eight.
> - 7 → So close! Count again, and don’t forget Reggie’s teapot: that was the last one. One gate of five, and three more. Eight.
> _For grown-ups: Kept a tally of the good things the committee listed and counted the total (one group of five and three more: 8)._

**Reggie Thistlewood**: …I propose a motion to thank the Keeper. All in favour.  
_A motion is an idea put to a meeting for a vote. Every hand goes up, Reggie’s last and slowly._  
_The crops beside the aqueduct will never need watering again._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): think question: why do people grumble about changes that help them?  
> _Reggie grumbled about the aqueduct, while quietly filling his teapot from it._  
> _Why do you think people sometimes grumble about changes that help them?_  
> - Change feels strange, even when it’s good. → That’s a fair answer. New things take getting used to, and grumbling is how some people get used to them.
> - Nobody asked Reggie first. → That’s a thoughtful answer. People like to be asked about changes to their home. Being asked feels respectful.
> - He just likes grumbling. → Ha! A fair answer. For some people, grumbling is a hobby. Reggie may be the champion.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why change can feel uncomfortable, even when it helps._


### Glossary

- **committee**: A small group of people who meet to talk things over and make decisions.
- **aqueduct**: A channel or bridge built to carry water a long way, sloping gently downhill.
- **wilting**: Drooping because a plant is short of water.
- **breakaway**: A group that splits off from a bigger group.
- **area**: How much flat space a shape covers, measured in squares.
- **motion**: At a meeting, an idea that someone suggests and everyone then votes on.

## Q9. The Gourd and the Shoe

- `q09-s1`: Go back for your shoe. · _You left it by the ditch on the long loop. The crowd will follow you there, whatever you do._
- `q09-s2`: Settle the argument between the gourd camp and the shoe camp. · _Wear the gourd and the shoe where both camps can see. Tap each in your bag and choose Wear._

#### `q09-intro`

_You are halfway round your evening walk when the strap on your bag snaps. A small gourd rolls into the ditch._  
_You bend to fetch it, and your shoe comes off in the mud with a noise like a kiss._  
_You leave them both. It has been a long day. You will come back for them._  
_When you look round, a small crowd of Nubbins has gathered by the gourd and the shoe, very quietly._  
_They look at you. Then they look at each other. Then they start following you, at a respectful distance._  
**Barty**: It is a sign!  
**You**: It’s a gourd. And a shoe.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): gourds: fruits with hard shells  
> _A gourd is a fruit that grows on a trailing vine. It belongs to the same plant family as pumpkins and squash._  
> _When a gourd dries out, its shell goes hard and light. It still rattles: the seeds rattle inside._  
> _People all over the world have used dried gourds as bowls, bottles and rattles for thousands of years._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that gourds are hard-shelled fruits in the pumpkin family, dried by people to make bowls, bottles and rattles._

**Barty**: It is TWO signs!  

**Choices**

- **Please stop following me.**
    - They stop. Then they all take one step after you, very slowly, in case that doesn’t count.
- **Walk faster.**
    - They walk faster. A little Nubbin at the front carries the gourd above its head like a lantern.

#### `q09-split`

_By the time you reach the ditch, the crowd has split in two._  
_Half are bowing to the shoe, which they have set on a rock. The other half are holding up the gourd and humming._  
**A Gourd Nubbin**: The gourd is round, like the sun. Round things are never wrong.  
**A Shoe Nubbin**: The shoe has laces. Nobody understands laces. Follow the laces.  
_A third, much smaller group has gathered round a pebble that was near the shoe. Neither of the other camps will speak to them._  
**You**: Has anybody actually checked? Is there any evidence for any of this?  
_Everyone stares at you. Checking had not occurred to anybody._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): evidence versus bad reasons  
> _“Round things are never wrong.” “Nobody understands laces.”_  
> _Which of these is the best reason to believe something?_  
> - ✅ I checked, and I found evidence. → Yes. Evidence is something you can check, that other people can check too. Being round, or having laces, or being followed by a crowd: none of those make anything true.
> - Lots of people believe it. → A crowd can be wrong. This crowd is bowing to a shoe! The best reason is evidence: something you can check and others can check too.
> - It sounds important. → Lots of nonsense sounds important. “Follow the laces” sounds very important. The best reason to believe something is evidence: something you can check for yourself.
> _For grown-ups: Told the difference between evidence (something you can check) and bad reasons for believing something._


#### `q09-mother`

_A Keeper in a headscarf marches up the path, rolling up her sleeves. This is Mother Brindle. She is not pleased._  
**Mother Brindle**: What’s all this, then? Barty! Is that you at the front?  
**Barty**: Mother! The signs!  
**A Gourd Nubbin**: Barty saw the signs first. Barty is very special.  
**Mother Brindle**: Special? He put a frog in the teapot this morning. He is going to BED.  
**Barty**: It was only a small frog.  
**Mother Brindle**: It’s past his bedtime. And yours, all of you.  
**Mother Brindle**: Keeper, sort this out. They won’t listen to me. Nobody listens to me. I’m only his mother.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): showing someone you are listening  
> _Mother Brindle says nobody listens to her. She sounds exasperated: fed up and worn out._  
> _How could you show her that you are listening?_  
> - ✅ Look at her, let her finish, then say back what she needs. → Yes. “You need everyone home and in bed.” Saying it back shows you really heard. Thank you, love. That’s all I wanted. Someone to actually hear it.
> - Nod while looking at the gourd. → Nodding is a start, but she can tell your eyes are on the gourd! Look at her, let her finish, and say back what she needs. Then she knows you heard.
> - Tell her not to worry. → That’s kind, but it skips over what she said. First show you heard: look at her, let her finish, and say back what she needs.
> _For grown-ups: Practised active listening: looking at someone, letting them finish, and saying back what they need._


**Choices**

- **Tell them both are signs.**
    - Both camps cheer, then look at each other suspiciously, then cheer again, slightly less.
- **Tell them it’s just things you dropped.**
    - Nobody believes you. Your modesty is taken as a further sign. Mother Brindle sighs.
- **Tell them to think for themselves.**
    - **You**: You don’t need to follow me. Any of you. You can all think for yourselves!
    - Everyone nods at once, perfectly together. Then they all wait for you to tell them what to think.
    - **Barty**: What should we think first?
    - Mother Brindle puts her face in her hands.

#### `q09-hats`

_You put the gourd on your head. It wobbles._  
_Then, after a moment’s thought, you balance the shoe on top of the gourd._  
_It slides left. The crowd gasps. You tilt your head. It slides right. The crowd gasps again._  
_You find the exact middle. You hold very, very still. The shoe stays._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, do): balance: keep the balance point over the base  
> _Tilt your head to keep the shoe steady. Find the spot where it stops sliding._  
> _Every object has a balance point. Keep that point right above whatever holds it up, and it stays put._  
> _Let it lean past the edge, and gravity tips it over. Stand tall. Breathe slowly. Don’t sneeze._  
> Check: `edu:balance:shoe:centre`
> _For grown-ups: Balanced a stack by keeping its balance point over its support, and learned how gravity tips things that lean._

_Both camps gasp. Both camps are right. Nobody can argue with that._  
**Barty**: Follow the Keeper!  

#### `q09-complete`

_The whole crowd falls in behind you in one long, happy, wobbling line._  
_There are nine of them, one behind the other, each exactly one metre behind the next._  

> **Lesson** (maths, ask): counting gaps in a line  
> _Nine Nubbins in a line, one metre apart. How long is the line, from the first Nubbin to the last?_  
> - ✅ 8 metres → Yes! Nine Nubbins, but only eight gaps between them. Eight gaps of one metre: 8 metres. Try it with your fingers: hold up three, and count the gaps. Two!
> - 9 metres → Lots of people say that! But count the gaps, not the Nubbins. Between 9 Nubbins there are only 8 gaps. So the line is 8 metres long.
> - 10 metres → Too many! Count the gaps between the Nubbins. Nine Nubbins have eight gaps between them: 8 metres.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that 9 Nubbins in a line have 8 gaps between them, so the line is 8 metres long._

_You walk to the pond. They walk to the pond. You turn round. They turn round, and bump into each other._  
_When you finally stop, they stop, sit down and fall asleep in a heap, with Barty on top._  
**Mother Brindle**: Thank you, love. Keep the gourd. And the shoe. I don’t want them in my house; they’ll only start something.  
_From now on, if you call “Follow me”, every Nubbin in the Grove will trail behind you in a parade until you stop._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think question: following and thinking for yourself  
> _The Nubbins followed you everywhere, just because others did._  
> _When is it good to follow someone, and when should you think for yourself?_  
> - Follow people you trust. Think for yourself when something feels wrong. → That’s a fair answer. Trust is earned, and a funny feeling inside is worth listening to.
> - It’s fine to follow, as long as you know where you’re going. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Following with your eyes open is very different from following with them shut.
> - Always think for yourself, even if you end up agreeing. → That’s a fair answer. You can still choose the same thing as everyone else, as long as it was your choice.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when it is wise to follow someone and when to think for yourself._


### Glossary

- **gourd**: A fruit with a hard shell, from the same plant family as pumpkins.
- **evidence**: Facts or signs you can check, that show whether something is true.
- **exasperated**: Very fed up and worn out, because something keeps going wrong.
- **balance point**: The spot where an object’s weight is evenly spread, so it can rest without tipping.

## Q10. Haggle

- `q10-s1`: Offer Harrow less than he is asking for the brass bell. · _Tap the bell and choose Haggle instead of Buy. Start low. Lower than feels polite._
- `q10-s2`: Haggle with Harrow through three full rounds. · _Each round, offer something between your last number and his. Agree too fast and he starts again._

#### `q10-intro`

_There is a new stall by the market path, piled with odds and ends. Behind it sits a Keeper with a pencil behind each ear._  
**Harrow Tuppence**: Morning! Harrow Tuppence. Everything a Grove could want, and several things it couldn’t.  
_You spot a little brass bell. Your Nubbin spots it too and makes a small, longing noise._  
**You**: How much is the bell?  
**Harrow Tuppence**: Twenty Shells.  
_You count out twenty Shells and hold them out._  
_Harrow stares at the Shells. Then at you. His face falls by about a mile._  
**Harrow Tuppence**: Twenty? Just like that? No haggling? Not even a little bit?  
**Harrow Tuppence**: Put those away. I can’t take that. It’s insulting. To both of us. To the bell.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, notice): markets and haggling around the world  
> **Harrow Tuppence**: To haggle is to bargain: we argue the price up and down until we both agree.  
> _In many markets around the world, haggling is normal and even expected. It can be friendly, like a game._  
> _In most shops, though, the price on the tag is the price. Haggling there just confuses people._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that in many markets people agree a price by haggling, while most shops have fixed prices._


**Choices**

- **Sorry. How does this work?**
    - **Harrow Tuppence**: You say a number. I say a bigger number. We weep. We meet in the middle. We shake. It’s beautiful.
- **Twenty is what the tag says.**
    - **Harrow Tuppence**: The tag is the OPENING. Nobody listens to the tag. The tag is a cry for help.

#### `q10-first-offer`

**Harrow Tuppence**: Right. Your turn. Say a number. Lower than twenty. Go on.  
**You**: …Eight Shells?  
**Harrow Tuppence**: EIGHT?  
_He clutches the stall. He clutches his heart. He clutches the bell, protectively._  
_Then, while you aren’t looking, he winks at your Nubbin._  
**Harrow Tuppence**: Now we’re talking. Oh, that’s lovely. Do go on.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): spotting exaggeration from clues  
> _Harrow clutched his heart at “eight”. Is he really shocked, or does he exaggerate?_  
> - ✅ No. He’s exaggerating for fun. He winked! → Yes. The wink and “that’s lovely” are the clues. He’s acting shocked because that’s part of the game. To exaggerate is to make something sound much bigger than it is. Harrow is an expert.
> - Yes, eight is a terrible offer. → Look at the clues: he winked at your Nubbin, then said “that’s lovely”. He isn’t hurt. He’s exaggerating: making it sound much bigger, for fun.
> - He might need a doctor. → Ha! He’s fine. Read on: he winks, then says “Oh, that’s lovely.” The heart-clutching is exaggeration: acting it up because haggling is a kind of performance.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues (the wink, “that’s lovely”) to tell that a character is exaggerating, not truly upset._


#### `q10-rounds`

**Harrow Tuppence**: Right. Proper rules. Three rounds. I go down, you go up, and we both pretend to leave at least once.  
**Harrow Tuppence**: Don’t meet me too quick, that’s rude. Don’t hold out too long, that’s also rude. Somewhere in between is an art.  
_Your Nubbin climbs onto the counter to watch. This is clearly the best thing that has ever happened in a shop._  
**Harrow Tuppence**: Twenty. For you. Because I like your face.  
**You**: Ten.  
**Harrow Tuppence**: Ten? For a BELL? It rings in two keys, you know. Eighteen.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): number patterns that follow a rule  
> _Harrow’s prices go 20, then 18. If he keeps the same rule, what will his next two prices be?_  
> - ✅ 16, then 14 → Yes. The rule is “take away 2” each time: 20, 18, 16, 14. A number pattern with a rule lets you guess what comes next. Very handy when haggling.
> - 17, then 16 → That takes away 1. Look again: 20 to 18 is a drop of 2. Keep taking away 2: 18, 16, 14. His next prices are 16, then 14.
> - 10, then 8 → Those are your numbers! Harrow’s go 20, then 18. That’s 2 less each time. So next comes 16, then 14.
> _For grown-ups: Found the rule in Harrow’s prices (take away 2) and used it to predict the next numbers: 16, then 14._


**Choices**

- **Pretend to walk away.**
    - You get three steps. Harrow calls out “Sixteen!” in a voice of real anguish.
- **Admire the bell, then go lower.**
    - **Harrow Tuppence**: Flattery AND a low offer. Who taught you that? Me. I did. Just now.

#### `q10-deal`

**Harrow Tuppence**: Fourteen. My final offer. I’ll be ruined. My children will eat gravel.  
**You**: You don’t have children.  
**Harrow Tuppence**: Fourteen, then, and nobody eats gravel.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think question: pretending in a game, or lying?  
> _Harrow said his children would eat gravel. He doesn’t have any children._  
> _Was that a lie, or part of the game?_  
> - Part of the game. Everyone knew he didn’t mean it. → That’s a fair answer. When everyone knows the rules, pretending is play, like acting in a play.
> - A bit of a lie, even if it was funny. → That’s an honest answer. Even a joke can blur the truth. You did call him on it, after all.
> - It depends whether the other person knows it’s a game. → That’s a wise answer. Pretending is fine when both people are in on it. It’s tricking when one isn’t.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between pretending inside a game everyone understands and telling a lie._

_You shake on it. Harrow’s eyes are a little wet. He says it’s the wind._  
_Fourteen is exactly halfway between his twenty and your first eight. Neither of you planned that. Probably._  
**Harrow Tuppence**: Halfway. The fairest spot there is. Lovely.  

#### `q10-complete`

_You hand over fourteen Shells. Harrow counts them twice, tenderly, like a man counting doves._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): money subtraction with Shells  
> _The tag said 20 Shells. You paid 14. How many Shells did you save?_  
> - ✅ 6 Shells → Yes. Count on from 14: 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20. That’s 6. Six Shells still in your pocket.
> - 4 Shells → Nearly! Count on from 14 to 20: 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20. Six counts. You saved 6 Shells.
> - 34 Shells → That adds them together. To find what you saved, take away: 20 − 14. Count on from 14 to 20, and you get 6 Shells saved.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the saving in Shells: 20 − 14 = 6, by counting on from 14 to 20._

**Harrow Tuppence**: That, Keeper, was a proper bit of business. Best I’ve had all week. Only one I’ve had all week.  
_He presses a small gourd into your hands as well. “Free. Nobody haggles over a gourd. Dreadful things, gourds.”_  
_Your Nubbin rings the brass bell. It does, in fact, ring in two keys._  
**Harrow Tuppence**: Tell you what. I’ve had a word with the shop. You can haggle there too, now. Anything you buy.  
**Harrow Tuppence**: They won’t go lower than a fifth off. And you have to mean it. Shopkeepers can tell.  
_From now on, any purchase in the shop can start with a bit of haggling, for up to 20% off._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): fairness: keeping your side of a deal  
> **Harrow Tuppence**: One more thing, Keeper. A deal is a promise. We both agreed fourteen, so fourteen it is.  
> **Harrow Tuppence**: If buyers and sellers didn’t keep their word, nobody could trust a market. Then where would we be?  
> **Harrow Tuppence**: Somewhere without bells, that’s where.  
> _For grown-ups: Heard why a deal is a promise both sides keep, and why that keeps trading fair._


**Choices**

- **Slip him the six Shells you saved.**
    - **Harrow Tuppence**: Don’t you DARE.
    - **Harrow Tuppence**: A deal’s a deal. Pay twenty now and the whole morning meant nothing. Put it away.
    - You put it away. He looks, for some reason, enormously proud of you.
- **Shake on it again, for luck.**
    - You offer your hand. He haggles you down to a slightly shorter handshake, and looks delighted.

### Glossary

- **haggle**: To bargain over a price, going up and down until buyer and seller agree.
- **exaggerate**: To make something sound bigger, worse or better than it really is.
- **tenderly**: Gently and lovingly.

## Q11. The Thinnest Slice

- `q11-s1`: Pick fresh mint for Mr Crisp. · _Mint grows in a small patch by the pond. Pick the top leaves, then give them to Mr Crisp._
- `q11-s2`: Stay and watch Gorbold with the last thin slice. · _Stay in the bathhouse. If you leave, Gorbold waits politely for you to come back._

#### `q11-intro`

_At the bathhouse the steam is thick, and the snack table is empty. Very, very empty._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): what steam really is: water vapour turning back into tiny drops  
> **Mr Crisp**: Mind the steam on my tray, please. Do you know what steam actually is?  
> - ✅ Tiny drops of water floating in the air. → Exactly. The warm pool water turns into an invisible gas called water vapour. When the vapour meets cooler air, it turns back into tiny drops. That cloud is the drops.
> - Smoke from a fire. → No fire here, thank goodness. Smoke comes from burning. Steam is just water. Warm water turns into invisible water vapour, which cools into tiny drops. That cloud is the drops.
> - A cloud that fell out of the sky. → Good thinking: real clouds are made of tiny water drops too! But this one rose up from the pool. Warm water turns into invisible water vapour, which cools into tiny drops. A little indoor cloud.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that the cloud above warm water is tiny water drops: water evaporates, then condenses in cooler air._

_In the warm pool floats a Nubbin so round it has stopped swimming. It just bobs._  
_This is Gorbold. Around it float fruit stones, a crust and one sad lettuce leaf._  
**Gorbold**: More.  
_A Keeper in a crisp white apron appears at your elbow, holding a silver tray._  
**Mr Crisp**: Good afternoon. Mr Crisp, in charge of refreshments. Gorbold has eaten the menu.  
**Mr Crisp**: Not the food on the menu. The menu itself. Both sides.  
**Mr Crisp**: Before that, the fruit. Then the fruit bowl. Then the table, and then a fern.  
**Mr Crisp**: I have one last treat to serve, but I need fresh mint. Could you fetch some?  
**You**: Is that wise? Gorbold looks very full.  
**Mr Crisp**: It is a VERY small treat.  

**Choices**

- **I’ll fetch the mint.**
    - **Mr Crisp**: Splendid. The patch by the pond. Only the top leaves, please. I am very particular.
- **Ask Gorbold if that’s all right.**
    - **Gorbold**: More.
    - That seems to be a yes. Gorbold says yes to most things.

#### `q11-mint`

_You pinch the top leaves off the mint plants by the pond. Your fingers smell amazing._  

> **Lesson** (science, do): how pinching the tips makes a plant grow bushier  
> **Mr Crisp**: Pinch just above a pair of leaves. The plant will grow new side shoots from there.  
> **Mr Crisp**: Pick the tips, and next week the mint is bushier than before. Gardeners call it pinching out.  
> Check: `edu:pick:mint:top-leaves`
> _For grown-ups: Picked mint from the tips and learned that this makes the plant send out new side shoots._

**Mr Crisp**: Perfect. Top leaves only. You have been listening.  
**Mr Crisp**: Now I shall make one small mint cake, and cut it into eight equal slices.  
_He vanishes into the steam. There is a sound of very fine, very careful slicing._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions: one slice of eight  
> _One cake, cut into 8 equal slices. Gorbold will get one slice._  
> _What fraction of the cake is one slice?_  
> - ✅ One eighth (1/8) → Yes. One slice out of eight equal slices is one eighth. A very thin eighth.
> - One half (1/2) → A half is one of 2 equal pieces. This cake has 8 equal pieces, so one slice is one eighth: 1/8.
> - 8 → 8 is how many slices there are altogether. One slice of the 8 is one eighth: 1/8.
> _For grown-ups: Named one slice of a cake cut into eight equal slices as one eighth (1/8)._

_Gorbold bobs a little closer, to listen._  
**Gorbold**: More?  
_A voice from the steam says, “Not yet.”_  

#### `q11-slice`

_Mr Crisp returns. On the silver tray lies one slice of mint cake, so thin you could read through it._  
**Mr Crisp**: For you, Gorbold. One more slice. Just a sliver.  
**Gorbold**: Full.  
**Mr Crisp**: It is barely a slice at all. You would hardly notice it.  
_Gorbold looks at the slice. The slice, somehow, looks back at Gorbold._  
_You look at the exits. There are two. Both are a long way off._  
_Mr Crisp holds out the tray. The steam goes very still._  

> **Lesson** (health, ask): listening to your body when it says “full”  
> _Gorbold said one word: “Full.” That is its tummy talking._  
> _What is the best thing to do when your tummy says “full”?_  
> - ✅ Stop eating, even if the food looks lovely. → Yes. Your tummy sends a message to your brain when you have had enough. Listening to it keeps you comfortable. The food will still be lovely later.
> - Finish it anyway. → Lots of people are taught to clear their plate! But eating past full can make you feel uncomfortable. It is fine to stop when you are full, and save the rest for later.
> - Eat it really fast, before the full feeling arrives. → Ha! The full feeling does take a little while to arrive. That is why eating slowly helps you notice it. When it arrives, it is fine to stop.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that feeling full is the body’s signal to stop eating, and that eating slowly helps us notice it._


**Choices**

- **Go on. It is very thin.**
    - **Gorbold**: …Fine.
    - Gorbold did say “full”, though. You make a note to listen better next time.
- **Take a big step back.**
    - Mr Crisp, without even looking, takes a big step back too. He has done this before.

#### `q11-pop`

_Gorbold eats the slice. There is a pause. Then a tiny hiccup._  
_Then a soft POP._  
_Glittering confetti fills the bathhouse and drifts down onto the water like snow._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): spotting a simile  
> _The confetti drifts down “like snow”. Comparing two things with “like” or “as” is called a simile._  
> _Which of these is a simile?_  
> - ✅ Gorbold bobs like a cork. → Yes. “Like a cork” compares Gorbold to a cork, which bobs on water too.
> - Gorbold is very round. → That describes Gorbold, but it doesn’t compare it to anything. “Bobs like a cork” is a simile.
> - The confetti is glittery. → A good describing word, but no comparison. “Drifts down like snow” is the simile.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a simile compares two things using “like” or “as”, and picked one out._

_When it clears, Gorbold is bobbing in the pool, normal-sized and blinking._  
**Gorbold**: Light!  
_Gorbold does a slow, happy spin. It is the first time in weeks it has been able to turn round._  

#### `q11-complete`

**Mr Crisp**: Ah. The usual result. Lovely.  
_Mr Crisp sweeps the confetti into a perfect pile. Not one speck lands on his apron._  
**Mr Crisp**: For your trouble. My own recipe.  
_He hands you a paper packet of thin mint slices, and a napkin bib with a tiny mint leaf sewn on._  
**Mr Crisp**: One slice fills a Nubbin to exactly full. Never over. I have had enough of over for one day.  
**Gorbold**: More?  
**Mr Crisp**: No.  
_Gorbold bobs over to your Nubbin and nudges a single fruit stone across the water towards it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): a fruit stone holds a seed  
> **Mr Crisp**: A fruit stone is not rubbish, you know. There is a seed inside it.  
> **Mr Crisp**: Plant it and water it, and in time a tree grows. The tree makes fruit with stones. Round and round.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a fruit stone has a seed inside that can grow into a new tree._

**Gorbold**: Yours.  
_Mr Crisp stops sweeping. In eleven years he has never once seen Gorbold give anything away._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): thinking about why someone shares  
> _Gorbold has only ever said “more”. Now it has given something away._  
> _Why do you think Gorbold shared, just this once?_  
> - It feels light and happy now, so it wants to share. → That’s a thoughtful answer. When we feel good, giving often comes more easily. Mr Crisp might agree.
> - To say thank you for listening when it said “full”. → That’s a kind way to see it. Being listened to can make someone want to give something back.
> - It just didn’t want the stone. → That’s fair! It might be true. But of everyone in the bathhouse, Gorbold chose your Nubbin. That seems to mean something.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why a greedy character might share for the first time; any reasoned answer was welcomed._


### Glossary

- **refreshments**: Food and drinks served to people, often at a party or event.
- **water vapour**: Water in the form of an invisible gas, floating in the air.
- **shoot**: A new stem growing out of a plant.
- **sliver**: A very thin, small piece of something.
- **simile**: A way of describing something by comparing it to something else, using “like” or “as”.

## Q12. The Very Quiet Nubbin

- `q12-s1`: Collect three pieces of evidence that the shop’s Nubbin isn’t real. · _Try feeding it, tickling it, and putting it in the pond. Watch carefully each time._
- `q12-s2`: Win the argument with Mr Fenwick Mull. · _Show him all three pieces of evidence at the counter, then stand firm._

#### `q12-intro`

_A parcel arrives from the shop. Inside, in a nest of wood shavings, lies a Nubbin._  
_The note says: “One Nubbin, quiet breed. Hand-raised. Do not overfeed.” The price tag says 12 Shells._  
_Your Nubbins crowd round and poke it. It does not move. It does not blink._  
_One of its eyes is a button._  
_You take it back to the shop. Mr Fenwick Mull is polishing the counter, which is already very shiny._  
**You**: This Nubbin you sent me doesn’t move.  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: Ah, no. That’s quite normal, for that breed.  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: It’s having a little lie-down. Very sleepy breed. Famous for it.  
**You**: It has a seam down its back.  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: Lovely stitching, isn’t it? Hand-sewn. Very rare.  

> **Lesson** (science, K-LS1-1, ask): the signs that something is alive  
> _Is this Nubbin alive? Scientists check for signs of life._  
> _Which of these is a sign that something is alive?_  
> - ✅ It eats, grows, breathes and reacts. → Yes. Living things need food, they grow, they breathe and they react to the world around them. So let’s test this “Nubbin”.
> - It has lovely stitching. → Stitching shows that someone MADE it! Living things aren’t sewn. They eat, grow, breathe and react. So let’s test this “Nubbin”.
> - It lies very still. → Living things lie still sometimes, like when they sleep. But a sleeping Nubbin still breathes, and wakes if tickled. Signs of life are eating, growing, breathing and reacting. Let’s test it.
> _For grown-ups: Named the signs of life (eating, growing, breathing, reacting) to plan how to test whether something is alive._


**Choices**

- **I want my Shells back.**
    - **Mr Fenwick Mull**: A refund? We don’t do refunds. Never needed to. Nothing has ever gone wrong.
- **Then I’ll wait for it to wake up.**
    - You wait. Mr Fenwick Mull waits. The Nubbin waits harder than either of you.

#### `q12-evidence`

_Time for a proper investigation. You test it three ways, and watch carefully each time._  

> **Lesson** (science, do): running a simple test and recording the results  
> _Test one: does it eat? Test two: does it react? Test three: does it breathe, and blow bubbles?_  
> _Write down what happens each time. Writing results down is how scientists keep track of evidence._  
> Check: `edu:test:plush:feed-tickle-float`
> _For grown-ups: Tested the toy for three signs of life and recorded each result, the way a scientist collects evidence._

_Evidence one: you offer it a heart fruit. It does not eat it._  
_No Nubbin has ever turned down a heart fruit. Not one. Not ever._  
_Evidence two: you tickle its feet. Nothing._  
_Your own Nubbin, watching, falls over giggling on its behalf._  
_Evidence three: you set it in the pond. It floats face down, with great calm. Not one bubble._  
_A price tag bobs up beside it._  

#### `q12-argument`

_Back at the shop, you lay out the evidence: one uneaten heart fruit, one damp Nubbin, one price tag._  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: Well. That’s shyness. Shy breed. It didn’t want to eat in front of you.  
**You**: It didn’t laugh when I tickled it.  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: Tired from the journey. Long way from the warehouse. Er. The nest. The wild nest.  
**You**: It floated face down in the pond.  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: Loves a swim. Very relaxed swimmer. Floats like a lily.  
_He gives it an encouraging pat. It topples slowly sideways off the counter._  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: Homesick. Misses its nest. They get homesick, this breed. Terribly sensitive.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): telling evidence apart from excuses  
> _Mr Fenwick Mull has an excuse for every clue. But an excuse is not evidence._  
> _Which of these is the strongest evidence?_  
> - ✅ The price tag: “Plush toy. Stuffed. Not alive.” → Yes. It is written down, and it answers the question directly. You can check a tag. You can’t check “shy breed”. That’s an excuse.
> - “It’s a shy breed.” → That’s Mr Mull’s excuse, and there’s no way to check it. The price tag is real, written evidence.
> - “It floats like a lily.” → A lovely simile! But it doesn’t prove anything. The price tag, in writing, is the strongest evidence.
> _For grown-ups: Picked the strongest evidence (a written label) over excuses that cannot be checked._

_You pick up the price tag and hold it in front of his nose._  
**You**: This Nubbin is, and always has been, a cushion.  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: That isn’t a cushion.  
**You**: I know. I got flustered. My point stands.  

**Choices**

- **Say nothing. Hold the stare.**
    - You hold the stare. He holds it back. Somewhere a clock ticks. He blinks first.
- **Read the price tag aloud.**
    - **You**: “Plush toy. Stuffed. Not alive. Made with love.”
    - **Mr Fenwick Mull**: …Made with love, though.
- **Then I’ll have a replacement.**
    - **Mr Fenwick Mull**: Out of stock, sadly. But my brother has a shop over the ridge. Lovely man. Nothing like me.
    - You walk over the ridge. The shop is identical. Behind the counter, in a false moustache, stands Mr Fenwick Mull.
    - **Mr Fenwick Mull**: Fenwick’s brother. Never met him.
    - The moustache falls off. He puts it back on, slightly higher. You walk back over the ridge together, in silence.

#### `q12-crack`

_Mr Fenwick Mull looks at the tag. Then at the toy. Then at the ceiling, for help._  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: All right. ALL RIGHT. It’s a toy. It has always been a toy.  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: A man who sells toys told me it was a Nubbin. I believed him. I wanted to believe him.  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: I’ll give you your Shells back. I’ll even open a returns counter. The first in the valley.  
_He takes a deep breath. His shoulders drop about an inch._  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: That’s better, actually. Saying it out loud.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): thinking about honesty: being fooled vs covering up  
> _Mr Mull believed a toy seller. Then he made excuse after excuse._  
> _Was he being dishonest, or was he fooled, or a bit of both?_  
> - Fooled at first, but the excuses were dishonest. → That’s a careful answer. Being tricked isn’t your fault. Covering it up afterwards is a choice.
> - He was just fooled. → That’s a kind way to see it. He did believe it at first. Some might say the excuses went too far.
> - Dishonest all along. → That’s fair: he made up a LOT of excuses. Notice how much better he feels once he tells the truth.
> _For grown-ups: Weighed whether a character was fooled, dishonest or both, and noticed how owning up made him feel lighter._


#### `q12-complete`

_Mr Fenwick Mull counts your Shells back into your hand, in neat piles of four._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, do): counting money in equal groups  
> _Count along with him: four, eight, twelve._  
> _Three piles of four make 12. That’s the 12 Shells on the price tag, all back._  
> Check: `edu:count:shells:12-in-fours`
> _For grown-ups: Counted 12 Shells as three equal groups of four (4, 8, 12)._

_He looks lighter for it, somehow._  
**Mr Fenwick Mull**: Keep the toy, though. No charge. It’s grown on me. In a way that isn’t growing.  
_You carry it home. Your Nubbins take it straight to the nest and pile round it._  
_By evening they are fast asleep, cuddled up to the plush Nubbin._  
_It is, at last, having a genuinely lovely rest._  
_From now on the shop gives refunds, if you can explain what is wrong with the thing you bought._  

### Glossary

- **breed**: A particular kind of animal, like a type of dog or sheep.
- **seam**: The line where two pieces of cloth are sewn together.
- **evidence**: Facts or clues that show whether something is true.
- **investigation**: A careful search for the truth about something.
- **excuse**: A reason someone gives to get out of blame, often not the real one.
- **flustered**: Muddled and a bit hot and bothered.
- **refund**: Money given back to you when you return something you bought.

## Q13. Grants for Silly Walks

- `q13-s1`: Show Mr Strutt a walk of your own. · _Tap a pattern of moves on the pad (up, down, left, right, spin), then press Walk._
- `q13-s2`: Show Mr Strutt a properly silly walk. · _Longer patterns score higher. Mix in spins, backward steps and pauses. The same move twice in a row counts less._

#### `q13-intro`

_A small wooden booth has appeared at the crossroads. The sign reads: GRANTS FOR WALKS (VERY SILLY ONLY)._  
_Behind the counter sits a tall Keeper in a bowler hat, stamping forms._  
_He stamps each form twice, for luck. There are seven forms in his pile._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> _Seven forms. Two stamps on each, for luck._  
> _How many stamps is that altogether?_  
> - ✅ 14 → Fourteen! Seven twos are fourteen. Fourteen helpings of luck.
> - 9 → That’s 7 add 2. But each form gets 2 stamps: seven lots of two. 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14.
> - 12 → So close! Count in twos, one for each form: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. Seven forms make 14 stamps.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out 7 forms × 2 stamps = 14 by thinking of equal groups._

**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Good morning. Hollis Strutt. I fund silly walks. Research, practice and showing off.  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Most walks in this valley are dreadfully sensible. It keeps me up at night.  
_He shows you his own walk to the filing cabinet._  
_It takes four minutes. It involves a sort of kick, a sort of sit, and a sort of question mark._  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Now. Show me yours. Use the pad. Make up a pattern. Surprise me.  

**Choices**

- **I’m not sure I have one.**
    - **Mr Hollis Strutt**: Everyone has one. Most people keep it hidden. Such a waste.
- **I’ve been practising.**
    - **Mr Hollis Strutt**: Marvellous. Don’t tell me. Show me.

#### `q13-first`

_You do your walk. It has a hop in it. You are quite proud of the hop._  
_Mr Strutt watches over steepled fingers. He makes a single note. It is a small note._  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Hmm. That is a rather ordinary walk, isn’t it?  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: The hop is fine. The hop is a start. But the rest of you was just walking, with a hop on top.  
_Your cheeks go a bit warm. You were proud of that hop._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): using feedback to improve  
> _Mr Strutt gave you feedback: the hop is good, the rest needs work._  
> _What is the most useful thing to do with feedback like that?_  
> - ✅ Keep the good bit, and try again. → Exactly. Keep the hop. Build round it. That is how all getting-better works.
> - Give up. I’m just not a silly walker. → Nonsense. Nobody gets it first time. Feeling a bit stung is normal. Then you keep the hop, and try again.
> - Argue that the hop was enough. → It’s fine to be proud of your hop! But listening to feedback is how you improve. Keep the hop, and try again.
> _For grown-ups: Chose to keep what worked and try again after hearing feedback._

**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Don’t look so glum. Every great silly walk began as a sensible one with ideas.  

#### `q13-notes`

**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Let me give you some notes.  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Use more knee. Knees are underused in this valley.  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Then do something with your elbows that nobody asked for.  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: And at least once, go backwards for no reason, and look as if there was a reason.  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: This year our budget was 2 Shells. The Ministry of Sensible Paths got forty times that. Forty. For gravel.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): multiplying by a tens number  
> _Silly Walks got 2 Shells. Sensible Paths got forty times as much._  
> _How many Shells did Sensible Paths get?_  
> - ✅ 80 → Eighty Shells. For gravel. Forty twos are eighty. I do this sum a lot, usually at night.
> - 42 → That’s 40 add 2. “Forty times” means forty lots of 2: 2 × 40 = 80.
> - 20 → That would be half of 40. “Forty times” means forty lots of 2, which is 80. Poor Mr Strutt.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that forty times 2 Shells is 80 Shells._

_Your Nubbin has been watching. It tries the walk itself, falls over, and carries on lying down._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): how we keep our balance  
> _Your Nubbin fell because its weight leaned out past its feet._  
> _To balance, keep your weight over your feet. Arms out wide help you stay steady, like a tightrope walker._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that we balance by keeping our weight over our feet, and that arms out wide help._

**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Now THAT is promising. Take notes from your Nubbin.  
_He slides a fresh form across the counter. It already has two stamps on it, for luck._  

**Choices**

- **Copy your Nubbin.**
    - You try walking lying down. It does not work, but it is extremely silly.
- **Make it your own.**
    - **Mr Hollis Strutt**: Bold. Original. I am already reaching for the stamp.

#### `q13-approved`

_You walk. Hop, crouch, spin, backwards. Hop, crouch, spin, backwards._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.OA.C.5, ask): continuing a repeating pattern  
> _Your walk repeats: hop, crouch, spin, backwards, hop, crouch, spin, backwards…_  
> _What is the 9th move?_  
> - ✅ Hop → Yes! The pattern repeats every 4 moves, so moves 1, 5 and 9 are all hops.
> - Spin → Let’s count: hop 1, crouch 2, spin 3, backwards 4, hop 5, crouch 6, spin 7, backwards 8, hop 9. A hop!
> - Backwards → Backwards is move 4 and move 8. The pattern starts again after that, so move 9 is a hop.
> _For grown-ups: Found the 9th move in a pattern that repeats every 4 moves._

_You go backwards with total confidence, as if there were an excellent reason._  
_You finish with the elbows. Nobody asked for the elbows. That is the point._  
_Mr Strutt rises slowly to his feet. He removes his bowler hat and presses it to his chest._  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: That is the silliest thing I have seen since Tuesday.  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Approved.  

#### `q13-complete`

_He stamps your form twice. Then a third time. He has never stamped a third time before._  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Your grant is approved. Use it well. Walk silly, often, and in public.  
_He hands you a spare bowler hat from under the counter. It is slightly too big and absolutely perfect._  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: You may switch the walk on and off as you please. I would leave it on. But then I would.  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: Between you and me, nobody needs a grant to be silly.  
**Mr Hollis Strutt**: But people do seem to like a form that says they may.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): thinking about courage and feeling free to be yourself  
> _Mr Strutt says nobody needs permission to be silly. But people still like a form that says they may._  
> _Why do you think that is?_  
> - They worry about what others will think. → That’s a wise answer. Worrying about being laughed at stops lots of people. A form can make it feel safer.
> - Being silly in public feels brave. → Good thinking. It does take courage! A stamp can feel like someone saying, “You’re allowed.”
> - They don’t need one. Just be silly! → Mr Strutt would cheer that answer. Still, lots of people feel shy, and that’s OK too.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why people want permission to be silly, and what makes it feel safe to be yourself._

_Your Keeper can now walk silly whenever you like. Switch it on in the settings._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): moving every day  
> **Mr Hollis Strutt**: One more thing. A silly walk is also exercise.  
> **Mr Hollis Strutt**: Children need about an hour of moving about every day. Hopping counts. Elbows count.  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that children need about an hour of active movement every day, and silly walking counts._


### Glossary

- **grant**: Money given to someone to help them do something.
- **feedback**: Comments that tell you what is working and what could be better.
- **steepled**: With the fingertips pressed together in a point, like a church steeple.
- **budget**: The amount of money set aside for something.
- **confidence**: Feeling sure of yourself.

## Q14. The Nap Patrol

- `q14-s1`: Carry the comfy chair over from the Workshop. · _It is the big red armchair by the Workshop door. Pick it up and carry it to the nest._
- `q14-s2`: Put your most tired Nubbin in the comfy chair. · _Tiredness shows on a Nubbin’s status card. Pick up the sleepiest one and put it on the chair._

#### `q14-intro`

_You are quietly brushing a Nubbin by the nest when the gate bangs open._  
_Three Keepers in long red robes sweep in. One trips on the step. They sweep in again, more carefully._  
**Brother Pouffe**: Surprise! It is the Nap Patrol!  
_There is a long silence. Your Nubbin, halfway through being brushed, stares at them._  
**You**: We… did not see that coming.  
**Brother Pouffe**: Exactly! We rely on surprise. Surprise, and cushions. Two things: surprise and cush—  
**Brother Bolster**: And blankets.  
**Brother Pouffe**: Three things! Hang on. Everybody out. We shall do the door again.  
_They go out. The gate bangs. They sweep in, nobody trips, and Brother Bolster raises two plump cushions, menacingly._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): working out a word from context  
> _Brother Bolster raises the cushions “menacingly”._  
> _What do you think “menacingly” means?_  
> - ✅ In a threatening, scary way. → Yes: as if he’s about to do something terrible. With a cushion. That’s the joke: cushions are not scary.
> - Very gently. → Good guess, cushions ARE gentle! But “menacingly” means in a threatening way. A threatening cushion is very silly.
> - Very slowly. → He might be slow too! But “menacingly” means in a threatening way. That’s what makes it funny.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in the scene to work out that “menacingly” means in a threatening way._

_Sister Tuft holds up three folded blankets, just as menacingly._  
**Brother Bolster**: Soft. Very soft. You have been warned.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): adding three numbers  
> _Bolster has 2 cushions. Tuft has 3 blankets. Soon there will be 1 big chair too._  
> _How many soft things will the Nap Patrol have?_  
> - ✅ 6 → Yes: 2 + 3 = 5, and 1 more chair makes 6. Six soft things. Very well armed.
> - 5 → That’s the cushions and blankets: 2 + 3 = 5. Don’t forget the chair! 5 + 1 = 6.
> - 3 → Three is how many robed Keepers there are! Soft things: 2 cushions + 3 blankets + 1 chair = 6.
> _For grown-ups: Added 2 cushions, 3 blankets and 1 chair to make 6 soft things._

**Brother Pouffe**: Your Nubbins look tired. Overworked. Under-napped. We shall see to that. Sister Tuft!  
**Brother Pouffe**: Bring forth… the big red chair!  
**Sister Tuft**: We left it at your Workshop. You said you’d carry it.  
**Brother Pouffe**: …Keeper. Would you be so good as to carry it over for us?  

**Choices**

- **Fine. I’ll fetch it.**
    - **Brother Pouffe**: Splendid. We shall wait here, being terrifying.
- **Can I hold a cushion?**
    - **Brother Bolster**: …Just for a minute.
    - It is extremely soft. You can see why he is so proud of it.

#### `q14-chair`

_You carry the chair back to the nest. It is deep, red and squashy, with a fringe round the bottom._  
_It is heavier than it looks. Most comfortable things are._  
**Sister Tuft**: Behold. The comfy chair.  
_Brother Pouffe cracks his knuckles. Brother Bolster raises the cushions._  
_Sister Tuft fluffs the chair twice, then a third time, to be safe._  
**Brother Bolster**: Feel that cushion. Go on. Feathers inside. Full of air.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, do): sorting materials by how they feel  
> _Sort what’s in the nest into soft and hard: cushion, blanket, gate post, pebble, feather, flowerpot._  
> **Brother Bolster**: Feathers and wool trap lots of tiny pockets of air. That’s why they squash. Wood and stone keep their shape.  
> Check: `edu:sort:materials:soft-hard`
> _For grown-ups: Sorted things into soft and hard and learned that soft things trap air._


#### `q14-sentence`

**Brother Pouffe**: Now. Bring us your most tired Nubbin.  
**Brother Pouffe**: It shall sit in the comfy chair until lunchtime. With a cushion behind it. And another cushion. Beside.  
**Brother Bolster**: And a blanket over its knees. A woolly one.  
**Sister Tuft**: And no getting up. Not even for a snack.  
**Brother Pouffe**: Unless it is a very small snack.  
_The Workshop clock says half past ten. Lunch in the Grove is at half past twelve._  
_They exchange grim nods. They have done this many times, and it always goes exactly to plan._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): time intervals  
> _It is half past ten. The nap lasts until lunch at half past twelve._  
> _How long will the nap be?_  
> - ✅ 2 hours → Yes. Half past ten to half past eleven is 1 hour. To half past twelve is 2 hours.
> - 30 minutes → Half an hour is a short nap! Count the hours: 10:30 to 11:30, then to 12:30. That’s 2 hours.
> - 12 hours → That’s a whole night’s sleep! From 10:30 to 12:30 is just 2 hours.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that half past ten to half past twelve is 2 hours._


**Choices**

- **Bring the sleepiest Nubbin.**
    - Your sleepiest Nubbin yawns so wide it nearly falls into itself.
- **Offer to sit in the chair yourself.**
    - **Brother Pouffe**: Ha! Keepers are safe from cushions today. Bring us a Nubbin.

#### `q14-asleep`

_The Nubbin sinks into the chair. Brother Bolster tucks in a cushion._  
_Sister Tuft lays a woolly blanket over its knees._  
_It is asleep before the blanket lands._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): why sleep matters  
> **Sister Tuft**: Sleep is not doing nothing. While you sleep, your body grows and mends itself.  
> **Sister Tuft**: Your brain tidies up the day, too. Children your age need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sleep helps the body grow and repair, and that children need about 9 to 12 hours a night._

_It snores very softly, like a kettle thinking about boiling._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): what a simile tells us  
> _The Nubbin snores “like a kettle thinking about boiling”._  
> _What does that tell you about the snore?_  
> - ✅ It’s a soft, quiet, rising sort of sound. → Yes. A kettle about to boil makes a gentle, growing hum. The simile lets you hear the snore in your head.
> - It’s very loud and whistly. → A boiling kettle whistles! But this one is only THINKING about boiling, so it’s soft and quiet.
> - It’s hot. → Kettles are hot, but the simile is about the sound: soft and quietly rising, like a kettle not quite boiling.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out what a simile (“like a kettle thinking about boiling”) tells the reader about a sound._

**Brother Pouffe**: Shh. The Patrol is working.  
_All three tiptoe to the edge of the nest and stand guard. Nobody has ever guarded a nap so fiercely._  

#### `q14-complete`

_Two hours later, at half past twelve, the Nubbin wakes. It stretches. It glows._  
_It looks as if it has slept for a week._  
**Brother Pouffe**: Ha! Look at it. Utterly refreshed. Our work here is done.  
**Brother Bolster**: Best nap we have ever given. Possibly the best nap anyone has ever had.  
**Sister Tuft**: We should go. We have three more Groves to burst into before tea.  
_They sweep out. One trips on the step. Then they sweep back in, because they forgot the chair._  
**Brother Pouffe**: Keep it. We have another. We have a whole room of them.  
**Brother Pouffe**: One last question, Keeper. When did YOU last sit down?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): thinking about rest and looking after yourself
