_On the third wiggle there is a soft pop, and the Nubbin slides out in a shower of seeds._  
_It is orange up to the elbows, and it smells wonderful._  
_Mr. Tweed picks a seed off his eyebrow and studies it. Then he picks another one out of his ear._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): a fruit is the part of a plant that holds seeds  
> _Pumpkins are packed with seeds. So is a pumpkin a fruit or a vegetable?_  
> - ✅ A fruit, to a scientist. → Yes! To a botanist, a fruit is the part of a plant that grows from a flower and holds the seeds. So pumpkins, tomatoes and cucumbers are all fruits, even though we cook them like vegetables.
> - A vegetable. → In the kitchen, lots of people call it a vegetable, and that’s fine for cooking! But to a botanist, a fruit is the part that grows from a flower and holds the seeds. So a pumpkin is a fruit.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that to a scientist, a pumpkin is a fruit because it grows from a flower and holds seeds._

_The Nubbin looks back at the empty pumpkin. It was warm in there, and snug, and full of dinner._  
_Its bottom lip wobbles._  

#### `q23-complete`

_The Nubbin climbs straight back into the pumpkin. Head first, bottom up._  
_You and Mr. Tweed look at each other._  
_He lifts the pumpkin off and scoops it clean with a spoon from his top pocket. A butter knife from his sock cuts two neat eyeholes._  
_Then he cuts a round hole in the bottom for a neck, and pops it on the Nubbin like a hat._  
_It fits perfectly. The Nubbin turns slowly in a circle, delighted._  
_Then he tries one on himself, to show solidarity. It goes on with a squeak and a squash._  
_He walks into the fence post and says sorry to it. He walks into the scarecrow and shakes its hand._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): will it fit? comparing measurements  
> _Will it fit? The neck hole is 45 centimetres round. Mr. Tweed’s head is 57 centimetres round._  
> _How much too small is the hole?_  
> - ✅ 12 centimetres → Yes: 57 take away 45 is 12. That’s why it went on with a squash, and why it wouldn’t come off.
> - 22 centimetres → Let’s count on from 45. Add 10 to make 55, then 2 more to make 57. That’s 12 centimetres.
> - 102 centimetres → That’s the two added together. To find how much too small, take away: 57 take away 45 is 12.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted to find how much too small a hole was for a head, using centimetres._

**Mr. Tweed**: Mff.  
_It takes you, the Nubbin, a spoon and a firm tug on each ear to get it off._  
_He comes out orange to the eyebrows, and very dignified._  
_He gives you a third one: smaller, neater, with a curly stalk on top._  
_The Nubbin wears its pumpkin all afternoon, peering out of the eyeholes. Some creatures just like somewhere snug to be._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): knowing what makes you feel safe  
> _Some creatures just like somewhere snug to be._  
> _Where is your snug place? Why do you think snug places can feel safe?_  
> - Under a blanket. It feels like a hug. → Lovely. Being wrapped up can feel like a hug that lasts. Lots of people feel calmer that way.
> - Somewhere small, where nothing can sneak up. → That’s a clever thought. In a small space you can see everything around you, and that can feel safe.
> - I like big open spaces better. → That’s a fair answer too. Everyone is different. Some of us feel calm somewhere snug, and some under a big sky.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about a place that feels snug and safe, and why it might help._


### Glossary

- **concentration**: Thinking very hard about one thing and nothing else.
- **vine**: A long, bendy plant stem that creeps along the ground or climbs.
- **contented**: Happy and peaceful, not wanting anything more.
- **tempo**: The speed of the beat in a piece of music.
- **crescendo**: When music gets louder bit by bit.
- **botanist**: A scientist who studies plants.
- **solidarity**: Standing together with someone, to show you are on their side.
- **snug**: Warm, cosy and just the right size around you.

## Q24. The Exam

- `q24-s1`: Shuffle your Nubbin’s paper three times so Buttons can’t copy. · _When Buttons leans over, tap your Nubbin’s paper to slide it somewhere new. Three times does it._
- `q24-s2`: At break, help Buttons learn its shapes. Then make sure both Nubbins pass. · _Practise shapes with Buttons on the chalkboard, then let both Nubbins finish the test on their own._

#### `q24-desks`

**Mrs Inkwell**: Test day! Two Nubbins, two desks, one paper each. Shapes, colours and counting. No talking, please.  
_Your Nubbin takes the left desk. On the right sits Buttons, Mr. Tweed’s Nubbin, in a matching tweed waistcoat._  
_Mr. Tweed stands behind Buttons. He points at the paper, then at Buttons’ head, then makes a small, encouraging fist._  
**Mrs Inkwell**: Keepers may stay, but quietly. Very quietly. I am looking at you, Mr. Tweed.  
_He mimes zipping his lips shut, locking them, and posting the key into his pocket. Then he checks the pocket._  
_The test begins. Your Nubbin licks its pencil and draws a perfect circle._  
_Buttons draws nothing. Buttons leans very, very slowly to the left._  
_Behind Buttons, Mr. Tweed drops a pencil. He bends very slowly to pick it up, and reads your Nubbin’s paper upside down._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): why copying in a test isn’t fair  
> _Buttons wants to copy. Why isn’t copying in a test a good idea?_  
> - ✅ A test shows what each one knows, so the teacher can see who needs help. → Yes. If Buttons copies, Mrs Inkwell will think Buttons knows circles, and nobody will teach Buttons. Copying hides the help you need.
> - Because you might get caught. → That’s true: you might! But the bigger reason is this. A test shows the teacher what you need help with. If Buttons copies, nobody will know Buttons needs help with circles.
> - It’s fine if you’re friends. → Friends do help each other, and that’s lovely. But in a test, each one does their own work. That way the teacher can see who needs help. Helping comes afterwards.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that a test shows what each learner knows, so copying hides the help they need._


**Choices**

- **Nudge your Nubbin to cover its paper.**
    - Your Nubbin curls an arm round its work. Buttons leans further. Its chair creaks.
- **Let it look. Sharing is nice.**
    - **Mrs Inkwell**: Eyes on your own paper, please, Buttons.
    - Buttons sits bolt upright and tries to whistle innocently, which Nubbins cannot do.
- **Look at Mr. Tweed.**
    - Mr. Tweed is studying the ceiling, hands behind his back, with the face of a man who has never met Buttons.

#### `q24-shuffled`

_Buttons leans. Your Nubbin slides its paper to the right._  
_Buttons leans the other way. The paper slips under the desk._  
_Left, right, under the desk. Buttons follows the paper with its whole body._  
_On the third shuffle, Buttons falls off its chair._  
_Mr. Tweed, who has been leaning right along with Buttons, falls over too._  
_He stays on the floor and taps it with one knuckle, as if he came down to check the floorboards._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): working out a character’s feelings from actions  
> _Why does Mr. Tweed pretend to be checking the floor?_  
> - ✅ He’s embarrassed, and doesn’t want anyone to know he was leaning to look too. → Yes. Pretending to do something else is a way of hiding embarrassment. His actions give him away.
> - He really likes floors. → Ha! Maybe he does. But he only started after he fell. More likely he’s embarrassed, and hoping nobody noticed he was leaning to peek.
> - He hurt himself. → That’s a kind worry. But he’s tapping the floor, not rubbing a bump. He’s embarrassed, and pretending he meant to be down there.
> _For grown-ups: Used what a character does to work out a feeling he is trying to hide._

**Mrs Inkwell**: Buttons? Are you all right?  
_Buttons is fine. Buttons’ paper is still completely blank._  

#### `q24-break`

_Buttons climbs back onto its chair and looks at its blank paper. Its ears droop all the way down._  
_Behind it, Mr. Tweed’s ears somehow droop too._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Hnn…  
_He points at Buttons, then at the paper, then clasps his hands together, pleading._  
**Mrs Inkwell**: Pencils down, everyone. It’s break. You may help each other at break. That’s learning, not copying.  
**You**: Right, Buttons. Let’s start with a square. Four sides, all the same length.  
_You draw a square on the chalkboard. Buttons copies it. It has five sides, but it’s a start._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, ask): lines of symmetry in a square  
> _If you fold a paper square so both halves match exactly, the fold is a line of symmetry._  
> _How many lines of symmetry does a square have?_  
> - ✅ 4 → Yes: one up and down, one side to side, and two from corner to corner.
> - 2 → Good start: up and down, and side to side. But you can also fold it corner to corner, both ways. That makes 4.
> - 1 → There’s more than one! Up and down, side to side, and both corner-to-corner folds. That’s 4.
> _For grown-ups: Found all four lines of symmetry in a square: two straight across and two corner to corner._

_Buttons gazes up at you with the solemn trust of a creature that has never drawn a square._  

#### `q24-pass`

_Back at the desks, Buttons draws a square. It has four sides this time. Buttons counts them twice._  
_Then a triangle, then a circle, with its tongue poking out._  
_Your Nubbin finishes its paper and waits, swinging its legs._  
**Mrs Inkwell**: Two passes!  
**Mrs Inkwell**: Buttons, that is the roundest circle I have ever seen. It is very nearly a circle.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): being proud of effort  
> _Mrs Inkwell is honest: it isn’t a perfect circle. And she is kind: she praises how hard Buttons tried._  
> _This morning Buttons couldn’t draw a square. Now it can. That is something to be proud of._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that honest praise can be kind, and that effort is something to be proud of._

_Buttons holds its paper up to Mr. Tweed with both arms._  
_Mr. Tweed’s eyes go shiny. He blows his nose very loudly into a spotted handkerchief._  

#### `q24-complete`

_Mr. Tweed lifts Buttons into the air like a trophy and does a slow, silent lap of the classroom._  
**Mrs Inkwell**: Mr. Tweed. Please put the Nubbin down.  
_He puts Buttons down and shakes your hand. Then your Nubbin’s. Then Mrs Inkwell’s, who did not offer it._  
**Mrs Inkwell**: You know, these two learn better together. Bring them as a pair, and I’ll teach them both for one fee.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.D.8, ask): a two-step money problem with Shells  
> _A lesson costs 8 Shells for each Nubbin. Two lessons would cost 2 lots of 8._  
> _As a pair, they pay just one fee of 8 Shells. How many Shells do you save?_  
> - ✅ 8 Shells → Yes: 2 lots of 8 is 16. One fee is 8. And 16 take away 8 leaves 8 Shells saved.
> - 16 Shells → 16 is what two lessons would cost. But the pair pays only 8, so you save 16 take away 8, which is 8 Shells.
> - 4 Shells → Let’s go step by step. Two lessons: 8 and 8 makes 16. One fee: 8. 16 take away 8 is 8 Shells saved.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a two-step problem: found the cost of two lessons, then how much a shared fee saves._

_Buttons and your Nubbin are already sitting side by side, drawing circles on each other’s papers._  
_Mr. Tweed lingers. He looks at the little desks, then at Mrs Inkwell, and holds up one finger, hopefully._  
**Mrs Inkwell**: …One paper. Just the one.  
_He folds himself into the tiny desk, which takes some time. His knees end up near his ears._  
_He licks his pencil and draws a circle with his tongue out._  
_It is not a very good circle. He holds it up to Buttons anyway, both arms, and Buttons claps._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): cheering on someone else’s effort  
> _Mr. Tweed’s circle isn’t very good. But Buttons claps anyway. Why do you think that matters?_  
> - Because Mr. Tweed cheered for Buttons first. → That’s a sharp answer. Kindness often comes back round the same way it went out.
> - Because trying is what counts. → That’s a wise answer. It was hard for him, and he did it anyway, in front of everyone.
> - It doesn’t. It’s still a wobbly circle. → That’s honest! It is a wobbly circle. But the clap isn’t really for the circle. It’s for the person who was brave enough to draw it.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why it matters to cheer for someone’s effort, even when the result isn’t perfect._


### Glossary

- **encouraging**: Giving someone hope and confidence, so they want to keep trying.
- **innocently**: In a way that tries to look as if you have done nothing wrong.
- **embarrassed**: Feeling silly or awkward because of something others might have seen.
- **symmetry**: When one half of a shape is an exact mirror of the other half.
- **fee**: The money you pay for a service, like a lesson.

## Q25. The High Dive

- `q25-s1`: Get Mr. Tweed off the ledge: talk him down, or let a brave Swim Nubbin show him how. · _Call up to him with Talk to coax him down one step at a time, or take a strong swimmer to the ledge and tap Dive._
- `q25-s2`: Build a low diving board at the pond with Mr. Tweed. · _Set the plank on the flat rock at the pond’s edge, then hammer it in with three taps._

#### `q25-ledge`

_Mr. Tweed is at the waterfall in a striped bathing suit, doing warm-up stretches. Mostly with his eyebrows._  
_He points up at the high ledge beside the falls, then at himself, then mimes a perfect swallow dive._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Hup!  
_He climbs. It takes a while. Halfway up he stops to wave at you, and very nearly doesn’t start again._  
_At the top he walks to the edge, looks down, and turns into a statue._  
_A long time passes. A small bird lands on his head. He does not move._  
_A queue forms behind him: three small Nubbins, waiting politely for their turn._  
_One by one they squeeze between his ankles and dive. He watches each one go._  
_Then he looks at the water as if it has betrayed him._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Hnn.  
_Very carefully, without moving anything else, he mimes two fingers walking backwards. He would like to come down now._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): courage and changing your mind  
> _Mr. Tweed climbed all that way, and now he wants to come back down._  
> _Can it be brave to change your mind?_  
> - Yes. It takes courage to say “I’m not ready”. → That’s a wise answer. Doing something just because people are watching isn’t the same as being brave.
> - No. He should just jump. → That’s a fair thought: the Nubbins made it look easy! But everyone is ready at a different time. Coming down now and trying again later is a choice too.
> - It depends why he wants to come down. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Fear can be a useful warning. Listening to it, and then trying something smaller, can be clever.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether it can be brave to say “I’m not ready” and change your mind._


**Choices**

- **Talk him down, one step at a time.**
    - **You**: You’re fine! One foot back. Just one.
    - **Mr. Tweed**: Mm…
- **Ask a Swim Nubbin to show him how.**
    - Your Nubbin looks at the ledge, then at the water, then back at you, with growing delight.

#### `q25-down`

_Step by step, or splash by splash, Mr. Tweed gets off that ledge._  
_His first steps are tiny. He holds on to each rock as if it were a long-lost friend._  
_You call up to him after every step. Good. And another one. Breathe._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, do): slow breathing to calm a big feeling  
> _When we’re scared, our breathing goes fast and our muscles go stiff. That’s partly why Mr. Tweed froze._  
> _Slow breathing helps. Breathe in while you count to four, then out while you count to four._  
> _Do it three times, with Mr. Tweed. In, two, three, four. Out, two, three, four._  
> Check: `edu:breathe:slow:3`
> _For grown-ups: Practised slow counted breathing, a way to calm the body when feeling scared._

_The last bit is mostly sliding._  
_He lands in the shallows with a slap and sits up, dripping._  
_The bird is still on his head._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Mm!  

#### `q25-board`

_Back on dry land, Mr. Tweed dries off with a towel the size of a handkerchief._  
_He looks at the high ledge. Then he looks at the low, flat rock by the home pond._  
_He holds his hands a little apart. He mimes sawing, then hammering, then a gentle bounce._  
_A diving board: a low one._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): converting metres to centimetres  
> _The high ledge was 4 metres above the water. The new board will be just 40 centimetres._  
> _How many centimetres high was the ledge?_  
> - ✅ 400 centimetres → Yes: 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so 4 metres is 400 centimetres. That’s ten times higher than the new board!
> - 40 centimetres → 40 centimetres is the new board. The ledge was 4 metres, and each metre is 100 centimetres. So it’s 400.
> - 4 centimetres → 4 centimetres is shorter than your finger! Each metre is 100 centimetres, so 4 metres is 400 centimetres.
> _For grown-ups: Converted 4 metres into 400 centimetres, and compared it with a 40 cm board._

**Mr. Tweed**: Small.  
_Your Nubbin is already bouncing on the spot. It would like to go first._  
_Mr. Tweed pulls a plank from somewhere inside the towel and hands it to you._  
_You bend it over your knee. It bends, then springs straight back. Boing._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): a bent plank stores energy  
> _When you bend a springy plank, it stores energy. Let it go, and it pushes back as it straightens._  
> _That push is what bounces a diver up off a diving board._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a springy board stores energy when it bends and pushes back as it straightens._


#### `q25-complete`

_The diving board is low, springy and slightly crooked. It is perfect._  
_Your Nubbin goes first. Bounce, bounce, splash! It comes up grinning, and paddles back faster than before._  
_Then Mr. Tweed walks to the end and looks down at the water. It is about 30 centimetres below him._  
_He freezes._  
_You wait. Your Nubbin waits. The bird comes back and lands on his head again._  
_Then he holds his nose, shuts his eyes, and steps off like a man stepping off a kerb._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understanding a simile  
> _He steps off “like a man stepping off a kerb”. What does this simile tell you about the jump?_  
> - ✅ It was tiny and easy after all. → Yes. Stepping off a kerb is something you do every day without thinking. After all that fuss, the jump was that small.
> - He fell over. → He didn’t fall: he stepped! The simile compares the jump to stepping off a kerb. It was tiny and easy after all.
> - He was on a road. → Good noticing: a kerb is the edge of a pavement. Here the simile means the jump was as small as that one step.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile (“like a man stepping off a kerb”) tells us about how big the jump was._

**Mr. Tweed**: Ha!  
_He climbs out and does it again. And again. Nine more times._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): building courage in small steps  
> _Mr. Tweed didn’t beat his fear by jumping off the highest ledge. He started small, then did it again and again._  
> _Each time felt a little easier. Big brave things are often built out of lots of small brave things._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard how facing a fear in small, repeated steps makes it easier each time._

_The board is yours to keep. He will visit._  

### Glossary

- **statue**: A carved or cast figure of a person or animal that stands perfectly still.
- **betrayed**: Let down by someone you trusted.
- **shallows**: The part of the water that isn’t deep, near the edge.
- **kerb**: The raised edge of a pavement, next to the road.
- **crooked**: Bent, or not quite straight.

## Q26. The Park Bench Sandwich

- `q26-s1`: Hand Mr. Tweed the right things, in the right order, as he mimes for them. · _Watch his hands: a sawing mime means bread, a shake means pepper. Pass the wrong thing and he’ll hand it back politely._
- `q26-s2`: Spread the picnic blanket and share the sandwich with every Nubbin there. · _Lay the blanket on the grass by the bench, then tap each Nubbin on it and choose Feed._

#### `q26-bench`

_Mr. Tweed sits on the bench by the pond. It has a small brass plate with his name on._  
_He brought the plate himself, and screwed it on._  
_He opens his coat and begins unpacking lunch from places lunch should not be._  
_A whole loaf from his left sleeve. A lettuce from his inside pocket. A jar of jam from somewhere near his knee._  
_A tomato, a pepper pot, a pat of butter from his breast pocket, and a small, warm flask from under his hat._  
_He lines them all up along the bench and admires them. Then he spreads jam on the lettuce._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Hm?  
_He looks at the lettuce, then at the jam. Something has gone wrong, and he can’t say what._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, do): following instructions in order  
> _Instructions only work if you follow them in the right order. Mr. Tweed has jumped into the middle._  
> _Put the steps in order: bread, butter, lettuce, tomato, a shake of pepper, and bread on top._  
> _Words like first, next, then and last help us keep steps in the right order._  
> Check: `edu:order:sandwich-steps:6`
> _For grown-ups: Put six sandwich-making steps in order and used sequence words: first, next, then, last._

_Your Nubbin climbs up beside him, very interested in the jam._  

**Choices**

- **Offer to pass him things.**
    - He nods gravely and holds out one hand, palm up, like a surgeon waiting for a tool.
- **Try a bite of the jam lettuce.**
    - It is crunchy, sweet and wrong. Mr. Tweed watches your face closely, then nods. Wrong. He knew it.
- **Let your Nubbin have the jam.**
    - Your Nubbin puts its whole face in the jar. Mr. Tweed produces a second jar from his other knee.

#### `q26-sandwich`

_Bread first. Next, butter. Then lettuce, then tomato._  
_A shake of pepper. Last of all, bread on top. Pat, pat._  
_Mr. Tweed holds the finished sandwich up to the light, like a jeweller checking a diamond._  
_A duck lands on the bench. It looks at the sandwich. Then it looks at Mr. Tweed._  
_A long, silent negotiation takes place._  
_The duck leaves with the jam lettuce. Mr. Tweed lets it go. He never trusted the jam lettuce._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-LS1-1, notice): what ducks need to eat  
> _Here’s a surprise: lettuce is a better snack for ducks than bread. Torn leafy greens, peas and oats are all good duck food._  
> _Bread fills ducks up without giving their bodies what they need. The jam, though, was not a good idea._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that leafy greens, peas and oats are better food for ducks than bread._

**Mr. Tweed**: Ahh.  

#### `q26-share`

_He is about to take the first bite when he notices: you have no sandwich. Your Nubbin has no sandwich._  
_Five wild Nubbins have gathered quietly behind the bench. They have no sandwich either._  
_Mr. Tweed looks at his sandwich, then at all of them. He sighs a sigh from the bottom of his boots._  
_He takes a ruler from his coat, because of course he has a ruler._  
_The sandwich is 16 centimetres long and 8 centimetres wide. He cuts it into exact squares, 4 centimetres on each side._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.C.7, ask): counting squares in rows and columns (area)  
> _16 centimetres long makes 4 squares along. 8 centimetres wide makes 2 squares down._  
> _How many squares are there altogether?_  
> - ✅ 8 → Yes: 2 rows of 4 is 8. Now count the eaters: you, your Nubbin, Mr. Tweed and five wild Nubbins. That’s 8. Exactly one square each!
> - 6 → Let’s count the rows. The top row has 4 squares, and so does the bottom row. 4 and 4 makes 8.
> - 12 → That’s 4 and 8 added together. But we want rows of squares: 2 rows of 4 is 8 squares.
> _For grown-ups: Found the number of equal squares in a rectangle by multiplying rows by columns._

_He points at a flat patch of grass, then flaps an imaginary cloth._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Picnic.  
_He pulls a checked blanket out of his coat. It is bigger than the coat._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Eco.1.K-2, notice): scarcity means choosing  
> _One sandwich, eight hungry mouths. When there isn’t enough of something for everyone to have lots, we have to choose._  
> _Mr. Tweed chose small, equal shares, so that nobody goes without._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard that when there isn’t enough for everyone to have lots, people have to choose how to share._


#### `q26-complete`

_Everyone gets a square._  
_Mr. Tweed takes the last one, which is mostly crust, and eats it as if it were cake._  
_The brass plate on the bench has only ever had one name on it._  
_It is the first time in years he has needed the ruler._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): why sharing can feel good  
> _Mr. Tweed got the smallest, crustiest piece. Yet he looks happier than he did with the whole sandwich._  
> _Why do you think that is?_  
> - Sharing feels good. → That’s a lovely answer. Giving can feel even better than getting.
> - He isn’t eating on his own any more. → That’s a thoughtful answer. A crust with friends might taste better than a whole sandwich by yourself.
> - He just really likes crusts. → Ha! Maybe he does. Some people do. But look at his face. It might not only be about the crust.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why someone might be happier with a small shared piece than a whole thing eaten alone._

_The Nubbins lie in a sleepy pile on the blanket: sticky, full and very happy._  
_Mr. Tweed goes to fold the blanket. He looks at the pile of sleeping Nubbins, and quietly leaves it where it is._  
_He tips his hat to you. The blanket is yours now. The Nubbins have decided._  

### Glossary

- **admires**: Looks at something and thinks how good it is.
- **surgeon**: A doctor who does operations, and is handed tools by a helper.
- **jeweller**: Someone who makes, mends or sells rings, necklaces and precious stones.
- **negotiation**: A talk where two sides try to agree on a deal.
- **imaginary**: Not real; only pictured in your mind.

## Q27. The Ruined Portrait

- `q27-s1`: Bring three Nubbins into the hall and line them up like the Nubbins in the portrait. · _Carry or call Nubbins into the hall. Mr. Tweed’s chalk crosses on the floor show where each one sits._
- `q27-s2`: Take a Photo mode picture that matches the Founders’ Portrait. · _Use the self-timer in Photo mode and sit in the empty chair. The outline turns green when everyone’s pose lines up._
- `q27-s3`: Hang the frame back on its hook before the Warden walks in. · _Tap the hook to hang the frame, then tap it again to straighten it. Two quick taps._

#### `q27-hall`

_The Keepers’ Hall smells of floor polish. On the far wall hangs the Founders’ Portrait: two serious old Keepers and three Nubbins._  
**Warden Pryce**: Mr. Tweed is cleaning the portrait today. Supervised. I’ll be back within the hour. Touch nothing but the frame.  
_The Warden leaves. The hall clock says quarter past two._  
_Mr. Tweed bows to the portrait and dabs it with a wet cloth. His nose begins to twitch._  
_He holds the twitch in. Then he holds it in harder. His face goes through every colour._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Hah… hah…  
_The sneeze is enormous. The wet cloth flies out of his hand and lands across both founders._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): why we sneeze, and catching sneezes  
> _Dust and strong smells, like polish, can tickle the inside of your nose. A sneeze blows them out, very fast._  
> _A sneeze sprays tiny droplets a long way. Catch it in a tissue or your elbow. Not on a painting._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sneezes clear dust from the nose and spray droplets, so we catch them in a tissue or elbow._

_When he peels it off, the founders have smudged into one very wide founder with four ears._  
_He dabs at it with his handkerchief. Now there is a nose where one of the ears was._  
_He tries the pencil from behind his ear. The founder now has spectacles, and a look of total surprise._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Oh.  
_He looks at the door, then at the clock. Then he looks at you, and mimes a small, desperate prayer._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): working out a time one hour later  
> _The Warden left at quarter past two. She said she’d be back within the hour. By what time will she be back?_  
> - ✅ Quarter past three → Yes. One hour after quarter past two is quarter past three. The minute hand goes all the way round once.
> - Half past two → That’s only 15 minutes later! One hour means the minute hand goes all the way round. Quarter past three.
> - Quarter past four → That would be two hours. One hour after quarter past two is quarter past three.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the time one hour after quarter past two._


**Choices**

- **We can fix this. Probably.**
    - He grips your hand gratefully, and gets cleaning fluid all over it.
- **We should tell the Warden.**
    - He nods slowly. Then he points at the clock, the portrait and you. Try first, then tell.

#### `q27-lined`

_Mr. Tweed draws a plan on the floor in chalk: two chairs, three Nubbins, one camera. Yours._  
_He draws a little cross for each Nubbin to sit on, and numbers them 1, 2 and 3 in very neat handwriting._  
_You bring in three Nubbins. Getting them onto the crosses takes a while._  
_One sits on cross 2. One sits on cross 3, facing the wrong way._  
_One is asleep on cross 1, and has been since before you arrived._  

> **Lesson** (art, do): composition: planning where everyone goes in a picture  
> _Painters plan where everyone goes before they start. This plan is called the composition._  
> _In the Founders’ Portrait, the tall Keepers sit at the back and the small Nubbins sit in front, so every face can be seen._  
> _Match the portrait: turn the backwards Nubbin round, so all three faces show._  
> Check: `edu:place:nubbins:chalk-marks:3`
> _For grown-ups: Learned that artists plan a picture’s composition so every face can be seen, and arranged the Nubbins to match._

_Three Nubbins in a row, more or less._  
_Mr. Tweed looks from the portrait to the Nubbins and back again, and gives a small, satisfied nod._  

#### `q27-pose`

_Mr. Tweed hangs a dark curtain behind the Nubbins and drags two chairs into place, just like the portrait._  
_He sticks on a grey moustache and offers you one. It is the same moustache: he has torn it in half._  
_He sits, rests one hand on his knee, and gazes into the distance with the face of a founder._  
_The Nubbins copy him. All three gaze into the distance. One falls asleep doing it._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Shh.  
_He nods at your camera, then the portrait, then holds up one finger. One go. The clock is ticking._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-2, notice): cameras catch light  
> _A painter makes a portrait slowly, by hand, with brushes and paint. It can take weeks._  
> _A camera catches light. Press the button, and it lets light in through the lens for a moment. That light makes the picture._  
> _That’s why the hall needs to be bright, and why everyone must hold still while it happens._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a painting is made slowly by hand, but a camera makes a picture by catching light._

**You**: Everybody look at the lens, and hold still…  

#### `q27-shot`

_Click._  
_You all wait while the picture slides slowly out of the camera._  
_It shows two stern founders and three Nubbins in front of a dark curtain._  
_It is dignified. It is serious. It is very nearly right._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): multiple-meaning words: stern  
> _The founders look “stern”. What does “stern” mean here?_  
> - ✅ Serious and strict-looking → Yes. A stern face doesn’t smile much. It looks as if it’s about to say “Sit up straight.”
> - Very old → They are old! But “stern” is about how they look: serious and strict.
> - The back of a boat → Good thinking! “Stern” really is the back of a boat. It’s a word with two meanings. Here, in a picture of faces, it means serious and strict-looking.
> _For grown-ups: Used context to choose the right meaning of “stern”, a word with more than one meaning._

_One Nubbin is yawning. But if you squint, so was one in the original._  
_Mr. Tweed holds the photo next to the portrait and squints at both, one eye at a time._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Mm!  

#### `q27-swap`

_Footsteps in the corridor. The Warden is early._  
_Mr. Tweed lifts the frame down, slides the smudged canvas out, and hides it up the back of his jacket._  
_You slot the photo into the frame. It is slightly too small._  
_Mr. Tweed stuffs the gaps with his handkerchief._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): finding a gap by subtracting  
> _The opening in the frame is 40 centimetres wide. The photo is 36 centimetres wide._  
> _How wide is the gap?_  
> - ✅ 4 centimetres → Yes: 40 take away 36 is 4. With the photo in the middle, that’s 2 centimetres each side. Just right for a handkerchief.
> - 6 centimetres → Nearly! Count on from 36: 37, 38, 39, 40. That’s 4 centimetres.
> - 76 centimetres → That’s the two widths added together. To find the gap, take away: 40 take away 36 is 4 centimetres.
> _For grown-ups: Subtracted two widths to find a gap, then halved it for each side._

_He hangs it. It is crooked. He straightens it, and the other side drops._  
_He straightens that, and the first side drops._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Quick!  
_The footsteps stop outside the door._  
_The door handle begins, very slowly, to turn._  

#### `q27-complete`

_The Warden walks in and looks at the portrait for a long, long time._  
**Warden Pryce**: It looks… brighter. Younger, somehow. That founder has your chin.  
_Mr. Tweed studies the ceiling. Half a grey moustache is still stuck to his lip._  
_Behind his back, he presses a stack of spare frames into your hands._  
_He mimes: your photos, your walls._  
_The Warden is still looking. You could tell her the truth. Or you could say nothing at all._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): owning up to an accident  
> _The painting is ruined, and the Warden may never find out._  
> _Should you tell her what really happened?_  
> - Yes. Telling the truth is right, even when it’s awkward. → That’s a brave answer. Owning up can feel scary. But it means nobody is fooled, and people know they can trust you.
> - No. It was an accident, and the photo is lovely. → That’s an honest answer: it was an accident, and the photo is lovely. But the Warden thinks she’s looking at the old painting. Is it fair to let her believe that? Something to think about.
> - Tell her, and explain it was an accident. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Accidents happen to everyone. Saying what happened, and that you tried to fix it, is often best.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether to own up to an accident when nobody would ever find out._


**Choices**

- **It’s a photo. There was a sneeze.**
    - **Warden Pryce**: A sneeze. Of course there was.
    - **Warden Pryce**: Honestly? I prefer this one. The old one always looked cross. It stays.
    - Mr. Tweed quietly pulls the canvas out of his jacket and hands it over, rolled up like a newspaper.
    - He looks lighter, somehow. Secrets are heavy things to carry up the back of a jacket.
- **Say nothing. Admire it.**
    - **Warden Pryce**: Well. Keep up the good work, both of you.
    - As the door closes behind her, Mr. Tweed breathes out for the first time in an hour.
    - The real painting is still rolled up in his jacket. Neither of you mentions it on the way out.

### Glossary

- **portrait**: A painting, drawing or photo of a person, or of a group of people.
- **founders**: The people who first started something, like a club, a town or a hall.
- **composition**: How the things in a picture are arranged.
- **lens**: A curved piece of glass that bends light, like the one in a camera or in glasses.
- **stern**: Serious and strict-looking. (It is also the back end of a boat.)
- **squint**: To look with your eyes partly closed.
- **corridor**: A long passage inside a building, with doors along it.
- **canvas**: Strong cloth that artists paint on.

## Q28. Do-It-Yourself

- `q28-s1`: Carry every Nubbin, and anything precious, out of Mr. Tweed’s cottage. · _Three Nubbins are napping inside, and his bear is on the mantelpiece. Carry each one out to the garden._
- `q28-s2`: Stand well back, behind the garden hedge, before the fuse runs out. · _Run to the far side of the hedge. The closer you stand, the yellower you get._

#### `q28-plan`

_Mr. Tweed’s front room is the colour of old porridge._  
_He stands in the middle of it with a tin of yellow paint and a very small brush._  
_On the mantelpiece stands a card in his best handwriting: TEA. SATURDAY. EVERYONE. It isn’t addressed to anyone._  
_He paints one stroke and steps back. He looks at four walls, a ceiling, and his one stroke._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.C.7, ask): area of a rectangle by multiplying  
> _One wall is 4 metres long and 2 metres high._  
> _How many square metres of wall is that?_  
> - ✅ 8 square metres → Yes: 2 rows of 4 square metres is 8. Four walls like that make 32 square metres. That’s a lot of tiny strokes.
> - 6 square metres → That’s 4 add 2. For area, multiply: 2 rows of 4 square metres makes 8 square metres.
> - 12 metres → That’s the perimeter: the distance all the way round the edge. The area inside is 4 times 2, which is 8 square metres.
> _For grown-ups: Found the area of a wall by multiplying its length by its height, and told area apart from perimeter._

_He tapes the brush to a broom. He paints the ceiling, the lampshade, a sleeping Nubbin and, briefly, himself._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Hnn.  
_He puts down the broom and picks up a firework from the mantelpiece. A light comes on behind his eyes._  
_He mimes it: firework in the tin, light it, run. Then a big BOOM with both hands, and paint landing everywhere, beautifully._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Boom.  
_He looks at you for approval. Your Nubbin is already hiding behind your legs._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): firework safety  
> _In real life, fireworks are only lit by grown-ups who know how, outdoors, following the instructions on the box._  
> _Everyone else stands well back. Never indoors, and never in a paint tin._  
> _Mr. Tweed’s plan breaks nearly every rule. That’s why the first job is getting everyone out._  
> _For grown-ups: Heard the real rules for fireworks: only grown-ups who know how, outdoors, following the instructions, with everyone else well back._


**Choices**

- **Absolutely not.**
    - He nods sympathetically and keeps unwrapping the firework.
    - Then he mimes carrying Nubbins out of the door. He has heard you: safety first, then boom.
- **Fine. But everyone goes outside first.**
    - He shakes your hand firmly. Then he points at your Nubbin, the door, and his eyebrows. He’d like to keep those too.
- **Can I light it?**
    - He looks at you very seriously and points to himself: his house, his firework. You may stand well back.

#### `q28-cleared`

_One by one you carry the sleepy Nubbins out into the garden. None of them wakes up._  
_Three Nubbins lie on the lawn now. One of them has a yellow stripe._  

> **Lesson** (art, notice): primary colours in paint  
> _Yellow is a primary colour in paint. You can’t make it by mixing other paints together._  
> _But you can mix it with others. Yellow and blue make green. Yellow and red make orange._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that yellow is a primary colour in paint, and what it makes when mixed with blue or red._

_Last of all, Mr. Tweed’s bear, from the mantelpiece. You prop it on the gate post, where it can supervise._  
_The front room is empty except for Mr. Tweed, the paint and the firework._  
_He tucks his trousers into his socks. This is his idea of protective clothing._  
_He gives you a thumbs up. You give him a long look._  

#### `q28-fuse`

_Mr. Tweed stands the firework in the paint tin, lights the fuse, and gazes at it with pride._  
_The fuse fizzes and crackles. He watches it fizz._  
_He keeps watching it fizz._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.1.4, ask): sound words (onomatopoeia)  
> _“Fizz” sounds like the noise it names. Words like that are called onomatopoeia._  
> _Which of these is a sound word too?_  
> - ✅ Crackle → Yes. Say it out loud: crackle. It sounds just like a fuse burning.
> - Fuse → A fuse makes a noise, but “fuse” doesn’t sound like one. “Crackle” does: say it out loud.
> - Yellow → Yellow is a colour word, not a sound word. “Crackle” sounds like the noise it names.
> _For grown-ups: Recognised words that sound like the noise they name, such as “fizz” and “crackle”._

_You wave at him through the window. He waves back, cheerfully._  
_You point at the fuse. He looks at the fuse. Then at you. Then at the door._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Oh!  
_He runs, and you run. Your Nubbin is somehow already behind the far hedge._  

#### `q28-complete`

_FWUMP. Every window goes yellow at once. The chimney puffs out a small yellow cloud._  
_You creep back and look inside. Walls, ceiling, floor, clock: all yellow. It is, honestly, a good job._  
_There is one perfect porridge-coloured rectangle on the wall, where the picture hung._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): objects block things that travel outwards, like a shadow  
> _Why is there a porridge-coloured rectangle where the picture was?_  
> - ✅ The picture was in the way, so no paint landed behind it. → Yes. The paint flew outwards from the tin, and the picture blocked it. It’s a bit like a shadow. Something in the way of light leaves a dark shape behind it.
> - He painted carefully round it. → He was busy running! The picture blocked the flying paint, a bit like an object blocks light to make a shadow.
> - Yellow paint doesn’t stick there. → It stuck everywhere else! The picture was in the way of the flying paint, so none reached the wall behind it.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a paint-free patch by comparing it to a shadow: something in the way blocks what travels towards it._

_A single drop falls from the lampshade onto Mr. Tweed’s head. He doesn’t notice. He is far too happy._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Ha!  
_He hands you a wide, flat brush and mimes one huge swish over the whole garden path. Big jobs, one go._  
_Then he mimes the firework, and shakes his head very firmly. The brush, yes. The boom, no._  
_On the way home, you mention the card on his mantelpiece to a few neighbours. They mention it to a few more._  
_On Saturday the yellow room is full of people, and Mr. Tweed has no idea where to put himself._  
_He ends up in the doorway holding the teapot, beaming at everyone. He forgets to pour anybody tea for nearly an hour._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): understanding shyness and loneliness  
> _Mr. Tweed wrote “TEA. SATURDAY. EVERYONE.” But he never gave the card to anyone._  
> _Why might someone find it hard to invite people?_  
> - They might be scared nobody will come. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Asking can feel risky: what if nobody says yes? That’s why it means so much when people do.
> - They might be shy. → That’s a kind answer. Shy people often want company just as much as anyone. The first step is just harder.
> - I don’t think it’s hard. → That’s great, if it feels easy for you! For some people it’s one of the hardest things. You could be the one who helps.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why inviting people can feel hard, and how others can help someone who is lonely._


### Glossary

- **mantelpiece**: The shelf above a fireplace.
- **approval**: Someone showing they think what you are doing is good.
- **supervise**: To watch over something to make sure it goes well.
- **protective**: Keeping you safe from harm.
- **fuse**: A string that burns slowly, to light a firework from a safe distance.
- **beaming**: Smiling a big, bright, happy smile.

## Q29. Mind the Egg

- `q29-s1`: Put Odette’s egg down somewhere flat in your garden. · _Set the egg on flat ground near your cottage. Not on the slope. Definitely not on the slope._
- `q29-s2`: Catch the runaway egg before it reaches the stream. · _Get ahead of it and wait on the path: tapping it from behind only makes it faster. Mr. Tweed’s hat counts as a catch._
- `q29-s3`: Give the egg back to Odette at the gate, safe and sound. · _Odette waits at your gate at sunset. Carry the egg to her and choose Give._

#### `q29-handover`

**Odette Pennant**: Hello! You must be Hazel’s grandchild. I’m Odette, from over the ridge. I hear you’re good with eggs.  
**Odette Pennant**: I’ve an appointment in the village this afternoon, and eggs aren’t allowed in the waiting room. Silly rule. Would you mind this one?  
_She puts a speckled egg in your hands. It is warm, and rounder on one side than eggs usually are._  
**Odette Pennant**: It’s an easy egg. It just likes to roll. Keep it on something flat and it’s no trouble at all. Back by sunset!  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-LS1-2, notice): parents keep eggs warm  
> _Many bird parents sit on their eggs to keep them warm. In lots of kinds of bird, both parents take turns._  
> _Warmth helps the baby inside to grow. A warm egg is a precious thing to be trusted with._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many bird parents sit on their eggs to keep them warm so the baby inside can grow._

_She waves and goes. The egg sits in your palm, perfectly still._  
_The moment you look away, it wobbles._  
_Mr. Tweed leans over the fence and looks at the egg. He mimes rocking a baby. Then he mimes it rolling away._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Hm.  

**Choices**

- **I’ll guard it with my life.**
    - Mr. Tweed nods gravely and salutes the egg. The egg wobbles.
- **Mr. Tweed, could you help?**
    - He points at himself, startled. Then he takes off his hat and holds it out like a nest. He is ready.

#### `q29-roll`

_You choose a flat spot in your garden and set the egg down. It sits. It considers._  
_Mr. Tweed lies flat on the grass and shuts one eye. He is checking whether the ground is level._  
_He squints along the grass one way, then the other._  
_It is level. He gives the egg a thumbs up._  
_The egg sits perfectly still._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): balanced forces on level ground  
> _Why does a round egg stay still on level ground, but roll away on a slope?_  
> - ✅ On level ground there’s no downhill for gravity to pull it towards. → Yes. On level ground the pushes and pulls on the egg are balanced, so it stays put. Tip the ground, or give it a nudge, and it’s off.
> - The egg gets tired on flat ground. → Ha! Eggs don’t get tired. On level ground gravity pulls straight down, so the egg has no downhill to roll towards.
> - Flat ground is sticky. → Grass does grip a little. But the big reason is gravity: on level ground, there’s no downhill for it to pull the egg towards.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that a round object stays still on level ground but rolls on a slope, because of gravity._

_Somewhere nearby, a Nubbin sneezes._  
_The egg sets off._  

#### `q29-chase`

_The egg rolls down the garden path, gathering speed and looking, somehow, delighted._  
_It bumps off a fence post and takes the left fork, towards the bridge._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions: left and right facing north  
> _The garden path runs north. The egg takes the left fork. If you face north, which way is left?_  
> - ✅ West → Yes. Face north, and west is on your left and east is on your right. To remember the order going round clockwise, try: Never Eat Shredded Wheat. North, east, south, west.
> - East → East is on your right when you face north. Your left is west.
> - South → South is behind you when you face north. Your left is west, and your right is east.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out that when you face north, west is on your left and east is on your right._

_Mr. Tweed vaults the fence, mostly, and sets off after it, holding his hat out in front of him._  
**Mr. Tweed**: Egg!  
_It rattles over the bridge and past the dojo, where three karate Nubbins bow to it as it goes by._  
_Mr. Tweed takes a shortcut through a hedge. He comes out ahead of the egg, wearing most of the hedge._  
_Beyond the dojo is the stream. You would rather not find out whether this egg can swim._  

#### `q29-caught`

_You dive. Mr. Tweed dives._  
_The egg bounces off your hands, then off his head, and lands neatly in his hat._  
_For a moment, nobody moves._  
_Then Mr. Tweed holds the hat up high, muddy and triumphant._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): teamwork  
> _Neither of you could have caught it alone. Your hands slowed it down, and his hat caught it._  
> _That’s teamwork: each person does their part, and together it works._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how two people each doing their part achieved something neither could do alone._

**Mr. Tweed**: Ha!  
_The egg sits in the hat and wobbles, very slightly. It looks as if it enjoyed that._  

#### `q29-afternoon`

_For the rest of the afternoon, nobody puts the egg down._  
_Mr. Tweed knits it a little woolly cosy with a hole for the top. It is lumpy. The egg seems to like it._  
_You line an old fruit box with a blanket and put it on wheels._  
_Then you wedge a stone against the wheels at each end, for brakes._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): how a wedge works as a brake  
> _Why do the stones stop the box from rolling away?_  
> - ✅ They press against the wheels, so the wheels can’t turn. → Yes. A wedge jammed against a wheel pushes back on it. The pushes balance, and the box stays put.
> - They make the box heavier. → The stones aren’t in the box, though! They’re jammed against the wheels, pushing back, so the wheels can’t turn.
> - The egg cosy holds it still. → The cosy is very good at being lumpy, but not at holding things still! The stones push against the wheels so they can’t turn.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that a wedge pressed against a wheel pushes back on it, so the wheel can’t turn._

_The egg wobbles once, tries the box, and decides to stay._  
_There is room in the box for two. Your own eggs look at it with interest._  
_As the sun goes down, Odette comes back over the ridge._  

#### `q29-complete`

**Odette Pennant**: There it is, safe and sound. And wearing a jumper!  
_Mr. Tweed bows modestly. The cosy has his initial knitted on it, a T. Upside down._  
_You tilt your head to read it. It looks like a lamp post standing on a pavement._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.G.A.3, ask): lines of symmetry in letters  
> _Upside down, Mr. Tweed’s T turned into a lamp post._  
> _Which of these letters would look exactly the same knitted upside down?_  
> - ✅ H → Yes. An H has a line of symmetry straight across the middle. Flip it top to bottom and it matches itself. Nobody would ever know. Except Mr. Tweed.
> - T → That’s the one he tried! A T’s only line of symmetry runs up and down, so upside down it turns into a lamp post. An H has a line of symmetry straight across the middle, so it matches itself upside down.
> - R → An R has no line of symmetry at all, so upside down it looks very odd indeed. An H has a line of symmetry straight across the middle, so it matches itself upside down.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that an H looks the same flipped top to bottom because it has a line of symmetry straight across the middle, and a T does not._

**Odette Pennant**: Keep the cosy, it suits your eggs. And keep that box. Two eggs side by side, on wheels? That’s a pram, that is.  
_She slips the cosy off and hands it back to you. Mr. Tweed passes her the egg last of all._  
_He holds on a moment longer than he needs to, pats it twice, and lets go. She tucks it into her basket._  
**Odette Pennant**: So. Was it good?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): honesty when someone trusts you  
> _Odette asks if it was good. The egg did go rolling off, but it’s safe now. What would you tell her?_  
> - Tell her it went for a roll. → That’s an honest answer. Odette trusted you, and the truth helps her know her egg better.
> - Say it was perfect. It’s safe now, after all. → That’s a kind thought: you don’t want to worry her, and the egg is safe. But she might like to know her egg is a roller. Something to think about.
> - Tell her, and tell her the funny bits too. → That’s a great answer. The truth can be told kindly, and even with a laugh.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to answer honestly and kindly when someone who trusted you asks how it went._


**Choices**

- **It went for a little roll.**
    - **Odette Pennant**: They always do. That’s why I asked a good Keeper and not the waiting room.
- **A perfect angel.**
    - Behind you, Mr. Tweed slowly picks a twig out of his hair.
    - Odette notices. Odette, kindly, says nothing. But she glances at the twig, and then at you.

### Glossary

- **appointment**: A time you have agreed to meet someone, like a doctor.
- **speckled**: Covered in lots of tiny spots.
- **level**: Perfectly flat, with no slope either way.
- **fork**: A place where a path splits into two. (It is also something you eat with.)
- **vaults**: Jumps over something, often pushing off with the hands.
- **triumphant**: Full of joy and pride after winning or succeeding.
- **wedge**: To jam something tightly into a space so it holds firm.
- **initial**: The first letter of a name.

## Q30. The Three-Wheeler

- `q30-s1`: Meet Rufus at the start line and enter the ridge race in your hand cart. · _Ride your hand cart to the start line on the ridge track, and talk to Rufus._
- `q30-s2`: Win the race. Each time you draw level with the Bluebell on a bend, it tips over: make that happen three times. · _Draw level with the Bluebell on a bend and Mr. Tweed will wave. Do it three times, then cross the line first._

#### `q30-meet`

_A bright blue three-wheeled cart rattles up the lane. It has one wheel at the front and a great deal of confidence._  
**Rufus Crankshaw**: Afternoon! Rufus Crankshaw. And this is the Bluebell. Fastest three wheels this side of the ridge.  
_Mr. Tweed is riding in the back of your hand cart, the one he gave you. He looks at the Bluebell’s single front wheel._  
_He smiles a very small smile._  
**Rufus Crankshaw**: Is that a race face? That’s a race face. One lap of the ridge track. Winner gets bragging rights.  
_Mr. Tweed points forward like a ship’s captain. Then he holds up three fingers and tips his flat hand gently onto its side._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): why a narrow base tips more easily  
> _Mr. Tweed thinks the Bluebell will tip over three times. Why might a cart with one front wheel tip on a bend?_  
> - ✅ Its wheels make a narrow triangle, so its weight can lean out past the edge. → Yes. Join up the three wheels and you get a triangle, narrow at the front. On a bend, the weight swings outwards. If it leans past the edge of that triangle, over it goes.
> - Blue carts are tippy. → Ha! Colour makes no difference. It’s the narrow triangle of wheels: on a bend, the weight can lean past its edge.
> - Three is an unlucky number. → Numbers can’t be lucky or unlucky! It’s the narrow triangle of wheels. On a bend, the weight can lean out past its edge.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that a three-wheeled cart’s narrow triangle of wheels lets its weight lean past the edge on a bend._

**Mr. Tweed**: Three.  

**Choices**

- **You’re on.**
    - **Rufus Crankshaw**: Splendid! Mind your wheels. All four of them, show-off.
- **Is the Bluebell… stable?**
    - **Rufus Crankshaw**: Stable as a table! A three-legged table, which is the steadiest kind. Ask anyone.
    - Behind him, the Bluebell tips gently onto its side, all by itself.
    - **Rufus Crankshaw**: …It does that.
    - Rufus is half right. Three legs never wobble on bumpy ground. But a narrow base can still tip over sideways.

#### `q30-grid`

_Two carts on the start line._  
_Rufus revs the Bluebell by saying “brrm” quite loudly._  
_Mr. Tweed climbs out and polishes the front of your cart with his sleeve._  
_Then he walks over and polishes the front of the Bluebell too, just as carefully._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): fairness: treating both sides the same  
> _Why does Mr. Tweed polish the Bluebell too?_  
> - ✅ To be fair: both carts get the same. → Yes. A fair race starts with both sides treated the same. Then whoever wins, wins properly.
> - He just likes polishing. → He probably does! But he did it just as carefully as yours. He wants both carts treated the same, and that’s fair.
> - To trick Rufus. → Good suspicious thinking! But a shiny front doesn’t slow anyone down. He’s treating both carts the same, to be fair.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that a fair contest starts with both sides treated the same._

**Rufus Crankshaw**: Very sporting of you!  
_Mr. Tweed climbs back in, folds his hands, and nods. Now it’s a race._  

#### `q30-race`

_The flag drops. Rufus shoots off the line, waving._  
_In the back of your cart, Mr. Tweed points at the Bluebell, then at a gap on the inside of the bend._  
_Every time you draw level, he leans out and gives Rufus a cheerful little wave._  
_Every time, Rufus waves back. The Bluebell leans, and leans, and gently tips over._  
**Rufus Crankshaw**: Not to worry! It does that!  
_He rights it with one hand and is off again. He is very, very good at righting it._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): adding time across a minute  
> _Each tip costs Rufus 2 seconds. Without tipping, his lap would take 3 minutes 58 seconds._  
> _After three tips, what is his time?_  
> - ✅ 4 minutes 4 seconds → Yes. Three tips cost 6 seconds. 3 minutes 58 seconds and 2 more makes 4 minutes. Then 4 more: 4 minutes 4 seconds.
> - 3 minutes 64 seconds → Good adding! But 60 seconds make a minute, so 3 minutes 64 seconds is really 4 minutes 4 seconds.
> - 4 minutes 0 seconds → That’s just one tip: 2 seconds. Three tips is 6 seconds, which takes him to 4 minutes 4 seconds.
> _For grown-ups: Added seconds to a lap time and crossed into the next minute, knowing 60 seconds make 1 minute._

**Mr. Tweed**: Ha!  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): what makes a win fair  
> _Is it fair to win because the Bluebell keeps tipping over whenever Rufus waves?_  
> - No. We should win fairly. → That’s a fair-minded answer. A win feels best when you know you earned it.
> - Yes. Rufus chooses to wave. → That’s a thoughtful point. Nobody is tricking him: he waves at everyone. Maybe the real problem is his cart.
> - It’s fine, because everyone is having fun. → That’s a lovely way to see it. Rufus is laughing more than anybody. Sometimes how you play matters more than who wins.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a win is fair when the other side keeps having bad luck, and why it matters._


**Choices**

- **Tell Mr. Tweed to stop waving. Win it fair.**
    - Mr. Tweed looks wounded, and sits on his hands.
    - On the next bend Rufus draws level, sees you, and waves anyway. The Bluebell tips over.
    - **Rufus Crankshaw**: Not to worry! I just like waving!
    - Mr. Tweed slowly takes his hands out from under him. It was never his fault. He looks enormously relieved.
- **Let him wave. It’s only friendly.**
    - Mr. Tweed waves so warmly that a Nubbin on the verge waves back, and also tips over.

#### `q30-complete`

_You cross the line first. The Bluebell crosses second, on its side, sliding._  
**Rufus Crankshaw**: Ha! What a race! Three tips! That’s a personal best. Or worst. One of those.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): being a good sport  
> _Rufus lost, and he’s laughing. That’s being a good sport._  
> _You try your hardest, you shake hands at the end, and you enjoy the game, whoever wins._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed what being a good sport looks like: trying hard, shaking hands and enjoying the game whoever wins._

_Mr. Tweed shakes his hand. Rufus shakes back so hard that the Bluebell, parked, tips over again._  
**Rufus Crankshaw**: Tell you what. I’ve an old one at home. Smaller. Tips if you breathe near it. Your Nubbins would love it.  
_Next morning there is a little blue three-wheeler in your garden._  
_A Nubbin bumps it. It tips. The Nubbin is thrilled._  
_It bumps it again. Then it stands with its feet wide apart, just in case._  

> **Lesson** (science, do): a wider base is steadier  
> _Try it like the Nubbin. Stand with your feet close together, and ask someone to give your shoulder a gentle nudge._  
> _Now stand with your feet wide apart, and try the nudge again. Much steadier!_  
> _A wider base is harder to tip. That’s why four wheels in a wide rectangle are steadier than three in a narrow triangle._  
> Check: `edu:stand:balance:feet-wide-narrow`
> _For grown-ups: Felt the difference between standing with feet together and feet apart when gently nudged._


### Glossary

- **confidence**: Feeling sure of yourself.
- **bragging**: Showing off about how good you are.
- **sporting**: Fair and generous to the other side in a game or race.
- **rights**: Stands something back up the right way. (It has other meanings too.)
- **thrilled**: Very excited and pleased.

## Q46. Not the Cabbages!

- `q46-s1`: Find all 8 cabbages that rolled across the meadow, and help put the cart’s wheel back on. · _Round things roll downhill. Look along the stream bank and under the bushes._
- `q46-s2`: Shake the big fruit tree until nothing else falls, then mend the cart with planks and rope. · _Tap the tree until it’s bare. The planks and rope are in the shed by the gate._
- `q46-s3`: Build the merchant a cart that can’t tip over. · _You need 4 planks, 2 wheels and a sack of stones. Keep it wide, and keep the heavy stones low. Tuk’s diagram is in your journal._

#### `q46-crash`

_A wooden cart creaks up the main path, piled high with cabbages. A man in a straw hat pushes it very, very carefully._  
**The cabbage merchant**: Afternoon! Fine cabbages, crisp cabbages, cabbages for every occasion. Weddings. Birthdays. Snacks.  
**The cabbage merchant**: I’ve pushed this cart all over the world, and I have a very good feeling about this Grove.  
_Behind you, a Nubbin in full racing stride comes round the bend. It is not looking where it’s going. It never is._  
_Thud. Wobble. A long, slow tip. Cabbages roll in every direction._  
**The cabbage merchant**: Ohhh, the cabbages! Somebody catch the cabbages!  
_Your Nubbin sits up in the wreck, wearing a cabbage leaf like a hat. It looks very pleased with itself._  
**The cabbage merchant**: The wheel’s come off. I had eight cabbages, and three have rolled into the stream!  
**The cabbage merchant**: The rest are scattered all over the meadow.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 1.OA.A.1, ask): subtract within 20 to solve a word problem  
> **The cabbage merchant**: Eight cabbages, and three are in the stream. So how many are out in the meadow?  
> - ✅ 5 → Five! Eight take away three is five. You’re quicker than my cart.
> - 11 → Eleven would mean adding. But three cabbages went away into the stream, so we take them away. 8 − 3 = 5. Five cabbages in the meadow.
> - 3 → Three is how many are in the stream. Take those three away from eight. 8 − 3 = 5. Five cabbages are in the meadow.
> _For grown-ups: Solved a take-away word problem: 8 cabbages, 3 in the stream, so 5 in the meadow._


**Choices**

- **Apologise for your Nubbin**
    - **You**: Sorry. My Nubbin is still learning about corners.
    - **The cabbage merchant**: Corners. Yes. Lots of people are still learning about corners.
- **Offer to buy the dented ones**
    - **The cabbage merchant**: Dented cabbages are still cabbages! That is my whole philosophy.
- **Point out that this is the race track**
    - **You**: To be fair, this is the race track.
    - **The cabbage merchant**: To be fair, I didn’t see a sign.
    - There is a sign. It is very large. He is standing on it.

#### `q46-crash-done`

_You collect the cabbages one by one. The last one has rolled all the way down to the stream bank._  
**The cabbage merchant**: Why do they always roll downhill? Not once has a cabbage rolled uphill to find me.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): gravity, and balanced and unbalanced forces  
> _Every cabbage is pulled towards the ground by a force called gravity._  
> _On flat ground, the ground pushes back up just as hard. The forces are balanced, so the cabbage stays put._  
> _On a slope, the pushes don’t balance any more. Gravity wins, and a round cabbage rolls downhill._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that gravity pulls things down, and that unbalanced forces make a cabbage roll down a slope._

_You slot the wheel back onto the axle. The cart stands up straight, and so does the merchant._  
**The cabbage merchant**: All eight! Only a little bit muddy.  
_Your Nubbin offers him the cabbage-leaf hat. He accepts it with great dignity._  
**The cabbage merchant**: You have a gift, friend. A cabbage gift. The rarest kind.  

#### `q46-fruit`

_The merchant parks his cart under the big fruit tree, a long way from the race track._  
**The cabbage merchant**: Shade, peace and quiet. Nothing can go wrong in the shade.  
_A breeze stirs the branches. High above the cart, something round and heavy wobbles on its stalk._  
**The cabbage merchant**: Is that tree looking at me?  
_The fruit drops. It is enormous. It lands right on the cart, which folds neatly in half._  
**The cabbage merchant**: …I’m not going to wail. I’m saving my best wail for something worse.  
_He picks the fruit out of the wreck, sniffs it, and gives it to your Nubbin, who eats it at once._  
**The cabbage merchant**: Right. Planks, rope, and someone to shake that tree bare before I park under it again.  

> **Lesson** (science, K-2-ETS1-1, ask): define the real problem before solving it  
> _Good builders start by asking: what exactly went wrong?_  
> _Why is shaking the tree bare a clever first step?_  
> - ✅ So any loose fruit falls now, and not on the mended cart later. → Exactly. The problem isn’t the shade. It’s heavy fruit hanging right over my head.
> - Because the tree is too noisy. → The tree is quite quiet, really. The real problem is the heavy fruit hanging above the cart. Shake it all down now, and nothing can fall on the cart later.
> - So your Nubbin gets a snack. → A lovely bonus! But the main reason is that heavy fruit was hanging right over the cart. Shake it down now, and nothing else can fall on it later.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the real problem (fruit hanging above the cart) before choosing a fix._


#### `q46-fruit-done`

**The cabbage merchant**: Good as new. Better than new. New had a squeak.  
_He ties the last knot in the rope and gives the cart a proud pat._  
**The cabbage merchant**: From now on I park in the middle of the meadow. Nothing falls on you in the middle of a meadow.  
_Somewhere very high above the meadow, a bird hears this, and thinks about it._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, ask): spot foreshadowing and predict what might happen next  
> _Writers sometimes drop a hint about what might happen later. That hint is called foreshadowing._  
> _Why do you think the writer tells us about the bird?_  
> - ✅ It’s a hint that something might fall from the sky after all. → That’s my guess too. The merchant says nothing can fall on him… and the writer shows us a bird.
> - No reason. It’s just a bird. → Could be! But writers don’t often mention a bird for no reason, just after someone says nothing can fall on them. It’s a hint: the middle of the meadow may not be as safe as he thinks.
> - The bird wants to buy a cabbage. → Ha! Maybe. But it’s more likely a hint that the middle of the meadow isn’t as safe as he thinks.
> _For grown-ups: Noticed foreshadowing: a small detail the writer uses to hint at what might happen next._

_Your Nubbins share the fallen fruit and watch him polish a cabbage on his sleeve._  
**The cabbage merchant**: Mark my words. My luck has turned.  

#### `q46-glider`

_Overhead, a shadow swoops in a wide, happy circle. A boy in orange and yellow is riding the wind on a wooden glider._  
**Pemba**: Hi! Hello! Nice Grove! Is that a vegetable stall? I love vegetables!  
_He leans to wave. The glider dips. You can see exactly where this is going, and so can the merchant._  
**The cabbage merchant**: No, no, no, no—  
_Pemba lands, rolls, and bounces off the cart. The cart does not bounce. It bursts into cabbages._  
**The cabbage merchant**: The cabbages! Again! Three times in one afternoon!  
**Pemba**: Oh no. That was me, wasn’t it? I’m Pemba. I’m really sorry. Can I help? I’m good at helping.  
_A boy with a boomerang on his back jogs up, out of breath, and looks at the mess._  
**Tuk**: Let me guess. You saw a cart and thought, “That looks soft.”  
**The cabbage merchant**: What I need is a cart that cannot tip. Not for Nubbins, not for fruit, not for flying boys.  
**Tuk**: Now that’s a problem I can plan for. I’ve got diagrams. I’ve always got diagrams.  
**The cabbage merchant**: Thirty-one carts I’ve lost. Every one taught me something. The first taught me wheels. The ninth taught me rope.  
**Tuk**: Here’s the secret. Things tip over when their weight leans out past the edge of whatever they stand on.  
**Tuk**: We want a stable cart. A steady one. One that hardly leans at all, whatever hits it.  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-5-ETS1-2, ask): compare designs: a wide, low base is more stable than a tall, narrow one  
> **Tuk**: So, which cart is harder to push over?  
> - A tall, narrow cart with the heavy stones on top → Ha! That one falls over if a butterfly sneezes. The weight is high up and the edges are close together, so it leans past them in no time. Wide and low is the steady one.
> - ✅ A low, wide cart with the heavy stones at the bottom → Exactly. Wide means the edges are far apart. Heavy stones down low mean the weight has a long, long way to lean before it gets past an edge.
> - They’re both just as easy to tip → Try it with two piles of books: one tall and thin, one low and wide. Give them each a little push. The tall one topples. The low, wide one just sits there. Wide and low is steadier.
> _For grown-ups: Compared two designs and explained why a wide, low base with weight at the bottom is harder to tip._


**Choices**

- **Make it wide**
    - **Tuk**: Wide. Good. Like a duck sitting down. Ducks never tip over.
- **Make it low**
    - **Tuk**: Low wheels, heavy bottom. You can’t knock over something that’s already nearly lying down.
- **Give it a warning bell**
    - **The cabbage merchant**: A bell! So they hear me coming!
    - **Tuk**: Fine. A bell. But it’s also going to be wide and low, because I have standards.

#### `q46-glider-done`

_Tuk unrolls his diagram on a flat rock. It has arrows, measurements, and one small drawing of a duck._  
**Tuk**: The cart bed is 2 metres long and 1 metre wide. I want a rope all the way round the edge, so no cabbage falls off.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.D.8, ask): find the perimeter of a rectangle  
> **Tuk**: So how much rope do I need to go all the way round? Long side, short side, long side, short side.  
> - ✅ 6 metres → Yes! 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6. The distance all the way round is called the perimeter.
> - 3 metres → That only gets you along one long side and one short side. The rope has to go all the way round. 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6 metres. That’s the perimeter.
> - 2 metres → That’s only one long side! Add all four sides: 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6 metres. The distance all the way round a shape is its perimeter.
> _For grown-ups: Found the perimeter of a 2 m by 1 m rectangle by adding all four sides (6 m)._

_You and your Nubbin drag the sack of stones into place. The cart sinks a little and settles, like a hen on a nest._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, do): keep the heavy part low to make something stable  
> **Tuk**: Now the stones. Put them at the very bottom, under the cabbages. Not on top!  
> _Drag the sack to the lowest spot on the cart. Then give the cart a nudge, and watch it hardly move._  
> Check: `edu:place:stones:low`
> _For grown-ups: Placed the heaviest load low down and saw that it made the cart harder to tip._

_The new cart sits low and wide, like a sensible duck._  
**Pemba**: Can I test it? I want to test it. Please let me test it.  
**The cabbage merchant**: Test it? With what?  
**Pemba**: With me!
