> - ✅ They only know a little about him, so they made him simple and funny. → Yes. The Players see Tuk from the outside. Tuk knows his own plans, worries and hopes. Same boy, two points of view.
> - Because Tuk really only thinks about meat. → HEY. Tuk does love meat! But he also plans, worries and cares. The Players only see the outside of him.
> - Because actors don’t like Tuk. → They probably don’t know him at all! That’s the point. They only see a little bit of Tuk from the outside, so they made him simple and funny.
> _For grown-ups: Compared how a character sees himself with how others see him (two points of view)._

_Then a huge, sweaty actor playing Bao strides out, flexing. He has a beard._  
**Bao**: Oh, I love him. Ten out of ten. No notes.  

#### `q55-act1-done`

_The interval bell rings. Kaito hasn’t blinked in twenty minutes._  
**Kaito**: They gave me a ponytail made of a mop.  
**Kaito**: And I was the villain. They had me shouting at the sea for a whole scene.  
**Kaito**: …It’s fair. That is how I was. It just isn’t how I am.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): understand how a character has changed  
> _Kaito says, “That is how I was. It just isn’t how I am.” What does he mean?_  
> - ✅ He used to make bad choices, but he has changed. → Yes. The play shows old Kaito. The real Kaito has grown, and he knows it.
> - He’s cross with the actors. → He was shocked about the mop! But then he says “It’s fair.” He means he used to be like that, but he has changed.
> - He doesn’t remember being the villain. → He remembers. That’s why he says “it’s fair”. He means he used to make bad choices, but he’s different now.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how a character has changed over time, using his own words as evidence._

**Bao**: Look at that. Growth. Gross. Pass the peanuts.  
**Pemba**: I think you’ve changed the most out of all of us, Kaito.  

#### `q55-finale`

_In the second act, an actor in a very shiny cape appears with a sign that says THE KEEPER. That’s you._  
**The Ember Bay Players**: Fear not, friends! The Keeper is here, and I have brought… my eight hundred Nubbins!  
_The eight hundred Nubbins are socks on sticks. One falls off and rolls into the sand._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide by sharing into equal pairs  
> _Really there are only 40 sock Nubbins, not eight hundred. Socks come in pairs._  
> _How many pairs of socks did the Players use?_  
> - ✅ 20 pairs → Yes. 40 ÷ 2 = 20. Twenty pairs of socks, and twenty very cold pairs of feet.
> - 80 pairs → That doubles 40. But each pair holds 2 socks, so we halve 40 instead. 40 ÷ 2 = 20 pairs.
> - 38 pairs → That takes 2 away from 40. Instead, put the socks into twos: how many twos make 40? Twenty. 40 ÷ 2 = 20 pairs.
> _For grown-ups: Divided 40 socks into pairs to find 20 pairs._

**Kaito**: That’s… honestly how you look when you walk in with the Nubbins. A bit less socky.  
_The finale begins. The Keeper slips on a banana skin and the villain wins. The curtain starts to fall._  
**Tuk**: THEY CAN’T END IT LIKE THAT.  
**Bao**: Your move, Keeper.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think about fair and kind ways to give an honest opinion  
> _The ending is terrible. But the Players did try very hard._  
> _What’s a fair way to show what you think of a show you didn’t like?_  
> - Be honest but kind: clap for the hard work, and say what could be better. → Ooh, a critic with manners. Rare.
> - Boo! A bad ending deserves boos. → Ha! Booing is honest, I’ll give you that. Just remember there are real people under those socks, and they tried their best.
> - Cheer anyway, so they feel happy. → That’s kind. Though if nobody ever tells them, the ending might never get better.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to be both honest and kind when giving an opinion on someone’s work._


**Choices**

- **Boo loudly**
    - You boo. The whole audience joins in, then starts booing each other. The Players bow anyway.
    - **The Ember Bay Players**: Thank you! The passion! We feed on it!
- **Cheer anyway**
    - You cheer. The actors look stunned, then delighted. The sock Nubbins take a bow.
    - **The Ember Bay Players**: A fan! We have a fan!
- **Storm the stage and fix the ending**
    - You climb up, rescue the fallen sock Nubbin and help the Keeper actor to his feet. The crowd goes wild.
    - **The Ember Bay Players**: This is improvised theatre now! Everybody, improvise!

#### `q55-finale-done`

_The curtain falls for the last time. Up and down the beach, people are arguing about it._  
**Kaito**: You know what? I’m glad we came.  
**Tuk**: I’m not. I’m writing a letter.  
**Bao**: I’m writing a fan letter. To the big guy with the beard. He gets me.  
**Pemba**: I’m still not sure if I’m “fun, and also fun”.  
_Same play, same seats, same peanuts. Four friends, four completely different opinions._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): compare different characters’ points of view on the same event  
> _Who liked the play the most?_  
> - ✅ Bao → Yes! Bao is writing a fan letter. Tuk is writing a cross one. Kaito is glad he came, and Pemba isn’t sure. One play, four points of view. What’s yours?
> - Tuk → Tuk is writing an angry letter! He liked it least. Bao is writing a fan letter, so Bao liked it most. One play, four points of view.
> - Kaito → Kaito is glad he came. But Bao is writing a fan letter, so Bao liked it most. One play, four points of view.
> _For grown-ups: Compared four characters’ points of view on the same play, and considered their own._


#### `q55-complete`

_Afterwards, the lead player hands out programmes at the stage door, still in his shiny cape._  
**The Ember Bay Players**: Take a mask or two! For the memories! We do the same show next week, only longer.  
**Bao**: Longer. Wonderful. I’m coming every week.  
**Pemba**: Do you think they’ll ever do one where we win?  
**Kaito**: If they did, I don’t think anyone would believe it.  
_You go home with two theatre masks, one smiling and one frowning, and a playbill with your name spelt wrong._  

> **Lesson** (art, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): the history of theatre masks  
> _Theatre masks are very old. In ancient Greece, more than two thousand years ago, actors wore masks on stage._  
> _Today a smiling mask and a frowning mask together stand for theatre: one for comedy, which is funny, and one for tragedy, which is sad._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that actors in ancient Greece wore masks, and that the comedy and tragedy masks are a symbol of theatre._


### Glossary

- **recognition**: Being noticed and praised for what you’ve done.
- **depth**: Having much more to you than people notice at first.
- **interval**: A short break in the middle of a play or show.
- **villain**: The bad character in a story.
- **improvise**: To make something up on the spot, without planning it first.
- **opinion**: What someone thinks or feels about something.
- **comedy**: A funny play or story.
- **tragedy**: A sad play or story.

## Q56. Earth Rumble

- `q56-s1`: Follow the flyer to the secret arena under the big boulder. · _The big boulder in the rocky section has a crack in it. Knock twice._
- `q56-s2`: Enter your Power Nubbin in a match against the Little Landslide. Win, or lose like a good sport. · _She feels your footsteps through the ground. Stand very still to puzzle her, then push._

#### `q56-flyer`

_A crumpled flyer blows across the Grove and sticks to your Nubbin’s face._  
**Tuk**: “RUMBLE NIGHT! Wrestling under the big boulder. Doors open at half past seven. Bring snacks.” Huh.  
**Tuk**: Secret wrestling under a boulder. Of course. Why would anything round here happen above ground?  
**Pemba**: We have to go! I’ve never seen wrestling. Is it like hugging, but crosser?  
**Tuk**: That’s… actually a perfect description. Two people push each other until one of them leaves the ring.  
_Your strongest Nubbin flexes its tiny arms at the flyer. It seems to think it has been invited._  
**Pemba**: It says the first match starts at eight o’clock. How long do we have to wait?  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): work out a time interval in minutes  
> **Tuk**: Doors open at half past seven. The first match is at eight. How long is that?  
> - ✅ 30 minutes → Right. Half an hour. Just long enough to eat all the snacks before it starts.
> - 1 hour → Not quite. From half past seven to eight, the minute hand goes from the 6 to the 12. That’s half the clock: 30 minutes.
> - 15 minutes → That would be quarter to eight. Half past seven to eight is half an hour: 30 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a half-hour time interval from half past seven to eight o’clock._


**Choices**

- **Pack snacks, as the flyer says**
    - **Tuk**: Finally, someone who reads the instructions. I’ll carry the noodles.
- **Bring your Power Nubbin**
    - Your Power Nubbin marches ahead of you, stomping on purpose so everyone knows it’s coming.
- **Ask whether this is a good idea**
    - **Tuk**: It isn’t. But I want to see it. Those are two different things.

#### `q56-flyer-done`

_At the big boulder you find a crack just wide enough for a fist. You knock twice._  
_With a deep, grinding rumble, the boulder slides aside. Stone steps lead down into the ground._  
_Below, a crowd roars by torchlight around a square ring of sand._  
**Tuk**: Okay. That’s a cool door. I’ll give them the door.  
**Pemba**: Listen! No, feel! I can feel the cheering in my feet!  
_He’s right. Every stamp and every cheer makes the stone steps tremble very slightly._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-PS4-1, do): sound is a vibration, and it travels through solid things  
> **Pemba**: Try this! Put your ear flat on a table, and gently tap the far end with one finger.  
> _The tap sounds louder through the table than through the air. Sound is a vibration: a very fast shaking._  
> _Vibrations travel well through solid things like wood and stone. That’s why the steps tremble when the crowd stamps._  
> Check: `edu:tap:table:ear-down`
> _For grown-ups: Listened to a tap through a tabletop and learned that sound is a vibration that travels through solids._

**Tuk**: Great. A room so loud the floor joins in.  

#### `q56-bout`

**Rumble Master Gorro**: WELCOME TO RUMBLE NIGHT! Tonight our champion defends her belt against the mighty Big Slab!  
**The Big Slab**: The Big Slab is feeling confident! The Big Slab is feeling enormous!  
**Tuk**: Why is he talking about himself like that?  
_The champion walks into the ring barefoot. She is tiny, dressed in green, with a fringe over her pale eyes._  
**Rumble Master Gorro**: THE LITTLE LANDSLIDE!  
**Bao**: Let’s get this over with. I have a bedtime.  
_The Big Slab charges. The champion plants her bare feet wide apart and doesn’t budge._  
_He pushes. She pushes back just as hard. For a long moment, nobody moves at all._  
_Then she shoves harder. The ground lifts like a trapdoor, and he sails out of the ring into the noodle stand._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): balanced and unbalanced forces  
> _When they pushed equally hard, nobody moved. Then the Little Landslide pushed harder._  
> _What happened to the Big Slab?_  
> - ✅ He moved, in the direction she was pushing. → Yep. Equal pushes are balanced, so nothing moves. A bigger push on one side is unbalanced, and something goes flying. Usually him.
> - Nothing. He’s bigger, so he stays put. → Being big helps, but the pushes decide. When her push became bigger than his, the forces were unbalanced, and he moved.
> - They both slid backwards. → Not this time. When one push is bigger, things move the way the bigger push goes. Out of the ring, into the noodles.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that equal pushes are balanced and a bigger push on one side makes something move._

**Bao**: Next! Anybody? Come on, I can feel you all shuffling.  
_Your Power Nubbin steps forward. The whole arena goes quiet._  
**Bao**: Huh. Small, heavy, walks like it means it. I like it already.  

**Choices**

- **Ask her to go easy on it**
    - **Bao**: Nope. Going easy would be an insult. Your Nubbin deserves a real match.
- **Tell her not to hold back**
    - **Bao**: Oh, I won’t. But I like that you asked.
- **Bow to her**
    - **Bao**: You know I can’t see that, right?
    - She grins anyway. She felt the floorboards creak as you bent.

#### `q56-bout-done`

_The match is short and very sandy. Your Nubbin stands perfectly still, and for a second she loses track of it._  
_Then it shuffles one foot, and she finds it at once._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): some animals sense the world through vibrations  
> **Bao**: I can’t see with my eyes, so I see with my feet. Every step sends a little shake through the ground.  
> _Some real animals do this too. A spider feels tiny shakes in its web, and knows where a fly has landed._  
> _When your Nubbin stood still, it made no shakes at all. So for a moment, it was hidden._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that some animals, like spiders, sense movement through vibrations._

**Bao**: Not bad! Not bad at all. Hardly anyone lasts that long.  
_Your Nubbin is either covered in glory or covered in sand. Possibly both._  
**Bao**: And you didn’t run. Most people run. Running’s loud.  
**Tuk**: Is it me, or did she just say “good job” in the grumpiest way possible?  
**Bao**: I heard that, Ponytail. And yes.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): being a good sport  
> _Your Nubbin gave it everything. What does a good sport do at the end of a match?_  
> - ✅ Shake hands (or paws) and say “good match”. → That’s the one. Win or lose, you thank the person who gave you a real fight.
> - Say the sand was unfair. → Blaming the sand? The sand was the same for both of us, Keeper. A good sport thanks the other player instead: “Good match.”
> - Stomp off without a word. → It’s fine to feel disappointed. But a good sport still says “good match” first, then has a sulk later if they need one.
> _For grown-ups: Practised what a good sport says and does at the end of a match._


#### `q56-complete`

_After the show, the Little Landslide finds you by the noodle stand, which has been rebuilt._  
**Bao**: The name’s Bao. Don’t tell anyone. Up there, I’m a nice quiet girl who has to wear shoes.  
**Bao**: Up there, everyone helps me across the road whether I want it or not. Down here, nobody helps me. It’s the best.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): think question: the best way to help someone  
> _Bao says people help her whether she wants it or not. Down here, she gets to do things herself._  
> _What do you think is the best way to help someone?_  
> - Ask first: “Would you like some help?” → Ha. Now there’s a question people forget. Asking means I get to choose.
> - Just help. Helping is kind. → It is kind, and you clearly have a kind heart. I’d just add: ask first, so the other person gets a say too.
> - Wait and watch, and only help if they get stuck. → That’s pretty smart. Lots of people like to try on their own first.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to offer help in a way that respects what the other person wants._

**Tuk**: You were incredible. How do you know where they’re going?  
**Bao**: I feel it through my feet. Your feet are louder than your mouth, Ponytail. Which is saying something.  
**Bao**: Here. A spare belt. I’ve got a cupboard full. Your Nubbin earned it, win or lose.  
_The belt is far too big. Your Nubbin wears it anyway, dragging it proudly behind like a tail._  
**Rumble Master Gorro**: And take a ring post! Every great champion needs an arena!  

### Glossary

- **flex**: To tighten your muscles to show how strong you are.
- **arena**: A big space where crowds watch sports or shows.
- **tremble**: To shake a little.
- **confident**: Sure of yourself, and not at all shy.
- **budge**: To move even a tiny bit, usually when someone is trying to move you.
- **glory**: Great praise and honour for doing something brave or difficult.

## Q57. The Painted Lady

- `q57-s1`: Take food and medicine to five houses in the river village. · _Fruit from the Grove and herbs from the healer’s shelf will both do. Knock gently; people are poorly._
- `q57-s2`: Clean the river by moonlight without the villagers seeing you. · _Steer the boat through the brown patches. If a lantern turns your way, drift into the mist and wait._

#### `q57-sick`

_Downstream from the Grove, the river turns a sickly brown. A village of stilt houses stands in the murk, quiet and grey._  
**Ma Reedy**: The fish are all gone. Half the village is coughing. It’s the works upstream. They pour their sludge in and call it progress.  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS3-3, notice): rivers carry pollution downstream to everyone below  
> **Nalu**: A river only flows one way: downhill. So whatever goes in upstream ends up with everyone downstream.  
> _That’s why this village is sick, even though the works is far away. A river is shared by everyone who lives along it._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that rivers flow downhill, so pollution put in upstream reaches everyone downstream._

**Nalu**: That’s awful. Someone has to do something.  
**Tuk**: Someone will. Probably not us. We have a schedule.  
**Nalu**: Tuk.  
**Tuk**: …I’m just saying the schedule exists.  
**Ma Reedy**: The old folk say a river spirit once watched over us. A lady in white with a painted face. She hasn’t come in years.  
_A little girl in a doorway holds up an empty fish basket, upside down, as if it might be hiding a fish._  
_Nalu goes very quiet. You can see an idea forming. Tuk can see it too, and he sighs._  

**Choices**

- **Promise to help**
    - **Ma Reedy**: You’re kind. But kind won’t clean a river, dear.
    - **Nalu**: Watch us.
- **Offer fruit from the Grove**
    - **Ma Reedy**: Real fruit! The children haven’t had any for weeks.
- **Ask about the river spirit**
    - **Ma Reedy**: She came at night. Mist on the water, a lantern on a boat. In the morning, the sick were well.

#### `q57-sick-done`

_You go from house to house with fruit and herbs. Five houses, five creaky ladders._  
_Each house gets three pieces of fruit: one for breakfast, one for lunch and one for supper._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> **Tuk**: Five houses, three fruits each. How many fruits did we carry? I need to know how sore my arms are allowed to be.  
> - ✅ 15 → Fifteen. Five groups of three: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. My arms were right to complain.
> - 8 → That’s 5 add 3. But every house got 3, so it’s five groups of three: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. Fifteen.
> - 12 → Close! That’s four houses. Count one more group of three, and you get 15.
> _For grown-ups: Solved 5 groups of 3 as a multiplication: 15 pieces of fruit._

**Ma Reedy**: Bless you. Nobody’s brought us anything but sludge for months.  
_At the last house, a little boy gives you a drawing of a lady with a painted face._  
_Underneath, in wobbly letters, he has written: COME BACK PLEASE._  
**Nalu**: That settles it.  
**Tuk**: I know that face. That’s your “I have a plan and it needs a costume” face.  

#### `q57-night`

_Midnight. Nalu steps into a boat wearing a white veil, a wide straw hat and red painted marks._  
**Nalu**: Well? Do I look like a river spirit?  
**Tuk**: You look like Nalu in a hat. But a really mysterious hat.  
**Pemba**: I think you look amazing. And spooky. Amazing-spooky.  
_Mist rises off the river and curls round the boat like steam from a bath._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): mist is made of tiny drops of water  
> **Nalu**: Mist is really a cloud sitting low on the water. It’s millions of tiny water drops, too small to see one by one.  
> _On a cold night, water rises off the river as an invisible gas. In the cold air it cools into those tiny drops._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that mist is a low cloud of tiny water drops that forms when water vapour cools._

**Nalu**: Here’s the plan. I lift the sludge out of the water. You and the Nubbins scoop it into barrels. Nobody gets seen.  
_Your Swim Nubbin slips silently into the river, then pops up holding a rusty can like a trophy._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understand a simile  
> _The Nubbin holds up the can “like a trophy”. A simile compares two things using “like” or “as”._  
> _What does this simile tell you?_  
> - ✅ The Nubbin is very proud of what it found. → Yes. People hold trophies up high when they’ve won. The simile shows how proud the Nubbin feels.
> - The can is made of gold. → Not at all: it’s rusty! The simile isn’t about the can. It shows how proud the Nubbin feels.
> - The Nubbin won a race. → No race tonight. The simile borrows the feeling of winning to show how proud the Nubbin is.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile (“like a trophy”) shows about a character’s feelings._

**Tuk**: And tomorrow, when the works start pouring again?  
**Nalu**: Then the Painted Lady pays them a visit too.  

**Choices**

- **Clean the river first**
    - **Nalu**: Right. Rescue first. Everything else can wait till morning.
- **Block the sludge pipe**
    - **Tuk**: Now that I can help with. I brought a very large cork.
- **Leave a stern note at the works**
    - **Nalu**: “Stop it. Love, the river.” Perfect.

#### `q57-night-done`

_All night you scoop. Barrel after barrel fills with brown gloop._  
_By dawn the water runs clear enough to see the stones on the bottom._  
_A fish flips up into the light, and someone on the bank gasps._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): fish need clean water to breathe  
> _Why did the fish come back? Fish breathe with gills, which take in oxygen from the water._  
> _Sludge clouds the water and blocks the sunlight that water plants need. Clean, clear water means fish can live here again._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that fish use gills to get oxygen from water, and need clean water to live._

**Ma Reedy**: The Painted Lady came back!  
_Ma Reedy turns towards your boat, half hidden in the mist. Nalu, still painted, freezes._  
**Nalu**: (whispering) Do we tell her?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think question: the truth or the legend  
> **Nalu**: Help me think. If we stay secret, the Painted Lady story gives them hope. If we tell, Ma Reedy knows the truth.  
> _Which matters more here: the truth, or the hope? There’s no wrong answer._  
> - The truth. People deserve to know. → That’s fair. Honest people are easier to trust, and Ma Reedy has been let down before.
> - The hope. The story helps them. → I think that too, sometimes. A story can keep people going.
> - Both: tell Ma Reedy, but let the story carry on. → Ooh. The truth for her, and the legend for everyone else. That’s clever.
> _For grown-ups: Weighed honesty against a hopeful story, with no single right answer._


**Choices**

- **Step out of the mist and tell her the truth**
    - **Ma Reedy**: I know, dear. I knew the first night. Spirits don’t sneeze.
    - **Ma Reedy**: The Painted Lady was always just somebody who decided to be her. Now it’s you.
- **Drift back into the mist**
    - You drift away. Behind you, the village is already telling the story, and it gets better every time.
    - **Nalu**: Maybe they need her more than they need to know who she is.

#### `q57-complete`

_The village wakes to clear water and full fish baskets._  
_The works upstream has hung up a nervous sign: PIPE CLOSED. SORRY._  
**Ma Reedy**: She came back. After all these years, she came back.  
**Nalu**: I bet she was happy to help.  
**Tuk**: She was very happy. And very wet. And she owes me new trousers.  
_Ma Reedy gives you a wide straw hat, still faintly marked with river-spirit paint._  
**Ma Reedy**: And these little fish. Put them in your stream. They nibble the muck and keep the water clear for good.  
**Nalu**: The fish can keep it clean. But it’s still up to us not to make it dirty.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, K-ESS3-3, ask): how people can look after rivers  
> _What’s one way people can help keep rivers and streams clean?_  
> - ✅ Keep rubbish and waste out of the water. → Yes. Bin it, don’t drop it. Everything in a stream ends up downstream.
> - Throw rubbish in. The fish will eat it. → The little fish nibble muck, but they can’t eat cans or sludge. Rubbish belongs in a bin, not a river.
> - Leave it to the river spirits. → Ha! Even the Painted Lady was just a person. Anyone can help, by keeping rubbish out of the water.
> _For grown-ups: Named a way people can help keep rivers clean for everyone._


### Glossary

- **downstream**: Further along a river, in the direction the water flows.
- **sludge**: Thick, dirty, sticky mud or waste.
- **veil**: A thin piece of cloth worn over the face or head.
- **mysterious**: Strange and hard to explain or understand.
- **gills**: The body parts a fish uses to breathe under water.
- **upstream**: Further back along a river, towards where the water comes from.

## Q58. The Fortuneteller

- `q58-s1`: Have Aunt Wen read the bones for you and your Nubbin. · _Join the queue at the house with stars on the door. Bring a fruit; it’s polite._
- `q58-s2`: Climb Mount Grumble and look inside the crater. · _Take the zigzag path, or call Puffin if you’ve found him. Keep your Nubbin well away from the edge._
- `q58-s3`: Help Pemba push the clouds into a giant angry-volcano shape over the village. · _Drag the cloud puffs into the outline. The wind blows the clouds east, so start on the west side._

#### `q58-reading`

_In the village of Hillstead, everyone queues outside a little house with stars painted on the door._  
**Aunt Wen**: Come in, come in! Aunt Wen sees all. Or most. Some of it is blurry.  
_She drops a bone into the fire. It cracks with a pop. She peers at the cracks and gasps happily._  
**Aunt Wen**: Your Nubbin will find something lovely today. Possibly a snack. Probably a snack.  
**Tuk**: That’s not a fortune. That’s just odds. Nubbins always find snacks.  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): testing a claim with evidence  
> **Tuk**: Everyone here believes her. But how could we actually test whether her fortunes come true?  
> - ✅ Write her fortunes down, then check later how many came true. → Exactly. Collect the evidence, then count. That’s how you test any claim, from fortunes to frogs.
> - Believe her. She sounds very sure. → Sounding sure isn’t the same as being right. A fairer test: write the fortunes down and check how many come true.
> - Ask her if she’s right. → She’ll say yes! Better to write her fortunes down and check them later. Evidence beats asking.
> _For grown-ups: Planned a fair way to test a claim by collecting evidence and checking it._

**Aunt Wen**: And you, young man, will have a very bad day if you keep saying things like that.  
_Outside, a villager carries an umbrella on a cloudless day. Another refuses to walk on the left of the road._  
**Pemba**: She’s amazing! She said I’ll have a great adventure! Do you think it’s today?  
**Nalu**: She says that to everyone, Pemba.  

**Choices**

- **Believe her**
    - **Aunt Wen**: A wise Keeper. Your Nubbin agrees. Look, it’s nodding.
    - Your Nubbin is nodding off.
- **Side with Tuk**
    - **Tuk**: Finally. Someone with a brain. Hello, brain.
- **Say you’ll wait and see**
    - **Aunt Wen**: Fair. The bones are patient. So am I. Mostly.

#### `q58-reading-done`

**Aunt Wen**: Oh, and the mountain won’t erupt this year. I read the clouds this morning. Nice and fluffy.  
**Tuk**: …The mountain can erupt?  
_Everyone turns to look at Mount Grumble, high above the village. A thin thread of grey smoke drifts from its top._  
**Aunt Wen**: Every few hundred years. Nothing to worry about. The clouds said so.  
**Tuk**: A volcano. You built your whole village under a volcano.  
**Aunt Wen**: The soil is wonderful for turnips.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): why people farm near volcanoes  
> _Aunt Wen has a point about the turnips. Ash from old eruptions breaks down into rich soil that plants love._  
> _That’s why people have farmed near volcanoes for thousands of years, even though it can be risky._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that volcanic ash makes rich soil, which is why people farm near volcanoes._


#### `q58-mountain`

_Above Hillstead, Mount Grumble sends up a thin grey thread of smoke. Tuk stares at it._  
**Tuk**: Everyone here trusts clouds over common sense. I’m going up there. I want to see with my own eyes.  
**Pemba**: I’ll come! Puffin can fly us most of the way.  
**Nalu**: I’ll stay and talk to the villagers. Just in case.  
_At the top, the air is hot and smells of boiled eggs. Inside the crater, red rock bubbles and hisses._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): magma, lava and volcanic gas  
> **Tuk**: That’s rock so hot it has melted. Under the ground it’s called magma. Once it pours out of a volcano, it’s called lava.  
> **Tuk**: And the eggy smell is gas coming up from deep underground. Volcanoes are famous for it.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the difference between magma (under the ground) and lava (above it)._

**Tuk**: That is not “nice and fluffy”. That is “very much about to go off”.  
**Pemba**: We have to tell everyone! Today!  
**Tuk**: They won’t listen to us. They only listen to Aunt Wen. And Aunt Wen only listens to clouds.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-ESS1-1, ask): some changes to the land are fast and some are slow  
> **Pemba**: Some changes to the land happen slowly, over thousands of years. Some happen fast.  
> **Pemba**: Which kind is a volcano erupting?  
> - ✅ Fast: it can change the land in hours or days. → Right. A river wearing out a valley takes ages. An eruption can reshape a mountainside in a day.
> - Slow: it takes thousands of years. → The mountain itself took a very long time to build up. But the eruption is fast: hours or days. That’s why we have to warn them now.
> _For grown-ups: Sorted a volcanic eruption as a fast change to the land, compared with slow changes like a river wearing a valley._


#### `q58-mountain-done`

_You hurry back down the zigzag path. A hot wind pushes at your back._  
**Pemba**: Wait. If they only listen to clouds…  
**Tuk**: …then we give them a cloud. Pemba, you wonderful little weather machine.  
**Pemba**: I can push clouds around with my wind. But I can’t make them out of nothing.  
**Tuk**: So where do clouds even come from?  
**Pemba**: From water! Every cloud started out in a river, a lake or the sea.  

> **Lesson** (science, do): the water cycle  
> **Pemba**: Help me put the water cycle in order! Then I’ll know which clouds to grab.  
> _Drag the cards: the sun warms the lake. Water rises as invisible vapour. High up, it cools into tiny drops._  
> _The drops crowd together into a cloud. The cloud rains, and the water runs back to the lake._  
> **Pemba**: And round it goes, again and again. The same water, over and over!  
> Check: `edu:order:water-cycle`
> _For grown-ups: Put the stages of the water cycle in order: warming, rising vapour, cooling into drops, clouds, rain._


#### `q58-clouds`

_The whole village has gathered in the square for Aunt Wen’s evening cloud reading._  
**Aunt Wen**: The clouds will now speak! Let us see. Yes. Ah. Hmm. That one looks like a duck.  
_High above, Pemba and Puffin swoop through the clouds, pushing great gusts of wind. Your Nubbins flap along behind._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Geo.2.K-2, ask): compass directions: east and west  
> **Tuk**: The wind is blowing the clouds towards the east. Which side should Pemba start from, so they drift into place?  
> - ✅ The west side → Yes! Start in the west, and the wind carries the clouds east, right into the shape.
> - The east side → Then the wind would blow them straight off the shape! Start in the west, and the wind carries them east.
> - The north side → North would send them sideways. The wind moves from west to east, so start in the west.
> _For grown-ups: Used compass directions to work out that wind blowing east carries things from the west._

**Tuk**: Okay. Steady. We need one shape. The village sign for “danger”. Big, clear, impossible to argue with.  
**Nalu**: And what is the village sign for danger?  
**Tuk**: A big angry mountain with a frowny face.  
**Nalu**: …That’s not a real sign.  
**Tuk**: It will be in five minutes.  
**Nalu**: Tuk. We’re tricking them. Is that really any better than what Aunt Wen does?  
**Tuk**: …Hm. I hate it when you ask the good questions while I’m busy.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think question: is a trick ever all right?  
> **Nalu**: Help me with this one. We’re tricking them to save them. Aunt Wen tricks them by accident.  
> _Is our trick okay? What do you think?_  
> - Yes: it keeps them safe, and we’ll show them the truth tomorrow. → That’s my thinking. A trick to keep them safe tonight, then the real evidence in daylight.
> - No: we should find a way to show them the truth tonight. → That’s brave. The truth might be slower, but it’s theirs to know.
> - I’m not sure. → Me neither. Not being sure means you’re thinking hard about it. That’s good.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a trick can be right if it keeps people safe._


**Choices**

- **Shape the frowning volcano. Get them moving.**
    - **Tuk**: Tonight we trick them out of danger. Tomorrow we walk them up and show them the crater.
    - **Nalu**: Promise?
    - **Tuk**: Promise. With diagrams.
- **Shape a giant arrow pointing at the mountain**
    - **Nalu**: Yes. Don’t tell them what to think. Show them where to look.
    - Below, a hundred heads turn from the sky to the smoking mountain, for the first time in years.

#### `q58-clouds-done`

_A huge cloud hangs over Hillstead, impossible to argue with._  
_Your Nubbins drift down out of it, damp and proud. Their fur is dotted with tiny drops of water._  
**Pemba**: See? Clouds are wet inside! It’s like flying through a cold bath.  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS2-1, ask): reading clouds for the weather  
> _Aunt Wen said fluffy clouds meant good news. For the weather, she was partly right!_  
> _Which clouds usually bring storms?_  
> - ✅ Tall, dark, towering clouds → Yes! Small, fluffy white clouds usually mean fair weather. Tall, dark ones can bring heavy rain and thunder.
> - Small, fluffy white clouds → Those usually mean a nice day. It’s the tall, dark, towering clouds that bring storms.
> - Thin, wispy clouds → Thin wispy clouds are very high up and don’t usually bring rain. The tall, dark, towering ones are the stormy ones.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that small fluffy clouds usually mean fair weather and tall dark clouds can bring storms._

**Aunt Wen**: Oh dear. Oh dear oh dear. The clouds have NEVER been this clear.  
**Aunt Wen**: Everyone, get your shovels!  
**Tuk**: Shovels. She said shovels. That’s the most sensible thing anyone’s said all day.  

#### `q58-complete`

_The villagers dig a trench all night. When Mount Grumble finally pops, the lava runs down the trench and away from the houses._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): lava flows downhill and can be steered  
> **Tuk**: Lava flows downhill, like very slow, very hot porridge. A trench gives it an easier path, away from the houses.  
> _In real life, people have built long walls of earth to steer lava away from their towns._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that lava flows downhill and that people build barriers to steer it away from homes._

**Aunt Wen**: I owe you, young man. Even if you don’t believe a word I say.  
**Tuk**: I believe one word. “Shovels.” That was a great call.  
**Aunt Wen**: Then let me give the Keeper something. Bring your Nubbins to me whenever you like. I’ll read the bones for them.  
**Aunt Wen**: I’m right more often than not. And much more often about Nubbins than about mountains.  
_Aunt Wen now reads bones at the Grove’s fortune tent. Tuk says he will never go. He goes twice a week, in a hat._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): work out a character’s motive from what he does  
> _Tuk says he’ll never go to Aunt Wen. So why do you think he goes twice a week… in a hat?_  
> - ✅ So nobody recognises him, because he said he never would. → Yes! The hat is a disguise. Tuk is a bit embarrassed to have changed his mind, so he hides it.
> - Because it’s raining. → Maybe! But twice a week, every week? The hat is more likely a disguise: Tuk doesn’t want anyone to know he goes.
> - Because he likes hats. → He might. But it’s funnier than that. He said he’d never go, so the hat helps him go without being spotted.
> _For grown-ups: Used a character’s actions to work out his hidden reason (he is embarrassed to have changed his mind)._


### Glossary

- **fortune**: What someone says will happen to you in the future.
- **odds**: How likely it is that something will happen.
- **erupt**: When a volcano bursts open and hot melted rock, ash or gas comes out.
- **crater**: The bowl-shaped hole at the top of a volcano.
- **magma**: Melted rock deep under the ground.
- **vapour**: Water as an invisible gas in the air.
- **gust**: A sudden, strong rush of wind.
- **sensible**: Showing good sense; wise and practical.
- **trench**: A long, narrow ditch dug in the ground.

## Q59. The Waterbending Scroll

- `q59-s1`: Keep Captain Hake talking while Nalu takes a closer look at the scroll. · _Ask about every item on the deck. The bison whistle is good for at least a minute._
- `q59-s2`: Escape the pirates down the river rapids. · _Steer between the rocks, and let your Swim Nubbins push on the straight bits._

#### `q59-market`

_A battered pirate ship is moored at the river market, its deck piled with “treasures” of every kind._  
**Captain Hake**: Step up! Rare goods, fair prices, absolutely no questions answered!  
**Pemba**: Look! A whistle shaped like a bison! It’s only 45 gold pieces, and I’ve got 100!  
**Tuk**: It’s a stick with a hole in it. You’re buying a stick.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.OA.A.1, ask): subtract to find change  
> **Tuk**: Fine. If you buy your stick for 45 gold pieces and pay with 100, how much change should you get back?  
> - ✅ 55 gold pieces → Right. 45 and 5 makes 50, and 50 more makes 100. So 55 back. Count it, he’s a pirate.
> - 65 gold pieces → Check it: 45 and 65 makes 110. Too much! 45 and 55 makes 100, so the change is 55.
> - 45 gold pieces → That’s the price, not the change. 100 take away 45 leaves 55.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out change from 100 by counting on: 100 − 45 = 55._

_Nalu has gone very still. In a glass case lies an old scroll covered in drawings of moving water._  
**Nalu**: That’s a waterbending scroll. A real one. It could teach me everything my village couldn’t.  
**Captain Hake**: Ah, the lady has taste. Two hundred gold pieces. Or your bison, your Nubbin and the boy with the boomerang.  
**Tuk**: That’s a lot of value for one scroll. I’m flattered, in a horrible way.  

**Choices**

- **Haggle**
    - **Captain Hake**: Two hundred! My final offer! Two hundred and ten!
    - **Tuk**: That’s not how haggling works. The price is meant to go DOWN.
- **Pretend to walk away**
    - **Captain Hake**: Fine! Nobody wanted it anyway! …Two hundred!
- **Ask where he got it**
    - **Captain Hake**: I found it. In a… temple. On a… shelf. That was open. Partly.

#### `q59-market-done`

_You turn round. Nalu is walking briskly towards your boat._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.2.4, ask): work out a word’s meaning from clues  
> _Nalu walks “briskly”. Look for clues: she wants to get away before anyone notices. What does “briskly” mean?_  
> - ✅ Quickly and with energy → Yes. Brisk walking is fast and purposeful. Not running, which would look suspicious.
> - Slowly and sleepily → Not with a pirate behind her! She wants to get away fast, so “briskly” means quickly and with energy.
> - Backwards → Ha! That would be quite a trick. “Briskly” means quickly and with energy.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in the story to work out the meaning of “briskly”._

_The glass case is empty._  
**Tuk**: Did you just—  
**Nalu**: Walk. Normally. Now.  
_Tuk walks normally. It is the least normal walk you have ever seen._  
**Captain Hake**: THIEVES! After them, lads!  

#### `q59-chase`

_You tumble into your boat and push off. Behind you, the pirate ship swings round, sails cracking._  
**Tuk**: You STOLE it? You tell me off for picking fruit from other people’s trees!  
**Nalu**: It was already stolen! I’m borrowing it from the thieves. That’s practically returning it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think question: is taking from a thief still stealing?  
> _Nalu says taking something from a thief is “practically returning it”. What do you think?_  
> - It’s still taking. It should go back to its real owners. → …You might be right. I need to think about who it really belongs to.
> - It’s fair. The pirates stole it first. → I can see that. But Nalu isn’t the owner either. So who should end up with it?
> - It depends what she does with it next. → Hm. That’s a good point. What I do next matters a lot.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether taking something from a thief is fair, and who it really belongs to._

**Pemba**: This is so exciting! Are we pirates now? Can I have a hat?  
**Captain Hake**: Bring back my scroll! And my whistle! He never paid for the whistle!  
**Pemba**: Oh. Oops.  
_The river narrows and tips downhill. The water speeds up and churns white around the rocks._  
_Your Swim Nubbins leap in and paddle hard, pushing the boat along like little furry engines._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): pushing water back moves a boat forward  
> _Your Nubbins push the water backwards with their paws, and the water pushes the boat forwards._  
> **Tuk**: Same as rowing. Push the water back, go forward. I knew that. I was just checking.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that pushing water backwards makes a boat move forwards._


**Choices**

- **Tell Nalu it was wrong**
    - **Nalu**: I know. I’ll make it right. After we don’t get caught.
- **Tell Nalu it’s for a good cause**
    - **Nalu**: Thank you. See, Tuk? The Keeper understands.
    - **Tuk**: The Keeper is now part of a crime. Congratulations, Keeper.
- **Make Pemba blow the whistle**
    - Pemba blows. Somewhere far upriver, a very confused sky bison turns his head.

#### `q59-chase-done`

_Ahead, two big rocks stick up out of the rapids with a narrow gap between them._  
_Your little boat slips through. The pirate ship, which is much wider, does not._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.2, ask): compare lengths in metres  
> **Tuk**: The gap is 3 metres wide. Our boat is 2 metres wide. The pirate ship is 6 metres wide.  
> **Tuk**: Which one fits through?  
> - ✅ Only our boat → Right. 2 metres fits in a 3-metre gap with 1 to spare. 6 metres is twice as wide as the gap. Crunch.
> - Both of them → The pirate ship is 6 metres: that’s twice as wide as the 3-metre gap. Only our 2-metre boat fits.
> - Only the pirate ship → It’s the other way round! 6 metres won’t fit in 3. Our 2-metre boat slips through.
> _For grown-ups: Compared widths in metres to decide what fits through a gap._

_It wedges itself between the rocks with a sad crunch. You sail on._  
**Captain Hake**: THIS ISN’T OVER! Also, does anyone have a long pole?  
**Tuk**: Small boat, big win. I’m putting that on a flag.  
**Pemba**: Bye! Sorry about the whistle! I’ll pay you back!  

#### `q59-complete`

_That night by the fire, Nalu unrolls the scroll and practises one move over and over: a whip of water, snapping out and back._  
**Nalu**: Look! I did it! I actually did it!  
**Tuk**: Great. Now do the move where we don’t steal things.  
**Nalu**: I’ll take it to the water villages once I’ve learned it. It belongs to them. I promise.  
**Nalu**: And I won’t forget how my tummy twisted when I picked up that case.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): noticing feelings in your body  
> **Nalu**: That twisty feeling in my tummy was my conscience. It’s the part of you that knows when something isn’t right.  
> _Feelings often show up in our bodies first. Noticing them can help you make a better choice next time._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a “twisty tummy” can be a feeling worth listening to before making a choice._

_Your Swim Nubbins have been watching closely. One flicks its tail at the stream, and a ribbon of water snaps through the air._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, notice): liquids take the shape of their container  
> _Water is a liquid. It has no shape of its own: it takes the shape of whatever holds it._  
> _In a cup, it’s cup-shaped. In a river, it’s river-shaped. That’s what makes it so good at bending and whipping._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that liquids like water take the shape of their container._

**Pemba**: Your Nubbin can do it too! Your Nubbin learned waterbending!  

### Glossary

- **moored**: Tied up so it can’t float away, like a boat at a dock.
- **haggle**: To argue about a price to try to make it lower.
- **briskly**: Quickly and with energy.
- **practically**: Almost, or very nearly.
- **churns**: Stirs and swirls about roughly.
- **wedges**: Gets stuck tight in a narrow space.
- **conscience**: The feeling inside you that tells you whether something is right or wrong.

## Q60. The Winged Lemur

- `q60-s1`: Follow the winged lemur through the old temple ruins. · _It glides from high ledge to high ledge. Climb where it lands, and keep your eyes on its tail._
- `q60-s2`: Make friends with the lemur: feed it three fruits by hand. · _Hold the fruit out and stay still. It comes closer each time, as long as you don’t grab._

#### `q60-thief`

_Your fruit basket is empty. Again. There are tiny footprints in the dew, and a peach stone on the fence._  
**Pemba**: Third time this week? That’s no bird. Birds don’t leave the stones in a neat little pile.  
_Above you, something with huge ears and leathery wings sits on a branch, eating your last peach._  
**Lumi**: Chirrup!  
**Pemba**: A winged lemur! I haven’t seen one since I was little. They used to live at the old temple.  
_The lemur stuffs the peach in its cheek, launches off the branch and glides away towards the hills._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, ask): body parts that help animals survive  
> **Pemba**: Look at it! Big ears, big eyes, wings and a long tail. Which part helps it get away from us so fast?  
> - ✅ Its wings → Yes! Its wings let it glide from tree to tree. Every part of an animal’s body helps it survive somehow.
> - Its ears → Its big ears help it hear us coming! But for getting away fast, it’s the wings.
> - Its tail → The tail helps it balance on branches. But for getting away fast: wings!
> _For grown-ups: Matched an animal’s body parts to the jobs they do, like wings for escaping._

**Pemba**: Come on, let’s follow it! Gently! Wingy little things scare easily.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): a real gliding animal: the colugo  
> _In our world there’s an animal called a colugo, sometimes nicknamed a “flying lemur”._  
> _It isn’t really a lemur, and it can’t really fly. It glides between trees on a cape of stretchy skin between its legs._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned about the colugo, a real gliding animal sometimes called a “flying lemur”._


**Choices**

- **Run after it**
    - You run. The lemur looks back, and seems to decide this is a game.
- **Leave a fruit out as bait**
    - **Pemba**: Smart! It’ll come back for more. Then we follow it home.
- **Ask what you should call it**
    - **Pemba**: Not yet. A name should fit, and we hardly know it.
    - From up the hill, the lemur chirrups, as if it agrees.

#### `q60-thief-done`

_You follow the lemur up the hill to the ruins of an old temple._  
_Under the broken roof you find its nest. You tip it out carefully to see what’s inside._  
_Twelve fruit stones. Five buttons. Three shiny pebbles. And one of your spoons._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 2.MD.D.10, do): make and read a tally chart  
> **Pemba**: Let’s make a tally chart before we put it all back!  
> _Draw a tally mark for each thing: fruit stones, buttons, pebbles, spoons. Four marks and a line across makes five._  
> **Pemba**: Fruit stones win by a mile. Twelve! That’s more than all the others put together.  
> Check: `edu:tally:nest-treasures`
> _For grown-ups: Made a tally chart of the nest’s treasures and compared the totals (12 is more than 5 + 3 + 1)._

**Pemba**: Oh. It lives up here all alone.  
**Pemba**: Let’s put everything back exactly how we found it. It’s its home, after all.  
_Your Nubbin puts the spoon back in the nest. Then, after a long think, it takes the spoon out again._  

#### `q60-friends`

_The temple is quiet and cold. Faded paintings on the walls show monks laughing with lemurs on their shoulders._  
**Pemba**: This is where I learned to fly. It used to be full of people. Now it’s just… this.  
_The lemur peeks down from a beam. It watches Pemba, then you, then your Nubbin._  
**Pemba**: It’s been on its own for ages. It isn’t really stealing. It’s just hungry and lonely. Like me, a bit.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): showing empathy to a sad friend  
> _Pemba is sad about the empty temple. What could you say to help?_  
> - ✅ “It sounds like you really miss it.” → …Yeah. I do. Thanks for noticing.
> - “Let’s talk about snacks instead.” → Snacks are nice. But I think I needed someone to notice I was sad first.
> - “Don’t be sad.” → I can’t just switch it off. But it helps when someone says it’s okay to miss things.
> _For grown-ups: Practised noticing and naming a friend’s sad feelings._

_Your Nubbin takes a fruit from your bag, walks to the middle of the floor and sits holding it up high._  
_It doesn’t move a whisker. It doesn’t grab. It just waits._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): how to be calm around a wild animal  
> _Wild animals are often frightened by sudden movements and loud noises._  
> _Staying still and quiet, like your Nubbin, shows an animal you are not a danger. Then it can choose to come closer._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that staying still and quiet helps a wild animal feel safe._

**Lumi**: …Chirr?  

#### `q60-friends-done`

_The lemur creeps closer. One fruit. Two. Three. On the third, it lands on your shoulder._  
_It wraps its long tail round your neck and falls asleep. It is warm, and it smells faintly of peaches._  
**Pemba**: It likes you! Ha, it really likes you!  
**Pemba**: So… do we take it home? Or is this its home? It’s the only one it’s ever had.  
**Pemba**: It can’t tell us in words. We have to work out what’s fair to it.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): think question: being fair to animals  
> _Animals can’t say yes or no in words. How can we be fair to them when we decide things for them?_  
> - Watch what it does. If it follows us, it wants to come. → Good thinking. Animals “talk” with what they do.
> - Take it where there’s food and friends. That’s good for it. → That’s caring. Food and friends matter a lot to a lonely lemur.
> - Let it stay. This is its home. → That’s fair too. Home matters, even when it’s a bit broken.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how to be fair to an animal that can’t say what it wants._

_The lemur snores. It is not helping._  

**Choices**

- **Carry it home to the Grove**
    - **Pemba**: The Grove has fruit and friends. That’s a good kind of home to be carried to.
- **Set it down, leave the door open and let it choose**
    - You set it on a beam and walk away slowly. Halfway down the hill, there’s a flap of wings, and a weight on your shoulder.
    - **Pemba**: It chose you! It chose us!

#### `q60-complete`

**Pemba**: Right. Shiny things, sneaky snacks, enormous eyes. I’ve got it. You’re Lumi!  
**Pemba**: Welcome home, Lumi. The Grove has fruit and friends, and nobody’s alone there.  
**Lumi**: Chirrup chirrup!  
_Lumi rides home on your shoulder, nibbling your hair._  
_That night it sleeps curled up in the fruit basket, which explains a lot._  
_Its huge eyes stay open long after everyone else is asleep, watching the dark garden._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): nocturnal animals and big eyes  
> _Big eyes are a clue! Many animals that are busy at night have very large eyes, to catch every bit of dim light._  
> _Real colugos come out at night too. Animals that are awake at night are called nocturnal._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many nocturnal animals have large eyes to see in dim light._

**Pemba**: Every Grove needs a little thief. Just… count your spoons.  

### Glossary

- **leathery**: Tough and smooth, a bit like leather.
- **glide**: To move smoothly through the air without flapping.
- **ruins**: What is left of an old building that has fallen down.
- **tally**: A mark you make to keep count of things.
- **faded**: Lost its colour slowly over a long time.
- **nocturnal**: Awake and busy at night, and asleep in the day.

## Q61. Avatar Day

- `q61-s1`: Search the Kettleby records hall for the true story of Marshal Brag. · _Records are filed by year, with the oldest at the back. Your Nubbin can squeeze behind the dusty shelves._
- `q61-s2`: Show the evidence at Pemba’s trial. · _Choose your strongest piece. Any of them will do; some get a bigger cheer._

#### `q61-trial`

_Kettleby is having a festival. There is bunting, there are sweets, and there is a straw statue of a past Avatar._  
_People are hitting the statue with sticks._  
**Pemba**: Hey! That’s Avatar Kesh! She was me, a long time ago. Sort of. It’s complicated.  
**Mayor Tibbs**: He admits it! Four hundred years ago, Avatar Kesh ruined our founder, the Great Marshal Brag!  
**Pemba**: Wait, what? What did she do?  
**Mayor Tibbs**: She split the land in two, and Marshal Brag fell into the sea! Now you shall stand trial for it!  
**Tuk**: Hold on. He’s twelve. Four hundred years ago he wasn’t even a thought.  
**Mayor Tibbs**: Under Kettleby law, every past life counts. It’s in the rules. We wrote the rules.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, ask): think question: judging the past fairly  
> **Tuk**: Kettleby wants to punish Pemba for something Kesh did four hundred years ago.  
> _Is it fair to blame someone today for what someone else did long ago? What do you think?_  
> - No. You can only be blamed for your own choices. → That’s how I see it. Pemba wasn’t there. He didn’t choose any of it.
> - Maybe, if he really is the same person. → Hm. That’s a real puzzle. Is someone with a past life the same person? Even grown-ups argue about that.
> - We need to find out what really happened first. → Yes! Before anyone blames anyone, get the facts. That’s exactly what we’re going to do.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether people today can be blamed for what others did in the past._

_Two guards walk Pemba to a cage. It has bunting on it. Pemba waves at you through the bars, smiling a small smile._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): reading a brave face  
> _Pemba is smiling, but his wave is small and slow. Sometimes people smile even when they feel scared._  
> **Nalu**: Hang on, Pemba. We’re coming back for you.  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that a smile can hide a worried feeling, and that a kind word helps._

**Nalu**: We need proof that Kesh wasn’t the villain. Where do they keep the old records?  

**Choices**

- **Ask for a fair trial**
    - **Mayor Tibbs**: Of course! Fair, quick, and finished by lunch.
- **Let Tuk do the talking**
    - **Tuk**: Mr Mayor. Your Honour. Sir. I represent the defence.
    - **Mayor Tibbs**: Do you have any experience?
    - **Tuk**: I’ve read a book.
- **Buy a festival sweet**
    - It is shaped like a smashed statue. It tastes of peppermint and guilt.

#### `q61-trial-done`

_The records hall is dark and dusty. Shelves stretch back and back, each one labelled with a year._  
**Nalu**: Newest at the front, oldest at the back. It’s 1425 now, and Kesh lived four hundred years ago.  
**Tuk**: So we want 1025. Right at the back. Of course it’s right at the back.  

> **Lesson** (maths, do): put years in order, oldest first  
> _Help your Nubbin find the way. Put these shelf labels in order, oldest first: 1400, 1025, 1250, 1180._  
> _Oldest means the smallest year number: 1025, 1180, 1250, 1400._  
> **Nalu**: So the very back shelf is 1025. That’s where Brag’s papers will be.  
> Check: `edu:order:years:oldest-first`
> _For grown-ups: Ordered four-digit years from oldest (smallest) to newest (largest)._

_Your Nubbin squeezes behind the oldest shelf. There is a sneeze, a scrabble and a cloud of dust._  
_It comes back out holding a scroll sealed with Marshal Brag’s own stamp._  
**Nalu**: It’s his diary. Written by Brag himself. Look at this entry. And this one.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): a diary is evidence from the time  
> **Nalu**: A diary is one of the best kinds of evidence. It was written at the time, by someone who was really there.  
> _Stories told later can grow and change as people pass them on. A diary stays just as it was written._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why a diary written at the time is strong evidence about the past._


#### `q61-evidence`

_The trial is held in the village square. The judge is Mayor Tibbs. The jury is also Mayor Tibbs._  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.Civ.8.K-2, notice): what makes a trial fair  
> **Tuk**: Hang on. One person is the accuser, the judge AND the jury? That hardly seems fair.  
> _In a fair trial, the people who decide should listen to both sides before they make up their minds._  
> _That’s why real courts have a judge, and often a jury, who did not bring the case._  
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why fair trials need people who listen to both sides before deciding._

**Mayor Tibbs**: The prisoner may speak, but briefly. We have a parade at four.  
**Tuk**: Your Honour. We have found Marshal Brag’s diary, written in his own hand.  
**Nalu**: “Today I shall march onto Avatar Kesh’s island and take it. Then the next island. Then all the islands.”  
**Tuk**: “Note to self: build a bigger hat.”  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): describe a character from his own words  
> _Brag’s own words tell us what he was like. Which word fits him best?_  
> - ✅ Greedy: he wanted island after island. → Yes. Take one island, then the next, then all of them. That’s greed, in his own handwriting.
> - Kind → Kind people don’t plan to take everyone’s islands. His words show he was greedy.
> - Shy → A shy person doesn’t want a bigger hat! His words show he was greedy, and a bit of a show-off.
> _For grown-ups: Described a character’s traits using evidence from his own words._

_The crowd murmurs. Someone at the back takes off a Marshal Brag hat and quietly puts it in a bin._  
**Mayor Tibbs**: That… does sound a bit like a bully.  
**Nalu**: Kesh didn’t attack anyone. She protected her home. Brag fell in because he wouldn’t step back when the cliff cracked.  
**Mayor Tibbs**: One more piece of evidence and I’ll be convinced. Keeper? What else did you find?  

**Choices**

- **Show the founding stone that thanks Avatar Kesh**
    - **Mayor Tibbs**: “Thank you, Kesh, for our peace.” It was under the statue all along!
- **Show the old map with Kettleby on Kesh’s side**
    - **Mayor Tibbs**: We were… on her island. Oh dear. She was protecting us.
- **Point out that Pemba has been nice to everyone all day**
    - **Mayor Tibbs**: That is not evidence. That is, however, very true.

#### `q61-evidence-done`

**Mayor Tibbs**: The court finds the prisoner… not guilty! Release the Avatar!  
_The guards open the cage. Pemba steps out, still wearing a strand of bunting like a scarf._  
**Pemba**: Yay! Can I keep the bunting?  
**Mayor Tibbs**: Take it! Started at quarter past three, finished at twenty to four. The fastest trial in Kettleby history!  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.A.1, ask): find a time interval to the minute  
> **Tuk**: Quarter past three to twenty to four. How long did the trial take?  
> - ✅ 25 minutes → Yes. Quarter past three is 3:15. Twenty to four is 3:40. From 15 to 40 is 25 minutes.
> - 20 minutes → Close! 3:15 to 3:35 is 20 minutes, and five more gets to 3:40. That’s 25.
> - 45 minutes → That would be 3:15 to 4:00. But it finished at twenty to four, which is 3:40. That’s 25 minutes.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the time from 3:15 to 3:40: 25 minutes._

**Pemba**: Keeper? Even if Kesh had done something bad… should I say sorry for it? It wasn’t me. But it sort of was.  
_Pemba waits for your answer. For once, he is completely still._  

**Choices**

- **“You’re not to blame for what she did.”**
    - **Pemba**: Okay. Then I’ll just try to be someone who deserves a nicer statue.
- **“It isn’t your fault. But you can still help fix things.”**
    - **Pemba**: Oh. I like that better than blame. Blame just sits there. Fixing gets to do things.
    - **Tuk**: Write that down. That’s going on a sign.

#### `q61-complete`

_That evening the straw statue comes down. In its place the villagers build a new one. It looks a lot like Pemba._  
**Mayor Tibbs**: From now on, Avatar Day will be Pemba Day! With fewer sticks and more sweets.  
**Pemba**: That’s the best day I’ve ever heard of!  
**Tuk**: You realise you’re a holiday now. That’s going to go straight to your head.  
**Pemba**: It’s already in my head. It’s having a party.  
**Mayor Tibbs**: And from now on, we read our own records before anyone picks up a stick. We should have done that years ago.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): find the theme of a story  
> _Every good story teaches something. What lesson did Kettleby learn today?_  
> - ✅ Find out the facts before you blame someone. → Exactly. We had the truth on our own shelves all along. We just never looked.
> - Statues are a bad idea. → The statue wasn’t the problem. Blaming without checking was. The lesson: find out the facts first.
> - Never have festivals. → Ha! They’re having a bigger festival than ever. The lesson is to find out the facts before you blame someone.
> _For grown-ups: Named the theme of the quest: find out the facts before blaming anyone._

_The mayor hands you a painted festival mask, and an invitation: Pemba Day will come once to the Grove._  

### Glossary

- **founder**: The person who started a town, a club or a business.
- **trial**: A meeting where someone decides whether a rule or law has been broken.
- **evidence**: Facts or things that help show what is true.
- **entry**: One piece of writing in a diary, usually for one day.
- **jury**: A group of people who listen at a trial and decide what is true.
- **murmurs**: Talks in low, quiet voices.
- **guilty**: Having done the wrong thing you are accused of.

## Q62. Penguin Sledding

- `q62-s1`: Break Pemba out of the block of ice. · _Tap the glowing cracks. Your Nubbins warm the ice when they huddle close._
- `q62-s2`: Make friends with a penguin and race Pemba down the snowy hill. · _Offer a fish first, then lean left and right to steer. Lying flat on your tummy is fastest._

#### `q62-iceberg`

_Snow covers the Grove. On the bank of the frozen pond, Nalu and Tuk are poking at a huge block of ice that wasn’t there yesterday._  
**Tuk**: For the record, I said leave it. Mysterious glowing ice is never good news.  
**Nalu**: It’s Pemba! He sat down by the pond last night to meditate, and he just… didn’t stop.  
**Tuk**: Or, hear me out, we fetch a grown-up with a chisel. And nobody sets foot on that pond. Pond ice is thinner than it looks.  
_Your Nubbin presses its paws to the ice and looks up at you. Under the surface, a blue arrow glows faintly._  
**Nalu**: Please. He could be freezing in there.  
**Tuk**: He’s inside a block of ice, Nalu. I think it’s a bit late to worry about that.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): melting and freezing can be reversed  
> **Nalu**: Think! How can we turn this ice back into water?  
> - ✅ Warm it up → Yes! Heat melts ice into water. And if the water gets cold enough, it freezes back into ice. It works both ways.
> - Shout at it → I’ve tried. It doesn’t listen. Warmth is what melts ice.
> - Pile more snow on it → More snow would keep it cold! We need warmth to melt it.
> _For grown-ups: Learned that warming melts ice into water, and cooling can freeze it again._


**Choices**

- **Crack it with a stone**
    - You strike. A thin crack zigzags across the ice.
- **Get your Nubbins to huddle round it**
    - Your Nubbins press together against the ice. It starts to drip, then trickle.
- **Hand Tuk his boomerang**
    - **Tuk**: Fine. FINE. But once he’s defrosted, he’s hearing all about who said leave it.

#### `q62-iceberg-done`

_Drip. Trickle. Crack! The ice splits with a whoosh of air._  
_Pemba sits up and blinks. His eyebrows have gone white with frost._  
**Nalu**: Are you all right? Are you cold? Are you hurt?  
_Your Nubbins huddle round him in a warm, furry heap._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS2-1, notice): animals in groups keep each other warm  
> **Nalu**: Huddling is clever. Emperor penguins do it all winter, crowding together to share warmth in the freezing wind.  
> _They even take turns. The ones on the cold outside shuffle slowly into the warm middle._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that emperor penguins huddle and take turns to survive the cold together._

**Pemba**: Morning, everyone! Have I missed breakfast? And, important question: any penguins?  
**Tuk**: Of all the questions. OF ALL THE QUESTIONS.  

#### `q62-sled`

**Nalu**: Do we have… what?  
**Pemba**: Penguins! A whole row of them waddled past while I was meditating. Round ones. Slippy ones.  
**Tuk**: He spent the whole night as an ice cube, and his first question is about penguins.  
**Pemba**: What would your first question be?  
**Tuk**: …Probably “where’s the food”. Okay, fair.  
**Nalu**: Pemba… how long were you stuck in there?  
**Pemba**: All night, I think. It was lovely and calm. And then it was very, very cold.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, ask): think question: too much of a good thing  
> _Meditating is good for Pemba. It makes him calm. But he did it for so long that he froze._  
> _Can a good thing turn into too much? What do you think?_  
> - Yes. Even good things need a stopping point. → That’s fair. Next time I’ll set an alarm. A loud one.
> - No. Good things are always good. → Lots of good things stay good. But too much sun, or too much cake, or too much sitting in the snow… I think how much matters too.
> - It depends on the thing, and on how you feel. → That’s wise. Your body usually tells you when to stop. Pemba just wasn’t listening.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether a good thing can become too much, and how to notice when to stop._

**Pemba**: I need warming up. Do you think a penguin would let me sit on it?  
_On the snowy hill, a line of penguins waddles past, sleek and round and not at all in the mood._  
**Pemba**: The trick is fish. You give them a fish, they give you a ride. Everyone knows that.  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): penguins are birds that swim and slide  
> **Nalu**: Penguins are birds, but they can’t fly. They swim instead, and they catch fish to eat.  
> **Tuk**: And on ice, penguins sometimes slide along on their tummies, pushing with their feet. It’s faster than waddling.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that penguins are flightless birds that swim, eat fish and slide on their bellies._

_Your Nubbin is already holding out a fish to the smallest penguin. The penguin considers it carefully._  

#### `q62-sled-done`

_The penguin flops onto its tummy. You flop onto its back. Your Nubbin flops onto you._  
_Down the hill you whizz, over the snow, then across a long, glassy frozen puddle at the bottom and into a snowdrift._  
_On the snow you were fast. On the ice you were even faster, and you hardly slowed down at all._  
_Pemba lands beside you, laughing too hard to stand._  
**Pemba**: Again! Again! AGAIN!  
**Tuk**: Hang on. Why did we go so much faster on the ice than on the snow?  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): friction slows things down  
> **Nalu**: Good question. What do you think?  
> - ✅ Ice is smoother, so there’s less friction to slow us down. → Exactly. Friction is a force that slows things when they rub together. Smooth ice has very little of it.
> - Penguins like ice better. → They probably do! But the real reason is friction. Snow rubs and slows you more; smooth ice barely does.
> - The ice was pushing us. → Ice can’t push. It just has less friction, so there’s less to slow you down.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that smooth ice has less friction than snow, so sliders go faster on it._


#### `q62-complete`

**Nalu**: I haven’t seen anyone laugh like that in a long time.  
**Tuk**: I haven’t seen anyone eat that much snow in a long time. You’re a walking snowman.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understand a metaphor  
> _Tuk calls Pemba “a walking snowman”. Is Pemba really a snowman?_  
> - ✅ No. Tuk means he’s so covered in snow he looks like one. → Yes. That’s a metaphor: saying someone IS something, to show what they’re like.
> - Yes. He turned into a snowman in the ice. → Ha! He’d be a lot quieter if he had. It’s a metaphor: I mean he’s so snowy he looks like one.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a metaphor that calls a snow-covered friend “a walking snowman”._

**Pemba**: The penguins say you can come back any snow day. Well, they didn’t say it. But they looked it.  
**Pemba**: Thanks for defrosting me, everyone. And for the penguin. The penguin was the best bit.  
**Nalu**: Next time you meditate in the snow, take a blanket. And a friend.  
_The penguins waddle home over the hill. The smallest one turns back to stare at your Nubbin, who waves._  

### Glossary

- **chisel**: A metal tool with a sharp edge, for chipping wood, stone or ice.
- **meditate**: To sit quietly and still for a while, calming your mind.
- **huddle**: To crowd closely together, often to keep warm.
- **sleek**: Smooth and shiny.
- **considers**: Thinks carefully about something.
- **snowdrift**: A deep heap of snow piled up by the wind.
- **friction**: A force that slows things down when they rub against each other.

## Q63. King Rumbold’s Challenges

- `q63-s1`: Fetch the king’s key from the bottom of the waterfall. · _A Swim Nubbin can dive into the pool. Otherwise, wait for the water to drop at noon._
- `q63-s2`: Find Biscuit the goat-yak somewhere in Stonereach. · _Follow the bleating. Goat-yaks love high places and anything that looks like a cabbage._
- `q63-s3`: Ride the mail chutes to the bottom of Stonereach with King Rumbold. · _Lean into the bends and duck under the letter slots. The king will not slow down._

#### `q63-throne`

_In the city of Stonereach, carved into the cliffs, the king sits on a stone throne. He is very old, very wrinkled, and grinning._  
**King Rumbold**: Visitors! I love visitors. You will face three challenges. If you fail, you will be… hmm… sent home without pudding.  
**Tuk**: That’s… actually a pretty scary punishment.  
_King Rumbold throws back his head and laughs: a loud, honking bray, like a donkey that has heard a very good joke._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): understand a simile  
> _His laugh is “like a donkey that has heard a very good joke”. What does this simile tell you about it?_  
> - ✅ It’s loud, honking and silly. → Yes! Donkeys bray loudly. Adding “a very good joke” makes it sound happy and ridiculous too.
> - It’s quiet and polite. → Have you ever heard a donkey bray? It’s very loud! The simile tells you his laugh is loud and silly.
> - He looks like a donkey. → The simile is about how his laugh sounds, not how he looks. Loud, honking and silly.
> _For grown-ups: Explained what a simile tells the reader about a character’s laugh._

**King Rumbold**: Challenge one! I have dropped the key to my snack cupboard to the bottom of the waterfall. Fetch it!  
**Pemba**: How did it get down there?  
**King Rumbold**: I threw it. I wanted to see if it could fly. It could not.  
**Tuk**: And before you try it, Your Majesty: keys don’t float either.  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, notice): why some things sink and others float  
> **Tuk**: A metal key is heavy for its size, so it sinks. A wooden spoon is light for its size, so it floats.  
> _Whether something floats depends on what it’s made of, not just on how big it is. A huge log floats; a tiny pebble sinks._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that whether an object floats depends on its material, not just its size._


**Choices**

- **Accept the challenge**
    - **King Rumbold**: Wonderful! Off you go! Mind the fish, they nibble.
- **Ask why he needs the key**
    - **King Rumbold**: Because I am hungry, child. Why does anyone want anything?
- **Laugh along with him**
    - You laugh. He laughs harder. Your Nubbin brays. The guards look very tired.

#### `q63-throne-done`

_Your Nubbin climbs back up the cliff path, dripping, with the key in its mouth._  
**King Rumbold**: My key! My snacks are safe! Challenge one complete!  
_He unlocks the cupboard and takes out a whole round cake, already cut into eight slices._  
**King Rumbold**: Would you like some? There are four of us. That’s… hmm… a lot of maths.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.NF.A.1, ask): unit fractions: sharing into quarters  
> **Tuk**: Eight slices, four of us. If we shared fairly, what fraction of the cake would each of us get?  
> - ✅ Two slices each: one quarter of the cake → Yes! Eight shared by four is two each. Two out of eight is the same as one quarter. Not that it matters now.
> - One slice each: one eighth → That would leave four slices over! Eight shared by four is two each: one quarter of the cake.
> - Half each → Half each only works for two people. With four of us, it’s a quarter each: two slices.
> _For grown-ups: Shared 8 slices among 4 and named each share as one quarter._

_Before anyone can answer, he eats the whole cake in one bite, without breaking eye contact._  
**Tuk**: Eight slices. One bite. I’m impressed and upset at the same time.  

#### `q63-pet`

**King Rumbold**: Challenge two! My pet, Biscuit, has run away again. He is somewhere in the city. Find him!  
**Tuk**: What kind of animal is Biscuit?  
**King Rumbold**: He is a goat-yak. You will know him because he looks like a goat, and also like a yak.  
_A stone mail chute rattles past your head. Somewhere in the city, something bleats._  
**Tuk**: Stone city. Narrow streets. One goat-yak. Okay, we sweep from the top down. Pemba, you take the roofs.  
**Pemba**: I love roofs!  
**King Rumbold**: Or! Instead of looking for Biscuit, you could think like Biscuit.  
**Tuk**: I am not going to think like a goat-yak.  
_Your Nubbin is already climbing the highest wall in sight, chewing a leaf thoughtfully._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): mountain goats are built for climbing  
> _Thinking like Biscuit is good science! Real mountain goats are amazing climbers._  
> _Their hooves have hard edges, with soft, grippy pads underneath. That helps them cling to steep rock._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a mountain goat’s hooves help it climb steep rock._


#### `q63-pet-done`

_You find Biscuit on a rooftop, eating a cabbage from a cart that looks very familiar._  
_Somewhere far below, a familiar voice wails._  
**Tuk**: I know that wail. Somebody’s having a bad cabbage day.  
**King Rumbold**: Biscuit! You found him! That’s two!  
_Biscuit chews the last leaf, looks at you, and burps._  
**King Rumbold**: He says thank you. That is how goat-yaks say thank you.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): putting things right when your pet causes trouble  
> _Biscuit ate the cabbage merchant’s cabbage. What would be the fair thing to do?_  
> - ✅ Pay the merchant back for the cabbage. → Quite right! The royal purse shall pay. Biscuit, that comes out of your pocket money.
> - Nothing. Biscuit is only a goat-yak. → Biscuit didn’t know better, but his owner does. Fixing the harm is still fair: pay the merchant back.
> - Blame the merchant for leaving it out. → Leaving a cart in the street isn’t asking for it to be eaten! The fair thing is to pay him back.
> _For grown-ups: Decided that when your pet causes harm, the fair thing is to put it right._


#### `q63-opponent`

**King Rumbold**: Challenge three. The last, and the most dangerous. You must face an opponent. And you may choose who!  
_He points to a huge guard with a hammer, to a hulking rock beast in a cage, and to himself._  
**Tuk**: Okay. Easy. Don’t pick the beast. Don’t pick the hammer. Pick the very old man.  
**Pemba**: Tuk, I think the very old man is the scary one.  
**King Rumbold**: Choose wisely! Or unwisely! I enjoy both!  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): predict using what you know about a character  
> _So far, King Rumbold’s challenges have been a thrown key and a runaway pet. What do you predict challenge three really is?_  
> - ✅ Something silly and fun → Good prediction! Everything the king does is a bit silly. Let’s see if you’re right.
> - A real, terrible fight → It could be! But the king loves jokes. His challenges so far were silly, so this one probably is too.
> - A maths test → Ha! There was some maths with the cake. But the king seems to like fun more than tests.
> _For grown-ups: Used what a character has done so far to predict what he will do next._

_Your Nubbin points at the guard, then the beast, then shakes its head firmly at both._  

**Choices**

- **Choose the guard**
    - **King Rumbold**: Wrong! Your true opponent is… the MAIL CHUTES! Nobody beats the mail chutes!
- **Choose the rock beast**
    - **King Rumbold**: Wrong! Your true opponent is… the MAIL CHUTES! Nobody beats the mail chutes!
- **Choose King Rumbold himself**
    - **King Rumbold**: Ooh, closer! But still wrong!
    - **King Rumbold**: Your true opponent is… the MAIL CHUTES! And I am coming with you!

#### `q63-opponent-done`

_The mail chutes are long stone slides that carry letters from the top of the city to the bottom._  
_You sit at the top. King Rumbold sits behind you. Nobody asks if this is allowed. He is the king._  
_You start slowly. Then the chute tips steeply down, and you go faster and faster._  
_You shoot out of the last chute into a pile of letters. The king lands on top of you, honking with laughter._  
**King Rumbold**: Again! Oh, wait. I’m the king. I can do this whenever I like.  
**Tuk**: Why do the steep bits go so much faster than the flat bits?  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, ask): gravity and slopes  
> **King Rumbold**: Ah, a scientist! Well, Keeper? Why?  
> - ✅ Gravity pulls us down, and a steep slope lets it pull us along faster. → Exactly! Gravity always pulls down. The steeper the chute, the more of that pull sends you whizzing.
> - The letters push us. → Ha! Letters are lazy. It’s gravity: it pulls you down, and a steep slope turns that pull into speed.
> - The flat bits are sticky. → Not sticky! On the flat, gravity pulls you into the floor, not along it. On a steep chute, it pulls you along.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that gravity pulls things down a slope, and steeper slopes make them go faster._


> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, do): test a steep ramp against a gentle one  
> **King Rumbold**: Try it yourself! Lean a book on one other book to make a ramp, and roll a ball down it.  
> _Now add another book underneath to make the ramp steeper. Roll the ball again. Which run was faster?_  
> **King Rumbold**: The steep one! Gravity, at work. Now do it a hundred more times. I did.  
> Check: `edu:test:ramp:steep-gentle`
> _For grown-ups: Tested a ball on a gentle ramp and a steeper ramp and compared the speeds._
