_At the ring, the thin one wakes in your arms, sees her mother, and goes stiff all over with joy._  
_Bramble washes her, ear to ear. Then she noses the old brown ribbon off her folded ear and drops it at your feet._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-LS1-2, notice): parents help their young survive  
> _Lots of animal mothers wash their babies, the way a cat licks her kittens clean._  
> _It keeps the baby clean and warm, and tells it: you’re mine, and you’re safe._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that animal parents care for their young, for example by washing them._

_Behind her, three strays stand up and look at you, as if waiting to see where you go next._  
**Nova**: That’s you invited. Come whenever you like. Bring soft fruit.  

#### `s9-gate-family`

_First light. The pond is grey and still. Hazel sits beside it with a cup, her back to the gate._  
_Corvin is at the gate. He has been there all night._  
_There’s frost on his shoulders: the ordinary kind, the kind that melts._  
**Corvin Vale**: Hazel’s grandchild.  
_His hands rest on the top bar. They aren’t blue any more. They shake a little, the way warm hands do in the cold._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-PS2-1, notice): hinges, and why handles go far from them  
> _A gate swings on its hinges: the metal joints that hold it to the post._  
> _Push near the hinges and it barely moves. Push far from them, out by the latch, and it swings easily._  
> _That’s why latches and handles always go on the far side._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that a push far from a hinge turns a gate more easily, which is why handles sit far from hinges._

_At the edge of the long grass, a grey ear turns towards his voice, and goes flat._  
**Corvin Vale**: Things keep reaching me this week, from your side of the valley. Things people said. Things people found.  
**Corvin Vale**: I didn’t know what to do with any of it. I still don’t. I kept all of it anyway.  
**Corvin Vale**: I know who’s sitting by that pond. I know what I took from her. I’m asking anyway.  
_Behind you, Hazel drinks her tea and does not turn round. She is listening to every word._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): forgiveness and trust (think question)  
> _Corvin is sorry. He gave back the trowel. He asked, instead of taking._  
> _But the grey ear in the long grass still goes flat when he speaks._  
> _Can you forgive someone, but not trust them yet?_  
> - Yes. Forgiving and trusting are different. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Forgiving is letting go of the anger. Trust gets built slowly, one visit at a time.
> - No. If you forgive, you should trust them again. → That’s a fair answer, and a generous one. Some people feel that way. Others think trust takes longer than sorry.
> - It depends on what they did. → That’s a wise answer. Small things are easy to forgive and trust again. Big things, like taking Ash, can take years.
> - I’m not sure yet. → That’s an honest answer, and it’s allowed. Hazel took twenty-two years. You can take your time too.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between forgiving someone and trusting them (a think question with no wrong answer)._


**Choices**

- **Show him the trick. “Lift and push.”**
    - **You**: Lift and push. Both at once. It was never the latch.
    - He looks at you. Then he puts both hands on the bar, lifts the gate a finger’s width, and pushes.
    - It swings open. It sticks again behind him, the way it does for everyone who lives here.
    - **Corvin Vale**: …Oh.
    - **Corvin Vale**: That’s all it ever was.
    - He walks to the pond and sits down an arm’s length from Hazel. She hands him the cup without looking.
    - Neither of them says anything. He isn’t very good at it yet. She is.
    - In the long grass, the grey ear is still flat. Not today, then. Perhaps not this year.
- **Open it for him. Don’t show him how.**
    - You lift and push, and the gate opens. He watches your hands. You turn them so he can’t quite see.
    - **Corvin Vale**: Thank you.
    - **Corvin Vale**: I’ll have to knock, every time. That’s right. That’s more than right.
    - By the pond, Hazel lifts one hand a little and lets it fall. It might be a wave.
- **Leave it shut.**
    - You don’t move. He looks at you, then at the latch, and nods, as if you’ve told him the time.
    - **Corvin Vale**: Yes. All right. Yes.
    - **Corvin Vale**: It ought to cost something. I’d think less of this place if it didn’t.
    - **Corvin Vale**: Thank you for taking the trowel. I mean that.
    - He takes his hands off the gate one at a time. He goes down the lane, and is gone before Sparks arrives.
    - By the pond, Hazel finishes her tea. She sits a while longer than she needs to.

#### `s10-lanterns-kept`

_At the stream lantern, she laughs at nothing at all. Then she explains that Briar would have._  
**Gran Hazel**: Briar’s. You can’t stand here and be gloomy. People have tried.  
_At the old wall, she says nothing. She puts her hand flat on the post, the way you’d touch a sleeping friend._  
**Gran Hazel**: Hush’s. For keeping. I kept a great deal here, one way and another.  

> **Lesson** (social-studies, D2.His.2.K-2, notice): oral history: how stories carry the past  
> _Each post has a story. Gran learned them from people who learned them from people older still._  
> _The past, remembered in stories told out loud, is called oral history. It’s how the Grove remembers._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that oral history keeps the past alive through stories told aloud._

_Then the long grass. The fourth post flickers, the way it has for twenty-two years._  
_Hazel stops. She looks at it, and then at you, for a long time._  
**Gran Hazel**: Still flickering. Well.  
**Gran Hazel**: I stopped hoping, after a while. I never stopped looking. They’re different things. Remember that.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): hope and patience (think question)  
> **Gran Hazel**: Hoping and looking. I say they’re different. You tell me.  
> _Can you keep looking for something even after you’ve stopped hoping?_  
> - Yes. Looking can be a way of loving. → That’s how it felt. Looking was just what I did, every night, because I loved them. That’s a thoughtful answer.
> - No. If you’re still looking, you must still hope a bit. → Maybe you’re right. Maybe a tiny bit of hope stayed, hiding under the looking. That’s a fair answer, and Gran likes it.
> - I don’t know. → Neither did I, for twenty-two years. That’s allowed. That’s an honest answer.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the difference between hoping and keeping on (a think question with no wrong answer)._

_…_  
**Gran Hazel**: Can I ask you something? I’ve never asked anyone. There’s never been anyone to ask.  
**Gran Hazel**: Should I have gone after him? That night. Instead of wedging a gate and waiting.  

**Choices**

- **You were right to wait. He had to come back on his own.**
    - **Gran Hazel**: Maybe. It’s a very comfortable answer. I’ve been suspicious of it for twenty-two years.
    - **Gran Hazel**: But you can’t carry anyone back. I’ve tried, with Nubbins. They only ever walk.
    - **Gran Hazel**: Thank you for walking it with me. I mean that. Whatever else.
- **Somebody should have gone after him.**
    - **Gran Hazel**: Yes. Some nights I think so too.
    - **Gran Hazel**: I’d have dragged him home by the ear. He’d have hated me properly, and the valley might never have gone grey.
    - **Gran Hazel**: Or I’d have stood in that cold garden long enough to start liking the quiet. I don’t know. I never will.
    - **Gran Hazel**: Thank you for walking it with me. I mean that. Whatever else.

#### `s10-night-told`

_You walk her home. The Keepers have stayed late by the pond. None of them wants to be the first to go._  
_Hazel sends them home one at a time, like a teacher at the end of a very long day._  
**Gran Hazel**: Look at them. Lumps. Every one of them.  
**Gran Hazel**: Tomorrow you’ll tell them what the Grove is going to be.  
**Gran Hazel**: They can walk me to the bottom. Not one step further. Tell them. They listen to you.  
_She goes in. Down the lane, somebody is crying very quietly, and somebody else is passing them a handkerchief._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): comforting someone by staying close  
> _Nobody could make Gran better. So the Keepers did what they could: they stayed close._  
> _When someone is sad, being near them, and passing a handkerchief, is a real way to help._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that staying close is a real way to comfort someone who is sad._


#### `s10-foot`

_The foot of the hill path. The grass is long here. It’s the exact place she always stopped for breath._  
_She looks back at the Grove once: the pond, the gate, the four posts._  
**Gran Hazel**: It looks like somebody lives here. It hasn’t looked like that for a long time.  
_You both know what this walk is. Gran is going up the hill to stay. Her life is ending, and she won’t come back down._  
**Gran Hazel**: Now, then. I can walk up on my own. I’d rather not.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, notice): asking for company in a hard moment  
> _Gran could do this alone. But she’s asking for company._  
> _Asking someone to be with you when something is hard is brave. It’s never weak._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that asking for company and help in hard moments is brave._

**Gran Hazel**: Who’s coming?  

**Choices**

- **Just me, Gran.**
    - **Gran Hazel**: Good. The quiet way. I like the quiet way.

#### `s10-foot-c`

_The foot of the hill path. The grass is long here. It’s the exact place she always stopped for breath._  
_She looks back at the Grove once: the pond, the gate, the four posts._  
**Gran Hazel**: It looks like somebody lives here. It hasn’t looked like that for a long time.  
_You both know what this walk is. Gran is going up the hill to stay. Her life is ending, and she won’t come back down._  
**Gran Hazel**: Now, then. I can walk up on my own. I’d rather not.

#### `s10-letter-told`

_Morning. Your Nubbins are up before you. The gate is stuck. You lift and push._  
_Her lantern is back on the hook by the cottage door. Somebody carried it down at first light._  
_You haven’t lit it yet._  
_Gran Hazel died up on the hill in the night. Her body stopped working, and it won’t start again._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): grief: what it is and what helps  
> _The big, heavy sadness you feel when someone you love dies is called grief._  
> _Grief can come in waves: all right one minute, very sad the next. That’s normal._  
> _What helps is people, and remembering. Gran made sure you’d have both._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the word grief, that it comes in waves, and that people and remembering help._

_On the signpost, under the stone, where the first one was: a letter in your grandmother’s writing._  
**Gran Hazel**: “If you’re reading this, I’ve gone up the hill, and this time I’m staying. Don’t be dramatic about it.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “Be a little dramatic. I’ve earned a little.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “You kept my three rules, more or less, which is more than I did. Here’s a fourth, because I can’t help myself.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “Show up. Every morning, same stuck gate, same stubborn chin. That’s all a Grove ever was. The rest is fruit.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “Tell Fern to prune the trees. Tell Sparks the hair grows back. Tell Byte his shoelaces are untied.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “Leave fruit at the edge for the ones in the long grass. You won’t always see who eats it. Leave it anyway.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “If he came to the gate, you’ll have decided about Corvin by now. Whatever you decided, I’d have done it worse.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “I’m not sorry. I’m sorry it’s now. Both are true. You knew that already.”  
**Gran Hazel**: “Love, Gran. P.S. The gate sticks. You know the rest.”  

> **Lesson** (literacy, notice): how a letter is set out  
> _Gran’s letter talks straight to you, and ends with a sign-off: “Love, Gran.”_  
> _“P.S.” is short for postscript, which means “written after”. It’s for one last thing you think of after you sign._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how a letter is set out, including the sign-off and the P.S. (postscript)._

_The Keepers are already at the gate. By the look of them, none of them slept much._  
_You read it out to them, all of it. Clover cries. Byte checks his shoelaces._  
_They are untied._  

#### `s13-letter-given`

_Hazel turns the trowel over in her lap. You think of the letter in the tin box under your bed, and slip in to fetch it._  
_You go down the lane after him. Frost is coming down blue on the hedges, and your breath goes ahead of you._  
_He is at the bend by the stile, his hands pushed under his arms. He keeps stopping to feel them._  
**Corvin Vale**: Hazel’s grandchild. Twice in one evening. People will talk.  
_You hold out the letter. He sees the writing on the front, and doesn’t take it._  
**Corvin Vale**: That’s my father’s hand. He wrote as if he were being timed.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, ask): choose the right meaning of a multiple-meaning word  
> _Corvin says, “That’s my father’s hand.” “Hand” has more than one meaning._  
> _Which meaning does he use here?_  
> - ✅ His handwriting. → Yes. Your “hand” can mean your handwriting. Corvin knows his father’s writing at a glance.
> - His real hand, at the end of his arm. → That’s the usual meaning. But he’s looking at a letter, so here “hand” means handwriting.
> - A helping hand. → Good thinking, that’s another meaning. But he’s looking at the writing on the front, so here it means handwriting.
> _For grown-ups: Used context to pick the right meaning of “hand” (handwriting)._

**You**: It was in the mill cellar. Tobin kept it. Your father wrote it after you’d gone.  
_He takes it. His fingers are clumsy with the cold still coming out of them. It takes him three goes to unfold it._  
_He reads it by the last of the light. Then again, slower. You look at the hedge, so he doesn’t have to be looked at._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): give someone privacy when they have a big feeling  
> _Sometimes the kindest thing is to look away for a moment._  
> _When someone is having a big feeling, a little privacy helps them feel safe. You stay close, but you don’t stare._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed how giving someone privacy can be a way to show kindness and respect._

**Corvin Vale**: “Nobody would count.”  
**Corvin Vale**: He counted my hours at the sluice. In a book. I used to check his sums for him.  
_He folds the letter along its old folds, and puts it in his breast pocket, where the tin was for twenty-two years._  
_His hand rests there. When it comes away, it doesn’t hurry._  
**Corvin Vale**: Thank you. I don’t know what else. Thank you.  
_He goes on down the lane. You walk back up to the cottage, where Hazel is still on the step._  

#### `s13-letter-nomoss`

_The paper is good paper, the kind you’d buy for something that mattered. You unfold it._  
**Aldous Vale**: Corvin.  
**Aldous Vale**: I have started this nine times. The other eight went in the stove. You’d say that was waste. You’d be right. I taught you that.  
**Aldous Vale**: They say in the valley that you did a wrong thing at the old woman’s Grove, and left in the night. I don’t know what. I know how.  
**Aldous Vale**: Quickly. In the dark. Without once sitting down to think. I know whose hands those were. They were mine first.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): work out what a metaphor really means  
> _Aldous writes: “I know whose hands those were. They were mine first.”_  
> _He doesn’t mean real hands. What is he really saying?_  
> - ✅ Corvin learned his rushing, cold way of doing things from his father. → Yes. Here “hands” stands for a way of doing things. Saying one thing to mean another is called a metaphor. Aldous is owning up: Corvin learned it from him.
> - Corvin borrowed his father’s gloves. → Ha! Not quite. Here “hands” means how someone does things. Aldous means: you do things my way, quick and in the dark.
> - Aldous wants his hands back. → It’s a metaphor, so it isn’t about real hands at all. “Hands” means a way of doing things. Aldous is saying Corvin learned his ways from him.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the meaning of a metaphor in a letter (“they were mine first”)._

**Aldous Vale**: I can tell you the weight of every sack this mill ground the year you were born. I can’t tell you what you laughed at.  
**Aldous Vale**: Your mother used to sit by the mill race in the evenings, with her feet in the water. I called it idling.  
**Aldous Vale**: I would give the whole mill to sit there once with her now.  
**Aldous Vale**: I won’t say sorry. I don’t know how, and you’d hear it as one more order. You always heard me that way. I made sure of it.  
**Aldous Vale**: I’ve stopped the wheel. It’s very quiet. I think you’d hate it. I think you’d get used to it.  
**Aldous Vale**: If you ever stop, stop here. You could sit as long as you liked. Nobody would count.  
**Aldous Vale**: Your father.  
_…_  
**Old Tobin**: “Nobody would count.” He counted everything. His own boy’s hours, in a book. And then he wrote that.  
**Old Tobin**: It isn’t mine to decide what happens to it. It never was. I only held the door shut.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): think about whether we must become like the people who raised us  
> **Old Tobin**: Aldous had three rules, and the boy copied them out. Hazel had three rules too, and hers were kind ones.  
> **Old Tobin**: Here’s a hard one, and I’ve no answer to it. Do we have to turn out like the grown-ups who raised us? Or can we choose differently?  
> - We can choose differently, even if it’s hard. → That’s a hopeful answer, and a fair one. Aldous himself stopped the wheel, right at the end. Late. But he chose.
> - We copy them a lot, without even noticing. → That’s honest, and it’s often true. The boy copied those rules in his best writing. Noticing what you’ve copied is the first step to choosing what to keep.
> - A bit of both. → I think that’s where I’d land too. We carry what we’re given. Then we decide what to keep, and what to set down.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how habits pass down through families, and whether we can choose differently (a think question with no single right answer)._


**Choices**

- **Keep it for Corvin. Give it to him when he can feel again.**
    - You fold it along its old folds and put it inside your coat, next to Hazel’s notebook.
    - **Old Tobin**: When he can feel again. Yes. Cold hands can’t hold a thing like that. It would slip straight through them.
    - **Old Tobin**: You’ll know when. Your grandmother always knew when. It was infuriating.
- **Burn it. Some things should end with the person.**
    - **Old Tobin**: …That’s a real answer. I’ve thought it myself, most winters.
    - **Old Tobin**: He wrote nine and burned eight. You’d only be finishing what he started.
- **Read it aloud at Aldous’s grave, and leave it there.**
    - **Old Tobin**: Read aloud, and left with the man. Yes.
    - **Old Tobin**: Nobody ever read Aldous anything. He never had the time to listen. He has now.

#### `s13-settled-burned`

_The mill’s old stove still draws. Tobin gets it going with a handful of chaff and a great deal of advice._  
_He keeps charge of the stove door. You stand back from the heat, the way he tells you to._  
_The letter catches at one corner. Then all of it goes at once, quickly, the way Aldous did everything._  
_For a moment you can read “Your father” in the flame. Then you can’t._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, ask): some changes from heating can’t be undone  
> _When ice melts, you can freeze the water and get ice back._  
> _Can the ash and smoke ever turn back into the letter?_  
> - ✅ No. Burning is a change that can’t be undone. → That’s right. Burning makes new things: ash, smoke and heat. Melting can be undone. Burning can’t.
> - Yes, if you cool the ash down. → Cooling water turns it back into ice. But burning makes brand-new stuff: ash, smoke and heat. The paper is gone for good. Some changes can be undone, and some can’t.
> - Only if you glue the ash together. → Ash would just be gluey ash! Burning changes paper into new things that can’t change back.
> _For grown-ups: Compared a change that can be undone (melting) with one that can’t (burning)._

**Old Tobin**: Nine.  
_Tobin sits on the step with you until the stove is cold. Neither of you counts how long._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): notice mixed feelings after a big decision  
> _After a big choice that can’t be undone, it’s normal to feel a mix of things: sad, relieved, unsure._  
> _Sitting quietly with someone you trust is a good way to let those feelings settle._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that mixed feelings after a big decision are normal, and that quiet company helps._


#### `s13-settled-grave`

_Aldous Vale is buried under the alder trees by the mill race, where his wife used to sit with her feet in the water._  
_The race is running high and brown. An alder drops a yellow leaf on the stone, and then another, as if it’s keeping count._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): deciduous trees drop their leaves in autumn  
> _Alders, like oaks and beeches, drop their leaves in autumn and grow new ones in spring._  
> _Trees that do this are called deciduous. The leaves on the grave are this year’s, finished with._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that deciduous trees, like alders, drop their leaves in autumn and grow new ones in spring._

_Moss sits on the headstone and shuts his eyes. You read the letter aloud. He listens the way he listens to rain._  
**Moss**: He’d have hated that. Being read to. Sitting still for it.  
**Moss**: He sat still for it.  
_You weigh the letter down on the grave with a flat stone from the race._  
_Tobin takes his hat off, and then can’t remember why, and puts it back on._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): ways of saying goodbye to someone who has died  
> _People say goodbye to someone who has died in lots of ways: visiting their grave, reading to them, or telling stories about them._  
> _None of these are wrong. They are all ways of remembering._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned some of the different ways people say goodbye to, and remember, someone who has died._


#### `s13-settled-grave-nomoss`

_Aldous Vale is buried under the alder trees by the mill race, where his wife used to sit with her feet in the water._  
_The race is running high and brown. An alder drops a yellow leaf on the stone, and then another, as if it’s keeping count._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): deciduous trees drop their leaves in autumn  
> _Alders, like oaks and beeches, drop their leaves in autumn and grow new ones in spring._  
> _Trees that do this are called deciduous. The leaves on the grave are this year’s, finished with._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that deciduous trees, like alders, drop their leaves in autumn and grow new ones in spring._

_You read the letter aloud, the way you would have read it to Moss. Slowly, so the old one could keep up._  
_You miss him. He would have sat on the headstone with his eyes shut._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): missing someone who has died  
> _Missing someone who has died can come back suddenly, when you do something you used to do with them._  
> _That’s normal. Doing it the way they liked is one way of keeping them close._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that missing someone who has died often returns at familiar moments, and that this is normal._

**Old Tobin**: He’d have hated that. Being read to. Sitting still for it.  
**Old Tobin**: He sat still for it.  
_You weigh the letter down on the grave with a flat stone from the race._  
_Tobin takes his hat off, and then can’t remember why, and puts it back on._  

#### `s19-warmth-sable`

_Two days after the Long Night. The valley is white to the doorsteps, and very quiet._  
_Sable hasn’t eaten her breakfast. She sits at the top of the garden, facing north, where the snowfield climbs to the high pass._  
_She has sat like that since dawn. When you come near, she doesn’t move away. She doesn’t look round, either._  
_Beside her floats the pale light that was Moss’s. It stayed when Moss faded at the Long Night, when he died._  
_The pale light leans north too, like a candle flame in a draught._  
_Up there, the snow is the blue of skimmed milk, and quite empty. Then, for a moment, it isn’t: a speck of red, like a forgotten coal._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): the higher up a mountain, the colder the air  
> _High up, the air is colder. The higher you climb a mountain, the colder it usually gets._  
> _That’s why snow stays on a high pass long after the valley has thawed. The tops of very high mountains keep snow all year._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that air usually gets colder the higher up a mountain you go, so snow lasts longer up high._

_Sable stands. She looks at you, then at the pass, then at you, the way she looks at a gate she wants opened._  
**You**: All right. All right. We’ll ask Marina.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): read what a character wants from her actions  
> _Sable never says a word. How do you know she wants to go up to the pass?_  
> - ✅ She looks from you to the pass and back, like at a gate she wants opened. → Yes. Her eyes do the talking. Characters can show what they want through what they do, not only what they say.
> - She tells you. → Sable doesn’t speak. But she looks from you to the pass and back, the way she asks for a gate. Her actions tell you.
> - You can’t know. → You can, from clues! She skips breakfast, faces north, and looks from you to the pass and back. Her actions say it.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred what a non-speaking character wanted from her actions._


#### `s19-climb-sable`

_First light. Marina ropes you to her. Sable will not be roped._  

> **Lesson** (health, notice): staying safe together on a snowy mountain  
> **Marina**: On a snowy mountain, people rope together. If one slips, the others can hold them.  
> **Marina**: Only ever go up with a grown-up who knows the mountain, and stay close.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why climbers rope together and stay close to a grown-up who knows the way._

_She goes ahead, a grey shape on the white, as if she knows the way._  
_Moss’s pale light drifts along at her shoulder, where he used to walk._  
_The snowfield is crusted on top and soft beneath. Each of your steps goes through with a crunch like biting toast._  
**Marina**: Lovely, isn’t it? That wind. Takes your face right off.  
_Sable is light enough not to break the crust. She leaves a line of small prints, neat as stitches._  

> **Lesson** (science, ask): spreading weight helps you stay on top of snow  
> _Your boots break through the crust. Sable’s paws don’t. Why not?_  
> - ✅ She’s lighter, and her weight is spread over four paws. → Yes. Less weight pressing on each bit of snow means the crust holds. That’s why snowshoes are wide: they spread a person’s weight out, so they sink less.
> - She’s floating. → Not quite! She’s much lighter than you, and her weight is spread over four paws, so the crust holds her.
> - Her paws are warmer. → Warm paws would melt snow, not help her stay up! It’s about weight: she’s light, and spread over four paws.
> _For grown-ups: Explained that lighter, spread-out weight sinks less into snow (why snowshoes work)._

**Marina**: She’s not stopping. Is she always like this?  
**You**: Only when it matters.  

#### `s19-hollow-sable`

_Near the top, the rock leans out over the snow like a hand held over a cup. Under it is a hollow, out of the wind._  
_There is no snow in the hollow. There hasn’t been for a very long time, you think. The bare rock is dry, and faintly warm._  
_In the middle of it, on a flat stone, is a light. Red. Smaller than a fingernail. Almost nothing._  
**Marina**: I’ll be on the lip. Shout if you want the rope.  
_Marina goes back up to the lip without being asked. She turns her back, and looks at the view very hard._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): notice when someone is giving others privacy  
> _Marina turns her back without being asked. Why do you think she does that?_  
> - ✅ To give you privacy for something important. → Yes. Marina can tell this moment matters. Stepping back so others can have it is a quiet kind of kindness.
> - She’s bored of the hollow. → She says nothing about being bored. She went “without being asked”, and looks hard at the view. She’s giving you privacy.
> - She’s cross with you. → Nothing she says sounds cross. She offers you the rope, then steps away. She’s giving you privacy, which is kind.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred that a character was giving others privacy, and why that is kind._

_Sable goes into the hollow, and stops a tail’s length from the light. The fur lifts all along her back._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): animals’ fur can stand up when they are alarmed  
> _Many furry animals, like cats and dogs, raise the fur along their backs when they are alarmed or frightened._  
> _It makes them look bigger. Sable is telling you, without a word, that this place matters to her._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that many animals raise their fur when alarmed, which makes them look bigger._

_She knows it. You don’t know how. Something in her knows the shape of the cold that was made here, and who made it._  
_Moss’s pale light settles beside the red one. Two lights on a flat stone: one pale, one hardly there._  
_You remember what Moss told you. Eternals only speak to those who sit still long enough._  

#### `s19-question-sable`

_After a long time, the light grows a little. Not brighter. Bigger, the way a coal does when you breathe on it._  
**Cinder**: Are they safe?  
_Nobody answers. Moss would have. You can feel the shape of what he’d say, as if he were sitting in your coat._  
**You**: No. They’re well.  
_The light is quiet for a long time. You watch it understand._  
**Cinder**: …Well. Well is better, isn’t it. I didn’t know there was a better.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): find the big idea (theme) of a story  
> _Cinder asked if the Nubbins were “safe”. The answer was “well”. Those words aren’t the same._  
> _What is the difference?_  
> - ✅ Safe means nothing can hurt you. Well means you’re free to live, and grow, and be happy. → Yes. Cinder kept them safe by keeping them still. But still isn’t living. That is the big idea of the whole Grove story: safe is not the same as well. A big idea like that is called a theme.
> - They mean exactly the same. → They can sound alike. But a Nubbin frozen still is safe from harm, and not well at all. Well means free to live and grow. That difference is the story’s theme.
> - A well is a hole you get water from. → Ha! Different well. Here “well” means healthy and happy, free to live. Safe is not the same as well. That’s the story’s theme.
> _For grown-ups: Identified the story’s theme: being kept safe is not the same as being well._

_Then the light sees Sable, grey from her ears to her tail._  
**Cinder**: Oh, little one. That grey is mine, isn’t it. I didn’t do it to you. But I did it.  
**Cinder**: I loved them. It was so cold, and I was so frightened. I held them so tight.  
_Sable gets up and crosses the last of the stone, further than she has ever gone towards anything warm._  
_She lies against the flat stone and leans her whole weight on it, the way she leant on your shin in the autumn._  
**Cinder**: She isn’t still. She’s grey, and she isn’t still. She came to me. Nobody made her. Who undid it?  
**You**: Everybody. Slowly.  
**Cinder**: She has forgiven me. I don’t know how I know. I know.  
**Cinder**: You’re the Keeper. You live down there, with the grey ones in the grass, and what I did.  
**Cinder**: Am I forgiven? By the ones who have to live with it?  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): think about who can forgive, and for whom  
> _Before you answer her, think about this._  
> _Can one person forgive someone on behalf of other people? Or can only the ones who were hurt forgive?_  
> - Only the ones who were hurt can really forgive. → That’s a thoughtful answer. Many people believe forgiveness belongs to those who were hurt. You can still remember someone truthfully: the good they meant, and the harm they did.
> - Someone who cares for them can forgive for them. → That’s a kind answer, and a fair one. A Keeper speaks for the Grove in lots of ways. Maybe this is one of them.
> - I’m not sure. It’s hard. → Not being sure is honest. Grown-ups argue about this too. Whatever you say next, say it kindly.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about whether we can forgive on behalf of others (a think question with no single right answer)._


**Choices**

- **“You’re forgiven.”**
    - **You**: You’re forgiven.
    - The light says nothing for a while. Then it turns the colour of a hearth when the door is shut and the kettle is on.
    - **Cinder**: Oh.
    - **Cinder**: I didn’t know it would be so light. I thought being forgiven would be heavy. I thought I’d have to carry it.
    - Sable breathes out, long and slow, against the stone. The light warms her nose.
- **“It isn’t mine to forgive. But you’re remembered.”**
    - **You**: It isn’t mine to forgive. But you’re remembered.
    - The light holds very still.
    - **Cinder**: Remembered.
    - **Cinder**: That’s more than I asked for. It’s what I should have asked for.
    - **Cinder**: Will you tell them? That I loved them? Not only what I did.
    - **You**: All of it.
    - Beside her, the pale light that was Moss’s brightens once, the way he used to nod.

#### `s19-fade-sable`

_You stay. Sable doesn’t move from the stone. Moss’s pale light doesn’t either._  
_The light gets smaller. It doesn’t flicker, the way the fourth lantern used to. It just gets smaller, steadily._  
_Like someone walking away up a long road, who turns round once to wave._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): explain how a simile changes the feeling of a moment  
> _The light going is compared to “someone walking away up a long road, who turns round once to wave”._  
> _How does that simile make the moment feel?_  
> - ✅ Gentle and sad, like a goodbye. → Yes. A wave is how you say goodbye to someone you love. The simile makes her going sad, but not frightening.
> - Fast and scary. → A long road and a slow wave aren’t fast. The simile makes it feel gentle, like a goodbye.
> - Funny. → There are funny moments in this story, but not this one. A wave over the shoulder is a gentle goodbye.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how a simile shapes the feeling of a sad moment._

**Cinder**: Little one. It isn’t cold.  
_Sable shuts her eyes._  
_…_  
_Then there is only the flat stone, and the dry rock, and the wind going over._  
_Cinder has faded. That means she has died. Her light has stopped, and it won’t start again._  
_You hear Moss’s words in your own mouth before you know you’re going to say them._  
**You**: That is fading done right. Not stilled. Let go.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): remembering someone who has died by carrying their words  
> _When someone we love has died, we often carry their sayings with us. Using their words is one way of remembering them._  
> _Moss used to say, “We are made of being remembered.” Today, you remembered him._  
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how using a loved one’s words is a way of remembering them after they have died._

_Sable stays curled against the stone a long time. You let her._  

#### `s19-warmth-alone`

_Two days after the Long Night. The valley is white to the doorsteps, and very quiet._  
_You are at the cottage window with a cup of tea when you see it: high on the pass, a speck of red, like a forgotten coal._  
_You look away, and look back. It is still there, steady, in all that white._  

> **Lesson** (science, notice): the higher up a mountain, the colder the air  
> _High up, the air is colder. The higher you climb a mountain, the colder it usually gets._  
> _That’s why snow stays on a high pass long after the valley has thawed. The tops of very high mountains keep snow all year._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that air usually gets colder the higher up a mountain you go, so snow lasts longer up high._

_Nobody else is looking. Moss would have been. But Moss faded at the Long Night, which means he died._  
_You still look round for him. Before you have quite decided anything, you are reaching for your boots._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): notice how missing someone shows up in small moments  
> _When someone we love has died, we often miss them most in small moments: a seat they always sat in, a thing they would have spotted first._  
> _Looking round for them is part of grief. Doing what they would have done is one way of carrying them with you._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about how grief shows up in small, everyday moments, and how doing what a loved one would have done can help._

**You**: Marina. Marina knows the path.  

#### `s19-climb-alone`

_First light. Marina ropes you to her, checks the knot twice, and then checks your socks._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): multiplication as equal groups  
> **Marina**: Two pairs of socks, I said. A pair is two socks. So how many socks should I find on you?  
> - ✅ 4 → Four. Two pairs, two in each pair: 2 × 2 = 4. Two on each foot. You pass.
> - 2 → That’s one pair. I said two pairs. Two groups of two: 2 × 2 = 4 socks.
> - 3 → Three socks would be a very odd foot. Two pairs is two groups of two: 2 × 2 = 4.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out 2 × 2 = 4 by thinking of pairs as equal groups._

_The snowfield is crusted on top and soft beneath. Every step goes through with a crunch like biting toast._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-4, notice): melting and freezing again can make a hard crust on snow  
> **Marina**: That crust is sun and frost taking turns. By day the sun melts the top of the snow a little.  
> **Marina**: At night it freezes again, harder. Melting and freezing, over and over, and you get a lid on the snow.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that snow can melt in the sun and refreeze at night, making a hard crust._

**Marina**: Lovely, isn’t it? That wind. Takes your face right off.  
**Marina**: What are we looking for, exactly?  
**You**: Something warm.  
**Marina**: Up here? Well. You’re Hazel’s. I gave up asking years ago.  

#### `s19-hollow-alone`

_Near the top, the rock leans out over the snow like a hand held over a cup. Under it is a hollow, out of the wind._  
_There is no snow in the hollow. There hasn’t been for a very long time, you think. The bare rock is dry, and faintly warm._  
_In the middle of it, on a flat stone, is a light. Red. Smaller than a fingernail. Almost nothing._  
**Marina**: I’ll be on the lip. Shout if you want the rope.  
_Marina goes back up to the lip without being asked. She turns her back, and looks at the view very hard._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): notice when someone is giving others privacy  
> _Marina turns her back without being asked. Why do you think she does that?_  
> - ✅ To give you privacy for something important. → Yes. Marina can tell this moment matters. Stepping back so others can have it is a quiet kind of kindness.
> - She’s bored of the hollow. → She says nothing about being bored. She went “without being asked”, and looks hard at the view. She’s giving you privacy.
> - She’s cross with you. → Nothing she says sounds cross. She offers you the rope, then steps away. She’s giving you privacy, which is kind.
> _For grown-ups: Inferred that a character was giving others privacy, and why that is kind._

_You go into the hollow on your own, and sit down a little way from the light._  
_You remember something Moss told you once. Eternals only speak to those who sit still long enough._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): being brave on your own, and knowing help is near  
> _Doing something important on your own can feel lonely, and a bit scary. That’s allowed._  
> _It helps to remember what people taught you, and to know who is near. Marina is just up on the lip, with the rope._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about feeling brave on your own, and remembering that help is close by._


#### `s19-question-alone`

_After a long time, the light grows a little. Not brighter. Bigger, the way a coal does when you breathe on it._  
**Cinder**: Are they safe?  
_Nobody answers. Moss would have. You can feel the shape of what he’d say, as if he were sitting beside you._  
**You**: No. They’re well.  
_The light is quiet for a long time. You watch it understand._  
**Cinder**: …Well. Well is better, isn’t it. I didn’t know there was a better.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): find the big idea (theme) of a story

**Cinder**: I loved them. It was so cold, and I was so frightened. I held them so tight.  
**Cinder**: Do they still say my name, down there?  
_You know one way they do. You say it to her plainly, without the bounce the children give it in the lane._  
**You**: Cinder held them close and tight, kept them warm one winter night;  
**You**: when the morning came to call, they did not move at all.  
**Cinder**: That’s fair. Do they skip well?  
**You**: Badly. With great enthusiasm.  
_Something passes through the light that might, in a bigger creature, be a laugh._  
**Cinder**: You’re the Keeper. You live down there, with the grey ones in the grass, and what I did.  
**Cinder**: Am I forgiven? By the ones who have to live with it?

_You stay. The wind goes over the overhang, and you keep your hands in your lap._

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): explain how a simile changes the feeling of a moment  
> _The light going is compared to “someone walking away up a long road, who turns round once to wave”._

> - ✅ Gentle and sad, like a goodbye. → Yes. A wave is how you say goodbye to someone you love. The simile makes her going sad, but not frightening.

#### `s24-tea-moss`

_Spring. The memorial flowers on the hill have opened all at once, as if somebody gave a signal._  
_Hazel’s is the untidy one near Briar’s. It still faces the Grove, very firmly._  
_Somebody comes over the far ridge in the early light, under a pack so big it looks like a walking hedge._  
_It is Nova. She comes straight up the hill path, and at the top she stops, which is new._  
**Nova**: Morning. Don’t get up. I was passing. I’m always passing.  
**Nova**: I thought I’d sit here a minute and not pass.  
_She sits down by Hazel’s flower with her pack still on, like a tortoise that has decided to stay a while._  
_Moss is on the flat stone by the path, where he always sits. He watches Nova sit down, and then he climbs your leg, slowly._  
**Moss**: I’m coming. Wherever this is going.  
**Moss**: Don’t look like that. I’ve decided.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): what a character’s words show about them  
> _“Don’t look like that. I’ve decided.” What does this tell you about Moss?_  
> - ✅ He has made up his own mind, and won’t be talked out of it. → Yes. Moss chooses rarely, and when he does, it’s settled. Rather like the day he chose Hazel.
> - Somebody told him he had to come. → Nobody tells Moss anything! “I’ve decided” means the choice is his own.
> _For grown-ups: Used a character’s words to describe his personality._

_He settles on your shoulder, light as a hat, and shuts his eyes._  
_Your Nubbin runs to her, then back to you, then to her again, to check you are both still there._  
**Nova**: Is there tea? There’s usually tea. I usually say no.  
**You**: There’s tea.  
**Nova**: Then I’ll have some. I’d like to stay for tea.  
_Nobody in the valley can remember Nova staying for tea. Down by the hedge, Fern drops a whole tray of seedlings._  

#### `s24-tea-moss-stayed`

_Spring. The memorial flowers on the hill have opened all at once, as if somebody gave a signal._

_Somebody comes over the far ridge in the early light, under a pack so big it looks like a walking hedge._

**Nova**: I thought I’d sit here a minute and not pass.  
_Beside Hazel’s flower, so close the two of them lean together, is a small grey-green one by the flat stone where Moss always sat._  
_Moss faded up here, beside her. That means he died. His flower came up close to hers._  
_There is just room between them for one person, if she tucks her knees up. Nova does, pack and all._  
**Nova**: Both of you. Right. I’ll sit in the middle and not take sides.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, notice): humour as a way of coping  
> _Missing two people at once is a lot to carry. Nova makes a small joke to help carry it. Humour is one way people cope with sadness._  
> _For grown-ups: Noticed that people sometimes use humour to cope with sad feelings._

_Your Nubbin runs to her, then back to you, then to her again, to check you are both still there._  
**Nova**: Is there tea? There’s usually tea. I usually say no.  
**You**: There’s tea.

#### `s24-tea-sable`

_Spring. The memorial flowers on the hill have opened all at once, as if somebody gave a signal._  
_Hazel’s is the untidy one near Briar’s. It still faces the Grove, very firmly._  
_Somebody comes over the far ridge in the early light, under a pack so big it looks like a walking hedge._  
_It is Nova. She comes straight up the hill path, and at the top she stops, which is new._  
**Nova**: Morning. Don’t get up. I was passing. I’m always passing.  
**Nova**: I thought I’d sit here a minute and not pass.  
_She sits down by Hazel’s flower with her pack still on, like a tortoise that has decided to stay a while._  
_Sable comes up the path behind you and sits down two steps from Nova, facing the far ridge._  
**Nova**: Hello, grey one. That’s where I came from. Are you thinking of going?  
_Sable says nothing. Her ears stay up._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-2, notice): animals use their ears to gather information  
> _Many animals can turn their ears towards a sound. Ears held up and forward usually mean an animal is alert and paying attention._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how animals use their ears, and what ear positions can tell us._

_Your Nubbin runs to her, then back to you, then to her again, to check you are both still there._  
**Nova**: Is there tea? There’s usually tea. I usually say no.  
**You**: There’s tea.  
**Nova**: Then I’ll have some. I’d like to stay for tea.  
_Nobody in the valley can remember Nova staying for tea. Down by the hedge, Fern drops a whole tray of seedlings._  

#### `s24-moss-kept`

_Higher up, on the crown of the hill, Moss sits with his back to the Grove, the way he has sat since the Long Night._  
**Nova**: Hello, Moss.  
_He doesn’t turn round. After a while Nova stops waiting for him to, and looks at the flower instead._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, ask): giving someone space  
> _Nova stops waiting for Moss to turn round. Was that the right thing to do?_  
> - Yes. He might need space. → That’s thoughtful. Giving space can be a kindness, as long as the door stays open.
> - No. She should keep trying. → That’s caring too. Notice she says she’ll come back later. She does a bit of both.
> - I’m not sure. → That’s honest. It’s a hard one. Sometimes you only find out by trying gently, and watching.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about when to give someone space and when to keep trying._

_Some sadness looks like tears. Some looks like a back turned to everyone._  
**Nova**: …I’ll sit with you later, then.  
_Moss doesn’t answer. But he doesn’t move away, either._  

#### `s24-lantern-corvin`

**Nova**: One more thing. Can we take her lantern? And light it up there, at sunrise?  
**Nova**: So she sees it. From wherever she is, being difficult about something.  
_It is Sunday, so Corvin is by the pond, saying nothing, badly. He gets up when he sees where you are looking._  
_Hazel’s lantern hangs on the hook by the cottage door. He takes it down before you can, the way he does every Sunday._  
_He trims the wick with a penknife. His hands are steady now. He takes a long time about it, and doesn’t apologise._  
**Corvin Vale**: The far ridge. For the sunrise.  
_He holds it out to you. When you take hold of it, he doesn’t let go straight away._  
**Corvin Vale**: Bring it back lit.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): reading a character’s words for hidden meaning  
> _Why do you think Corvin says “Bring it back lit”, not just “Bring it back”?_  
> - A lit lantern would mean the trip went well. → That fits. A light still burning is a good sign: nobody gave up.
> - He wants Hazel’s light kept going. → A lovely reading. He looked after her lantern every Sunday. It matters to him.
> - He’s just fussy about lanterns. → He might be! But he holds on a moment too long. There’s more in it than fuss.
> _For grown-ups: Looked for the meaning behind a character’s short words._


#### `s24-stowaway-knows`

_The carrier’s cart goes up the ridge road on Tuesdays, and takes anyone who can lift their own luggage._  
_Nova can just about lift hers. The cart’s springs go down with a groan._  
_Under the tarp at the back, something says “ow”. Then, much more quietly: “Nobody heard that.”_  
_Then the tarp lifts, and a girl in big wellies, with a sash of home-made badges, sits up among the sacks and points at you._  
**Tilly**: It’s you. From Keeps & Critters. You sat next to the dragon.  
**Tilly**: This is a stowaway situation. You can’t send a stowaway back. That’s the law of the sea.  
**Nova**: We’re not at sea.  
**Tilly**: It’s the law of carts, then. It’s the same law.  
_Sparks comes down the lane at a run, waving both arms, and slows right down when she sees who Tilly has found._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.2.3, ask): how a character’s feelings change  
> _How does Sparks feel when she starts running, and how does she feel when she sees who found Tilly?_  
> - ✅ Worried at first, then relieved. → Yes. She runs flat out, then slows right down. Her body shows the change before she speaks.
> - Cross the whole time. → She might be a bit cross with Tilly! But watch her slow down. She goes from worried to relieved when she sees Tilly is with someone she trusts.
> _For grown-ups: Described how a character’s feelings change, using clues from the text._

**Sparks**: Oh, it’s YOU. Fine. Good. Take her. Bring her back with the same number of wellies.  

#### `s24-bun-moss`

_Before the cart goes, Nova climbs back up the hill on her own, with one of Fern’s lantern buns._  
_She puts it on the flat stone where Moss always sat, by his flower, and stands there with her hands in her pockets._  
_Moss faded. That means he died, and he isn’t coming back. His flower is how the valley keeps him._  
**Nova**: He told me once I walked like someone being chased. I said I was. He said, “By what?” I never answered.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): inferring a character’s feelings  
> _Nova “walked like someone being chased”. What do you think was chasing her?_  
> - Sadness she didn’t want to stop and feel. → That fits this whole story. Stopping for tea might have meant feeling things.
> - Wanting to see absolutely everything. → That’s true of Nova too. Hazel’s list sent her everywhere.
> - Being lonely. → A thoughtful answer. Remember: “I never had anyone to take.”
> _For grown-ups: Inferred what lies behind a character’s behaviour._

**Nova**: I’ll tell him when I get back.  
_Lots of people talk to someone who has died. It doesn’t need an answer to help._  

#### `s24-eternal-watch`

_On the western hill your Eternal sits where it always sits, and watches the cart go, very carefully._  
_It doesn’t follow, and it doesn’t need to. It already knows which way you’ll come home._  
_Eternals never grow old. In the Grove’s stories, that is what makes them so rare._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): every living thing has a life cycle  
> _Eternals are a Grove story idea. Real living things all have a life cycle: they are born, grow, may have young, and die._  
> _That cycle is part of what makes each life precious._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that all real living things have a life cycle, and told story from fact._

_You wave. It doesn’t wave back, exactly. It blinks, slowly, which is the same thing._  
_The cart turns the corner, and the hill goes out of sight._  
_Nova settles against her pack and shuts her eyes._  

#### `s24-bird-collector`

_Above the falls the ridge goes up into cloud, and the cloud is full of birdsong you don’t know._  
_You stop to eat, and set Fern’s bag of lantern buns on a rock. Then it is a bag of lantern buns minus one._  
_Something enormous is standing in the mist three strides off, with a bun in its beak._  
_It is taller than Nova and striped like a humbug, with legs like stilts and a little crest that won’t lie flat._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-LS1-1, notice): body parts that help an animal survive  
> **Nova**: Look at those legs. Long legs mean long strides, and a head high enough to see over anything.  
> **Nova**: And the stripes. In mist and shadow, stripes break up an animal’s outline, so it’s harder to spot.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned how long legs and a striped pattern can help an animal survive._

**Tilly**: Oh. Oh. Oh, he’s BEAUTIFUL.  
**Tilly**: He’s called Sir Reginald. That’s decided. Nobody else gets a go.  
_Sir Reginald swallows the bun whole. You can watch it go all the way down._  
_It looks at the bag, and then at you. It takes one step forward and two steps back._  
**Nova**: Don’t grab. Whatever you do. A thing like that, you only see once if you grab.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Responsible decision-making, ask): gentleness with wild animals  
> _Why does Nova say not to grab?_  
> - ✅ Grabbing frightens wild animals, and then they stop trusting people. → Yes. A wild animal that gets grabbed learns that people mean danger. Slow and gentle earns trust.
> - Because the bird might bite. → It might! But the bigger reason is trust. A wild animal that gets grabbed learns that people mean danger, and won’t come close again.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about why grabbing a wild animal breaks its trust._


**Choices**

- **Hold out a bun on your flat hand.**
    - You hold out a bun on your flat hand. The bird looks at your hand for a long time, and takes one step back.
    - Nova holds out a bun of her own without thinking. The bird walks straight past you and takes it from her.
    - **Tilly**: It doesn’t like you. That’s weird. Everything likes Keepers.
    - You think of your pens at home, full of fast grey runners that never make a sound. You don’t say anything.
- **Sit down on the path and wait for it to come to you.**
    - You sit down on the wet path. The bird stays where it is, three strides off, and comes no nearer.
    - Nova sits down too, a little way off. After a long while the bird goes and stands over her instead.
    - **Tilly**: It doesn’t like you. That’s weird. Everything likes Keepers.
    - You think of your pens at home, full of fast grey runners that never make a sound. You don’t say anything.

#### `s24-nest-waited`

_Under an overhang of rock there is a nest the size of a cart wheel, made of heather and string and most of somebody’s washing line._  
_In it are four striped chicks like knitted tea cosies. Beside it sits Tilly, perfectly safe and extremely cross._  
_Her badge sash is wound round the smallest chick, badges and all, so it doesn’t get cold._  

> **Lesson** (science, 3-LS1-1, notice): a bird’s life cycle, and why chicks need a parent  
> **Nova**: Egg, chick, adult, and then new eggs. That’s a bird’s whole life cycle, round and round.  
> **Nova**: Newly hatched chicks often can’t keep themselves warm yet. A parent sits over them, like a feather duvet.  
> **Nova**: Cage the mother, and the chicks get cold. That’s the real reason wild birds stay wild.  
> _For grown-ups: Learned the stages of a bird’s life cycle and why chicks need a parent nearby._

**Tilly**: You took AGES. I’ve been whistling for about a hundred years.  
**Tilly**: Sir Reginald’s a mother. That’s allowed. She can still be Sir.  
_Fairweather’s cage stands open and empty at the edge of the overhang. Out in the dark, a creaky two-note call._  
_You remember the wet path. You sit down by the nest with your Nubbin beside you, and you wait._  
_After a long while the mother comes out of the dark on her own, and stands over her chicks, and over your Nubbin._  
_She tidies the tuft on its head again. It wasn’t bothering it, and she does it anyway._  
**Nova**: There. She came straight home.

#### `s24-lights-told`

_The sun comes over the far rim and runs down into the valley one place at a time, as if it is calling a register._  
_The Tooth, then the Circuit’s square roofs, then the falls, smoking white; the Hollow, where the paths stop; the tide pools, flashing._  

> **Lesson** (science, 5-ESS1-2, notice): why high places catch the sunrise first  
> _At sunrise the Sun sits very low, so its light skims sideways across the land._  
> _The tallest places poke up into it first. The valley floor stays in shadow until the Sun climbs higher._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why the tops of hills light up before the valley at sunrise._

_Then the Grove: the pond, the cottage, the hill. All of it at once, small and bright, exactly as she wrote it._  
**Tilly**: Oh.  
**Nova**: There. The whole valley. At once.  
_Down in the Grove, four small lights are still burning, one at each post, as if somebody left them on for you._  
_Then more lights, all the way up the western hill: lanterns, a long line of them, climbing in the last of the dark._  
_The valley has walked up her hill to watch the far ridge. Fern saw the cart go, and Sparks told everyone else._  
**Nova**: They came. They all came up.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Social awareness, notice): showing up for each other  
> _Nobody asked them to come. They noticed, and they came. Sometimes that is the whole of being kind._  
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how simply turning up can show someone they are not alone._

_You lift Hazel’s lantern as high as it will go. Nova puts her hand under your elbow, to help hold it up._

#### `s24-shelf-moss`

_Moss has slept on your shoulder most of the way up. He wakes now, and looks for a long time without saying anything._  
**Moss**: Forty years I sat on that hill and looked at this ridge. I never once thought to look back the other way.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.6, ask): point of view  
> _Moss only ever looked one way. Is there something you have only seen from one side?_  
> - A place I’ve only seen from inside. → Try it from outside sometime. Moss would approve.
> - An argument, from my side only. → That’s a brave answer. The other side often looks different from over there.
> - A person I think I know well. → Lovely. People can surprise you, like Hazel at nineteen.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how a different point of view can change what we see._

**Moss**: She’d have liked it. She’d have talked all the way through it.  
_You look back the way he is looking: the western hill, the flat stone, very small._  
_Seeing a place from far away can make you see it new._  
_Moss shuts his eyes again, but he doesn’t sleep._  

#### `s24-shelf-sable`

_Sable has walked two steps ahead of you the whole way up, waiting at every bend._  
_Now she sits at the very edge of the Shelf, facing the Grove, and the sun comes up on her too._  
_She stays grey. She looks warm anyway._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.4.5, ask): words with more than one meaning: warm  
> _“She stays grey. She looks warm anyway.” What kind of “warm” is this?_  
> - ✅ Warm as in content and safe, not just the temperature. → Yes. Her colour hasn’t changed, but something inside her has settled. That’s “warm” used figuratively.
> - Warm as in hot from the sun. → The sun is on her, so that’s true too! But the line means more: she looks content and safe. That’s “warm” used figuratively.
> _For grown-ups: Explained a word used with a figurative meaning._

_Nova sits a little way off, and doesn’t make a fuss of her. Sable seems to like that._  
_Down in the valley the light reaches the Grove, and her ears come up._  
_Then she lies down, chin on her paws, and watches it all._  

#### `s24-tick-scarf`

_Nova sits on the lip of the Shelf with the atlas open at the front, and a stub of pencil worn almost to nothing._  
**Nova**: This was hers. The one she wrote the list with. She gave it me with the book. I’ve never once used it.  
_She ticks the last line. It is a very small tick, and it takes her a long time._  
**Nova**: Take someone. Done. I took two, and a stowaway.  
_Tilly is shivering. Nova unwinds the long scarf and winds it round her, three times, and there is still some left._  
**Tilly**: It’s too long.  
**Nova**: It was always too long. You’ll grow into it.  
_Then she ties the pencil stub to a bit of string, and hangs it round Tilly’s neck._  
**Nova**: Helping Someone Sad. You earned it. You were very annoying about it, but you earned it.  
**Tilly**: …It’s the best badge I’ve got.  
_Tilly checks the top of her welly, the way she always does, and leaves the note where it is._  
_Nova turns the atlas to its very last page, which is blank, and holds it out to you._  
**Nova**: Your turn.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): theme: what counts as an adventure  
> _Hazel wrote a list of faraway places. Then she spent most of her life in one garden._  
> _What do you think: did she miss her adventure, or have a different one?_  
> - She had a different one: the Grove, and everyone in it. → That’s how Nova reads it now. The back of the book is full of ordinary days, and Hazel called them the best.
> - She missed it, a bit. But she sent Nova instead. → That’s a fair answer, and a kind one. She gave the list away so somebody would go. That counts for something.
> - Both. You can miss one thing and love another. → A wise answer. People can be glad and sorry about the same life. Hazel probably was.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about the story’s theme: an ordinary life with people you love can be the adventure._


**Choices**

- **Write: “The Sunrise Shelf, again. Take someone.”**
    - **Nova**: Good. Somebody has to keep it in use.
- **Write: “Wherever Nova goes next. Tea after.”**
    - **Nova**: Then you’ll have to come and find me. I’ll leave the kettle on. Probably.
- **Write: “Here. Every morning.”**
    - **Nova**: That’s the hardest one on any list. She managed it forty years.

#### `s24-home-eternal`

_You come down off the ridge in the afternoon, slowly, because Augusta Fairweather is coming too, on Nova’s arm._  
**Augusta Fairweather**: Fifty years. I don’t suppose anybody has kept my room.  
_She takes the empty cottage at the foot of the falls path, for a week, she says. Nobody believes her, kindly._  
_Your Eternal is on the cottage step when you get in, as if it had been there all along. It probably had._  
_That night you light Hazel’s lantern by the cottage table and open the atlas, to read her list again._  
_In the margins there is writing, in faint pencil. It wasn’t there before, or it was, and it needed this light._  
_It is on every page. Beside a boy and a dragon: “I’d have fed the dragon.” Beside a building of endless counters: “Ha. Typical.”_  
_She read every story Nova ever brought her, and had something to say about all of them. Of course she did._  
_Nova stays three days, and has tea every afternoon. On the fourth she goes over the far ridge with a pack you could lift with a finger._  
_At the top she turns and waves, and doesn’t wait to see whether you wave back. She knows._  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.4.2, ask): finding the theme of a story  
> _Nova set off to see one last faraway place. What do you think this story is really about?_  
> - ✅ Learning that everyday life with people you love can be the adventure. → Yes. The list was the adventure Hazel planned. The back pages were the one she had.
> - Climbing a very tall ridge. → The climb happens! But it carries a bigger idea. The list was the adventure Hazel planned. The back pages, full of ordinary days, were the one she had.
> - Catching a rare bird. → Fairweather wanted that, and gave it up. The bigger idea is in the book. Ordinary days with people you love can be the adventure.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out the theme of the story._


#### `s24-home-corvin`

_Corvin is by the pond when you come in, though it isn’t Sunday. He looks at the lantern, lit in broad daylight._  
**Corvin Vale**: Good.  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Relationship skills, ask): trust and keeping promises  
> _Corvin says only “Good.” What do you think he means by it?_  
> - Thank you for keeping your promise. → Probably. For Corvin, one word can carry a lot.
> - He’s glad everyone came home safe. → A kind reading. A lit lantern means the night went well.
> - He trusts you a bit more now. → That might be the biggest meaning. Trust grows from small promises kept.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about how keeping promises builds trust._

_He hangs it back on its hook himself, and doesn’t trim the wick. It doesn’t need it._  
_A promise kept is a small thing. It is also how trust gets built, one small thing at a time._  
_Your Nubbin sits under the hook and looks up at it, the way it did before._  
_Corvin stays by the pond until the light goes, which he never does on a weekday._  

#### `s24-lecture`

_The museum is full, which it never is. Somebody has put out every chair, and some of the Nubbins have brought their own._  
**Professor Delve**: A lecture. Every plaque in this museum must be true. This one has taken fifty years to become so.  
**Augusta Fairweather**: I was called a liar. I have been wrong about a great many things. I was not wrong about the bird.  
**Augusta Fairweather**: I shan’t tell you where she nests. That is the whole of the lecture. Thank you.  

> **Lesson** (science, K-ESS3-3, notice): protecting the nests of rare birds  
> _Real wildlife experts often keep the nest sites of rare birds secret._  
> _That way, nobody disturbs the parents or takes the eggs. Sometimes the kindest thing to share is nothing._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned why the nest sites of rare birds are often kept secret._

_Professor Delve hangs the new plaque himself, on tiptoe, with his spectacles on the end of his nose._  
**Professor Delve**: “A tall striped bird nests on the far ridge. Augusta Fairweather saw it first. She was right.”  
**Professor Delve**: True. Entirely true. I checked.  
_Everyone claps. Fairweather sits down rather suddenly, and doesn’t say anything for a while._  

#### `s25-sill-late`

_The lamp comes on: a warm ring of light, and a small, satisfied tick every second._  
_Everyone goes down the ladder talking about the moth. You go last, with the toy and the book, and set them on the window seat for now._  
_For now turns into a week, and then a fortnight. The toy sits on the sill and gets the afternoon sun._  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.1, ask): a fortnight is two groups of seven days  
> _A fortnight is two weeks. How many days is that?_  
> - ✅ 14 days → Yes. Two groups of seven: 2 × 7 = 14. The word comes from an old way of saying “fourteen nights”.
> - 10 days → A week has seven days, so two weeks is 7 + 7. That makes 14.
> - 2 days → That would be two days, not two weeks. Two weeks is 2 × 7 = 14 days.
> _For grown-ups: Worked out a fortnight as two equal groups of seven days._

_Nobody looks at it. You don’t either, though you mean to._  
_Out of the window, on top of the western hill, Moss is looking this way. He would tell you he was looking at the weather._  

#### `s25-storm-nosable`

_Later that week your Nubbin finds the toy on the sill. It sniffs it, sneezes, and goes off after a moth._  
_Not yet, then._  
_Then, at the end of a hot week, a storm. It comes over the hill at bedtime, all at once, like a dropped tray._  
_Your Nubbin won’t settle. It goes from the basket to the hearth to the door and back, ears flat at every bang._  
_You look for the old sock it likes, and can’t find it. You warm a stone by the fire, and it pushes the stone away._  
_A flash, then thunder right overhead. The window seat lights up white, and the knitted toy on its sill with it._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): light travels faster than sound, so we see lightning before we hear thunder  
> _Lightning and thunder happen at the same moment. You see the flash first because light travels far faster than sound._  
> _Sound takes about three seconds to travel one kilometre. So you can count the gap to tell how far away the storm is._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that light travels faster than sound, which is why the flash comes before the thunder._


> **Lesson** (maths, 3.OA.A.3, ask): divide by 3 in a word problem  
> _Say you count six seconds between a flash and its thunder. About how far away is the storm?_  
> - ✅ About 2 kilometres → Yes. Six seconds, three seconds for each kilometre: 6 ÷ 3 = 2.
> - About 6 kilometres → Close thinking, but sound needs about three seconds per kilometre. 6 ÷ 3 = 2 kilometres.
> - About 18 kilometres → That’s 6 × 3. We need to share the seconds into groups of three: 6 ÷ 3 = 2 kilometres.
> _For grown-ups: Used division to turn the flash-to-thunder gap into a distance._


#### `s25-page-found`

_There is a page about clockwork toys in a nursery, and an old horse who has watched them come and go. You read it to him._  
_It says the clockwork toys were sure they would stay clockwork for ever, and never be anything more._  
_Clank listens with his chimney-light steady. His whistle doesn’t drop at all._  
**Moss**: The horse was wrong about that. I’m older than the horse.  
_You pass it on. Clank does a small spin on his one wheel, the way he does when he knew something already._  
**Clank**: Announcement: I found my word already. In Nova’s book. Next to a wooden boy.  
**Clank**: Is Real the same word? I don’t think it is the same word.  
**Moss**: No. It lives next door to it. He’s already knocked.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, L.3.4, notice): words with close but different meanings  
> _Some words live “next door” to each other: close in meaning, but not the same. Think of “glad” and “joyful”, or “alive” and “Real”._  
> _Finding exactly the right word, not just a nearby one, is something good writers work hard at._  
> _For grown-ups: Explored words with close but different meanings._

_You pass that on. Clank’s whistle rises, just a little, and holds._  
**Clank**: Next door. Announcement: I have a neighbour.  

#### `s25-byte`

_A wet afternoon. Moss is on the window ledge again; he says the hill is too damp for his knees._  
_You were not aware he had knees. You decide not to raise it._  
_Byte comes up the path under an umbrella, with his clipboard in a plastic bag, to return a pencil Hazel lent him nine years ago._  
**Byte**: She said bring it back when I’d finished with it. I’ve finished with it. It took longer than projected.  
_He sees the toy on the sill, and stops._  
**Byte**: Fern says your Nubbin made her apologise to that. Formally. With the good cups.  
**Byte**: And that you said it was Real. I’d like to know what you meant. Ideally in a unit.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 4.MD.A.1, ask): choosing the right unit  
> **Byte**: A unit is what you measure in. If I want to log how long the toy gets held, which unit should I use?  
> - ✅ Hours and minutes → Correct. Time is measured in hours, minutes and seconds. Noted.
> - Kilograms → Kilograms measure mass: how heavy. For how long, I need hours and minutes.
> - Metres → Metres measure length. How long in time needs hours and minutes. Confusing word, “long”.
> _For grown-ups: Matched a measurement to the right unit (time in hours and minutes)._

**Byte**: Hazel had a book for everything. Is there a book?  

#### `s25-page-byte`

_You find the page where the old horse explains it, and read it out. Byte writes it all down._  
_Then he reads back what he’s written, and frowns at it._  
**Byte**: There isn’t a single number on this page. Not one. How is anybody meant to check it?  
**Byte**: Can it be measured? Ask him. I know you can hear him. I’ve stopped pretending I think you can’t.  
**Moss**: Tell him to try.  
_You tell him. Byte looks at the toy for a long time, then at his clipboard, then turns to a clean page._  
**Byte**: Fine. A log. Hours held. Times carried. Times dropped, and gone back for in the dark. I’ll let you know.  

> **Lesson** (maths, 3.MD.B.3, do): reading a tally chart and finding a difference  
> **Byte**: A week later, the tally chart: carried 23 times, dropped 7 times, gone back for 7 times out of 7.  
> **Byte**: Read it with me. How many more times carried than dropped? 23 − 7 = 16. And every drop was gone back for.  
> Check: `edu:read:tally:s25-log`
> _For grown-ups: Read a tally chart and worked out a difference by subtracting._


> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-awareness, ask): thinking about what can and can’t be measured  
> _Byte’s numbers show something. Can they measure love?_  
> - Yes, a bit: they show care. → That’s a fair answer. Going back every time is a kind of evidence.
> - No. Love is a feeling, not a number. → Many people agree. Numbers can show what someone does, but not quite how they feel.
> - Some of it, but not all. → That’s a careful answer. Byte might even agree, eventually.
> _For grown-ups: Thought about what numbers can and can’t tell us about feelings._


#### `s25-shed-kept`

_You carry the bundle out to the shed without him. He is in the tin bath, under the cold water, waiting for your hands._  
_A whole slow evening: cold water, a sliver of soap, and squeezing, and never wringing. Clover checks, and says “again”._  
_Your hands go numb, and then they go patient._  

> **Lesson** (sel, CASEL: Self-management, notice): patience with slow, careful work  
> _Some jobs can’t be hurried. Rushing would felt the wool, and then there’d be no going back._  
> _Patience isn’t just waiting. It’s choosing to keep going carefully, even when you’d like to be finished._  
> _For grown-ups: Talked about patience as choosing to work carefully, not quickly._


#### `s25-line`

_It is past dark when Clover says that will do. Your fingers are white and wrinkled, and you can’t feel them._  
_You roll him in a towel and press, and never twist. Clover nods, which from Clover is a medal._  

> **Lesson** (science, 2-PS1-1, ask): materials that absorb water  
> _Why does rolling him in a towel and pressing help?_  
> - ✅ The towel absorbs the water from the wool. → Yes. Towels are made of loops that soak up water, so pressing moves the water out of the toy and into the towel.
> - The towel keeps him warm. → It might, a little. But mostly the towel absorbs the water, pulling it out of the wool.
> _For grown-ups: Explained how an absorbent material soaks up water._

**Clover**: Now you leave him. Overnight, flat, by the range. Not too near. Wool doesn’t like being rushed any more than the rest of us.  
_His loose eye came off in the rinse. Clover holds out her palm for it._  
**Clover**: I’ll sew it back tomorrow, with proper thread. It’ll outlast both of us.  
_Your Nubbin wakes on the step, looks round for him, and finds him on the towel by the range._  
_It lies down beside the towel: not on it, beside it._  

#### `s25-line-dry`

_In the morning you peg him on the line by his ears. By noon he’s dry: a size smaller, lumpier, and somehow more himself._  

> **Lesson** (science, K-PS3-1, notice): sunlight and wind dry wet things by evaporation  
> _Sunlight warms the wet wool, and the water in it turns into vapour and drifts away. That’s evaporation._  
> _A breeze helps by carrying the damp air off, so drier air can take its place. Sun plus wind is the best drying day._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that sunlight and wind dry wet things by evaporation._

_Clover sews his eye back on, tight, and gives you a spare button from her tin, the same brown, for your Nubbin to wear._  
_He goes back on your Nubbin’s bed, and stays there for good._  
_At teatime Moss comes down to the ledge and looks through the window at him on the bed for a long while._  
**Moss**: Then he’s Real to you. That’s how it ends for most of them. It’s the better ending, mostly.  

#### `s25-falls-kept`

_You come home from the Hollow with the notebook inside your coat. It’s late, and the cottage smells of cold ashes._  
_Moss is on the window ledge. He doesn’t ask about the notebook, and you don’t tell him yet._  
_On your Nubbin’s bed the toy is waiting, a size smaller, with both eyes on tight._  
_There is one thing you do want to tell him._  
_You went along the ledge behind the falls today. You put your hand on the rock, and the rock was warm._  

> **Lesson** (science, 4-PS3-2, notice): warm springs are heated from deep underground  
> _Deep under the ground, the rock is very hot. Rainwater can soak down a long way, get warmed, and rise again._  
> _Where it comes out, you get a warm spring. Heat from inside the Earth like this is called geothermal heat._  
> _For grown-ups: Learned that warm springs are heated by geothermal heat from deep underground._


#### `s25-twice-kept`

**You**: There’s a pool behind the falls. Warm. Steaming a bit. Lit from underneath, by nothing.  
**Moss**: The Wellspring. Yes.  
**Moss**: The first ones came up out of the warm water as small lights. Nobody ever told me where the lights came from.  
_He looks through the window at your Nubbin, asleep on its bed with its arms round the toy._  
**Moss**: I’ve a guess. It’s only a guess.  
**Moss**: He can stay where he is while I think about it.  

> **Lesson** (literacy, RL.3.3, ask): making an inference from clues  
> _Moss doesn’t say what his guess is. What do you think he is guessing?_  
> - That the lights were things that were loved a long time. → That fits the clues: the toy, the little light, and where Moss is looking. Moss would say you’re a good listener.
> - That the lights came from the warm water itself. → That’s a fair reading too. The water is warm and strange. Moss leaves room for more than one answer.
> - I don’t know yet. → That’s an honest answer. Moss doesn’t know either. That’s why it’s only a guess.
> _For grown-ups: Used clues in the story to make a guess about what a character was thinking._


#### `s25-coda-wild-button`

_Spring. The flowers on the hill are open, and the long grass at the edge of the Grove is new and green._  

> **Lesson** (science, 1-ESS1-2, notice): daylight grows longer in spring  
> _In spring the days grow longer and the sun climbs higher, so the ground warms up._  
> _More light and warmth wake the seeds and buds that waited through the winter._  
> _For grown-ups: Linked spring growth to longer days and more sunlight._

_A wild Nubbin is sitting right at the edge, where the mown grass stops. You haven’t seen it before._  
_Its coat is grey-brown, soft and a little lumpy, like knitting with a dropped stitch here and there._  
_The tuft on its head is a bit crooked. One of its eyes catches the light like a button._  
**You**: Button?  
_It turns its head._  
_It doesn’t come in, and it doesn’t run away. It looks at you the way you look at someone you’re nearly sure you know._  
_Then it hops, twice, high and neat, as if to show you that it can._  
_It goes back into the long grass. After that, in the mornings, it is often at the edge._
